Its matrix lists "Add store" and "Omit a store with empty journal" as supported outcomes. No document says a topology change forfeits migration lineage. 3. **Nothing re-keys lineage.** Entries are keyed by (TargetStoreIdentity, EntityTag) (migration_lineage.rs:108-110). The application is a NoOp and the stale keys stay. The next release carries a migration plan. preflight_ordinary_source_application (761) calls current_proposal_lineage_is_applied, which looks up the new identity, gets None and returns false (2066-2075). plan_schema_migration then returns Unadopted from resolve_transitions (migration_planner.rs:428-430) or validate_unchanged_lineage (492-494). Even if adoption succeeds, lineage_after_planned keeps the stale entries. highverifiedschema-application-1 · robustness · medium confidence
Missing cardinality is treated as corruption; during upgrade startup this persists a terminal failure that blocks the rebuild that would clear it
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/application.rs:2661

Failure scenario

Deploy N changes the schema, which publishes a new accepted root. The database becomes Ready and the watchdog starts rebuilding cardinality at 4096 entries per page, which takes minutes for a large store. Before that finishes, deploy N+1 is installed and its generated schema adds a check or targeted rule, or edits a rule operation, on any existing entity. In post_upgrade the driver completes recovery, then apply_generated_schema calls generated_row_local_constraint_proofs; exact_entity_count returns None, producing store_corruption. That is recorded as a terminal startup failure bound to (incarnation, submission key, head), and the watchdog stops. The failure never clears because cardinality is never rebuilt while not Ready, so redeploying the same wasm reproduces it and every db() call fails. The explicit apply_schema path also reports 'corruption' for removals or check additions issued shortly after any publication.

Evidence

generated_row_local_constraint_proofs: `authority.handle.exact_entity_count(*entity_tag).ok_or_else(InternalError::store_corruption)?` (2661-2664). require_exact_empty_entity_count maps None to store_corruption (2630-2631). The comment at 2620-2622 says missing cardinality 'is corrupt state'. But StoreHandle::exact_entity_count (registry/handle.rs:571-583) returns None whenever the ready cardinality generation does not validate: header not Ready, cursor present, effective root != canonical root, or source mismatch. Folding any AcceptedSchemaPublish invalidates the source (commit/recovery.rs:1058-1063, 1100-1104), and session/write.rs:8544-8549 asserts None right after a publication. Cardinality is only rebuilt by the startup driver's Ready branch (startup/driver.rs:52-60); before Ready the driver applies the generated schema (driver.rs:61). STORE_CORRUPTION is a persisted terminal SchemaReconciliation code (startup/mod.rs:116). By contrast, SQL DDL treats missing cardinality as conservatively nonempty (schema/sql_ddl.rs:350-362).

Recommendation

Do not treat unavailable cardinality as corruption. For generated_row_local_constraint_proofs, treat an unknown count as non-zero and use the existing bounded scan or pending-job path. For the removal proofs, return a retryable or 'not yet provable' error that the startup driver does not classify as terminal. Alternatively, drive cardinality pages before the generated application when a proof needs them.

Verifier (confirmed): I traced this end to end and it holds. At application.rs:2661-2664, a None from exact_entity_count becomes store_corruption, and require_exact_empty_entity_count (2630-2631) does the same. For journaled stores, StoreHandle::exact_entity_count (registry/handle.rs:571-583) returns None whenever ready_cardinality_counts_for_source (handle.rs:1007-1038) finds a header that is not Ready, a live cursor, or a source mismatch. Every AcceptedSchemaPublish marks the maintenance source invalid (commit/recovery.rs:1058-1063, 1100-1104). The test at session/write.rs:8544-8549 checks that the value is None right after a publication. Cardinality is only rebuilt in the Ready branch of drive_recovery_page (startup/driver.rs:52-60). A new submission key makes observe return Recovering, so the driver goes straight to drive_generated_schema_application and complete_generated_schema_handoff without building any cardinality pages. STORE_CORRUPTION is a terminal code for every kind (startup/mod.rs:116). The failure receipt is bound to the accepted head, which never changes, so observe keeps returning it. reconcile_startup_watchdog_from_durable_state then deactivates the watchdog, and redeploying the same wasm reproduces the failure. The in-file tests confirm the hidden dependency: they call drive_cardinality_to_ready right after a publication and before applying a check edit (application.rs:4196, 4540). The 0.213 decision to treat missing cardinality as corruption came before 0.230 made cardinality an optional, invalidated-on-publication generation, so that premise is stale. SQL DDL, by contrast, treats a missing count as nonempty (sql_ddl.rs:350-362). The canister can be recovered by deploying a wasm without the check addition and waiting for cardinality to rebuild, so this is high rather than critical.
Skeptic · reachability (upheld, high): I could not refute this. Every step from the post_upgrade lifecycle hook to the persisted terminal failure is reachable, and I found no guard that blocks it. For journaled stores, a missing cardinality count is a normal, expected state after any accepted-schema publication (0.230 made cardinality "optional" evidence that stays conservative while it is being rebuilt). Schema application, however, still classifies that state as STORE_CORRUPTION. That rule dates from the 0.213 design, which predates durable cardinality generations; SQL DDL (sql_ddl.rs:350-362) was updated to treat missing cardinality as conservatively nonempty, but this path was not. The startup driver only rebuilds cardinality in its Ready branch, while generated schema application runs in the not-Ready branch. So the failure keeps itself in place. The native test harness (__drive_native_database_for_tests) runs the watchdog until cardinality is Quiescent before each next step, which hides the window from tests. I rate it high rather than critical because it is not a permanent wedge: redeploying wasm N makes observe() report Ready (N's submission key is reconciled and the receipt's key does not match it), the driver then clears the receipt (driver.rs:53) and resumes the cardinality rebuild, and N+1 can be redeployed once that rebuild finishes. The cost is still real: after a valid upgrade, all database access fails with a misleading "store corruption" diagnostic, and redeploying the same wasm does not help. Explicit apply_schema calls and field/entity/index-removal proofs made during the rebuild window also return STORE_CORRUPTION (not persisted there). The correct fix is on the code side: treat None as "unknown/nonempty" (bounded scan or pending job for checks, store_unsupported or retryable for removals), not as corruption.
highverifiedschema-application-2 · durability · medium confidence
Capacity eviction can drop the deployed generated submission's receipt, flipping a Ready database to Recovering with no watchdog running
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/application_store.rs:336

Failure scenario

A canister is Ready after deploy D, holding receipt R_D. An operator or tool then submits 64 or more explicit apply_schema proposals with distinct submission keys over the canister's life (removals, which are only possible explicitly, or NoOp proposals). Each insert at capacity evicts the smallest-key terminal record, and eventually R_D. From then on every db() call returns startup-recovery-pending. If the evicting commit had no journal debt (for example a NoOp or control-only publication), nothing re-applies the generated schema until the next upgrade. If the watchdog does run, re-applying D fails with Unsupported whenever explicit removals made accepted state diverge from D's model, which persists a terminal startup failure. It also silently re-adds explicitly removed generated checks as new activations.

Evidence

MAX_SCHEMA_APPLICATION_RECORDS = 64 (line 39). When full, preflight retires `terminal_retention_candidate()` (308-316), which returns the first non-Pending key in map order (336-351), i.e. SHA-256 key order, with no protection for the current generated submission. Readiness requires that exact record: generated_submission_is_reconciled needs `load_schema_application_record_read_only(...).is_some_and(NoOp|Applied)` (application.rs:2977-2996), and observe returns Recovering when it is not reconciled (startup/observe.rs:98-106). Generated admission refuses all ordinary work unless Ready (icydb-model/src/build/actor/db/store.rs:121-130). The watchdog stops after Terminal and is only re-armed in init/post_upgrade or by a retained-marker/journal-debt wakeup (commit/guard.rs:314-336). Every explicit apply_schema with a new submission key inserts a record, including NoOp proposals (application.rs:713-716, 743-757).

Recommendation

Never evict the receipt for the currently registered generated submission key; exclude it in terminal_retention_candidate or keep a dedicated durable 'generated reconciled' marker per incarnation and key. Evict by insertion age rather than key hash. Consider making readiness independent of a retained idempotency receipt.

Verifier (confirmed): Confirmed from the code. When a new key arrives at capacity, preflight (application_store.rs:308-316) retires terminal_retention_candidate (336-351). That is the first non-Pending key in SHA-256 map order, and nothing excludes the currently registered generated submission. Readiness requires that exact record with a NoOp or Applied outcome (application.rs:2977-2996 via generated_schema_is_reconciled, and observe.rs:98-106). startup_state() is computed fresh on every db() call with no cache (icydb-model store.rs:807-817), so eviction immediately fails every call with recovery-pending (store.rs:121-130). Every explicit apply_schema with a new key inserts a record, including NoOp (application.rs:713-716, 743-757), and a NoOp goes through publish_database_control_atomically (schema_publication.rs:240-245), which leaves no journal debt and so wakes no watchdog. Generated deploys fill the 64 slots over a canister's life, so later explicit submissions evict the live receipt with meaningful probability. The 0.213 retention design (closeout P1-3) assumed that retiring a receipt only ends the replay window; it predates readiness depending on that receipt. When journal debt does wake the watchdog, it re-applies the generated proposal against the post-explicit head, which can re-add explicitly removed items or fail with Unsupported, a terminal code. It needs long canister life plus explicit apply usage, but the result is a full database outage until the next upgrade, so high stands.
Skeptic · reachability (upheld, high): I could not refute this. The whole path goes through supported public APIs, and nothing along it protects the generated receipt. 1. Deploy D: the generated driver calls apply_generated_schema_fragment (crates/icydb/src/db/session/catalog.rs:150-182), which reaches apply_schema_with_contract. That inserts a record R_D under ICYDB_SCHEMA_SUBMISSION_KEY (crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/application.rs:743-757). observe then returns Ready. 2. Any later explicit `DbSession::apply_schema` (catalog.rs:187) with a new submission key also reaches apply_schema_with_contract. - It inserts a new record even when the outcome is NoOp (application.rs:713-716 and 743-757). - An empty publication list goes through publish_database_control_atomically (crates/icydb-core/src/db/commit/schema_publication.rs:240-244, 777-787). - The only admission check is ensure_recovery_admitted (crates/icydb-core/src/db/commit/recovery.rs:130-151). Nothing checks generated ownership. 3. When the store is full, preflight retires the first non-Pending key in BTreeMap byte order (application_store.rs:308-316, 336-351; key iteration in control_store.rs:169-179). - Nothing excludes the current generated key. The contract says the same thing: "the lowest stable-key terminal receipt is recycled" (docs/contracts/PERSISTED_FORMAT_INVENTORY.md:31). So the code matches the contract, and the flaw is in the design. - The commit guard preflight (commit/guard.rs:251) and store.apply (application_store.rs:272-289) run this same logic. 4. Once R_D is removed: - generated_submission_is_reconciled returns false (application.rs:2977-2996). - observe returns Recovering (startup/observe.rs:98-106). - Every db() call fails in admit_ordinary_database_work (crates/icydb-model/src/build/actor/db/store.rs:121-130, 781-786). Admission re-observes on every call, with no cache. 5. Nothing wakes the watchdog up to repair this: - After the database became Ready, drive_recovery_page returned Terminal (startup/driver.rs:44-61), and the callback stopped the watchdog (store.rs:275-279). - A NoOp or control-only marker has no journal batches, so finish_commit fires no wakeup (commit/guard.rs:327-336). - Ordinary writes are refused, so they cannot create journal debt either. The only thing that re-arms the watchdog is init/post_upgrade (store.rs:247-255). Recovery: an upgrade re-applies D against the current accepted head. If accepted state still matches D, that is a NoOp that re-inserts R_D and restores Ready. If explicit changes made accepted state diverge from D, the re-apply may re-add removed items or record a terminal failure. I did not fully trace that branch. Reachability: there is no dead step, but the trigger needs a privileged operator making many explicit submissions over time. Schema-changing deploys also leave records behind, which lowers that number. Once the store is full, each insert at capacity removes the lowest key and adds a random one, so R_D's rank tends to drift down and it will almost certainly be evicted eventually. The impact is a database-wide outage that does not heal itself until someone upgrades. So I agree with high rather than critical: an upgrade normally recovers it, so it is not a permanent wedge.
highverifiedschema-application-3 · correctness · medium confidence
Generated reconciliation rejects entities with any live activation, including SQL-DDL-owned ones, and persists it as terminal while the only way to finish the activation needs Ready
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/application_lowering.rs:1624

Failure scenario

An operator runs `ALTER TABLE Order ALTER COLUMN note SET NOT NULL` (or creates a SQL unique index) on a large generated entity, which publishes a durable Forward/Verify activation that is advanced over many calls. Before it completes, a new wasm is deployed whose model changes anything, even another entity, giving a new submission key. Generated reconciliation lowers Order, hits the activation check, returns store_unsupported, and records a persisted terminal startup failure. Every db() call now fails, including the SQL DDL endpoint needed to finish or abort the activation. The only way out is rolling back to the previous wasm.

Evidence

lower_existing_entity starts with `if !current.constraint_activations().is_empty() || !current.candidate_indexes().is_empty() || !current.candidate_relations().is_empty() { return Err(InternalError::store_unsupported()); }` (1624-1629). It runs for every entity in the generated proposal (finish, 824-846), even when that entity's fragment is unchanged, and does not check origin. RUNTIME_UNSUPPORTED is a terminal SchemaReconciliation code (startup/mod.rs:133). complete_generated_schema_handoff records the failure (icydb-model/src/build/actor/db/store.rs:337-352). The SQL DDL endpoint, the way to advance or abort a SQL SET NOT NULL or unique-index activation, dispatches through db(), which requires Ready (icydb-model/src/build/actor/db/sql.rs:74-77).

Recommendation

In lower_existing_entity, compare the fragment first and only reject when the generated fragment actually changes an entity that has a live activation, or ignore SQL-owned activations when generated-owned facts are unchanged. Alternatively, classify this as a retryable, non-terminal reconciliation wait instead of a persisted failure.

Verifier (confirmed): Confirmed. lower_existing_entity rejects with store_unsupported whenever the current snapshot has any activation, candidate index or candidate relation (application_lowering.rs:1624-1629). It does this before checking origin and before comparing fragments. The generated proposal carries every model entity, and lower_generated_existing_store_candidate then finish (842-846) calls it for each one. ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK ... NOT VALID leaves a durable SqlDdl-origin activation in the catalog indefinitely (sql_ddl/constraint.rs:51-80; SQL_SUBSET.md:524-526), and unique-index and SET NOT NULL activations do the same until they finish. RUNTIME_UNSUPPORTED is terminal for SchemaReconciliation (startup/mod.rs:133), and complete_generated_schema_handoff records it (icydb-model store.rs:337-352). The SQL DDL endpoint dispatches through db()?, which requires Ready (icydb-model sql.rs:74-77), so the operator cannot VALIDATE or DROP the activation. I found no test or contract saying that unchanged entities with SQL-owned activations must block generated reconciliation; the documented rejections are for the removal lanes. Rolling back to the prior wasm is the only exit. High is appropriate.
Skeptic · reachability (upheld, high): I could not refute this. I traced the path from the post_upgrade watchdog to a persisted terminal startup failure, and no step is blocked. The activation guard in lower_existing_entity (application_lowering.rs:1624-1629) is the first thing it checks. It does not look at origin or at whether the entity's fragment changed. The generated proposal always carries the whole fragment with every entity assignment (icydb/src/db/session/catalog.rs:315-347). Nothing filters out entities whose lineage digest is unchanged (application_lowering.rs:620-656). So every entity in every store gets lowered. SQL DDL has no rule against generated entities when it creates live activations. The ADD CHECK binder has no origin guard (sql/ddl/constraint.rs:137-177). With NOT VALID, sql_ddl/constraint.rs:78-85 publishes a SqlDdl-origin activation and leaves it in place until VALIDATE runs. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX works the same way: it publishes a candidate index plus an activation (SQL_SUBSET.md:438-441). NOT VALID makes the scenario stronger than the claim says. It is a legitimate long-lived state, so an operator never has to be in the middle of a multi-call activation to hit this. store_unsupported becomes ErrorClass::Unsupported, then RUNTIME_UNSUPPORTED (error/mod.rs:1730, 3198). That code is terminal for SchemaReconciliation (startup/mod.rs:133). There is only one way out. `continue_schema_application` and `abort_schema_application` accept only Generated-origin activations (application.rs:394-401, 530-541). The migrate endpoints only act on migration plans. The SQL DDL endpoint needs Ready. This is not permanent, so it is not critical. Redeploying a wasm whose generated model equals the old one works. The old submission key still has its Applied receipt, and the failure receipt's submission-key binding no longer matches, so observe returns Ready. The operator can then validate or drop the activation and redeploy. The 0.213 design notes say live activation state should reject generated reconciliation, so the rejection itself is intended. What the design does not address is the total outage: the rejection is terminal and the only remedy sits behind the Ready gate. The result is an outage of every db() entry point under a realistic operator workflow. That meets the high bar (a DoS, and recovery that fails under plausible conditions).
highverifiedschema-migration-1 · robustness · high confidence
Entity-local `page.rows == 0` oversize check under a page-global leftover budget deterministically wedges RewritingRows/FinalValidation (non-abortable) and Validating
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/migration_execution.rs:398

Failure scenario

Physical plan with two transformed entities A < B (same or different stores). A's last rewrite page resumes at cursor P. A's remaining rows (e.g., 2 x 300 KiB) exhaust A and leave 424 KiB of row-byte budget. B's first candidate row is 450 KiB. rewrite_entity_page(B) sees page.rows==0 for B and returns store_unsupported. Nothing is committed, so every later Advance recomputes the same page and fails the same way. Abort returns AbortTooLate, and deploying any other Wasm yields PlanChanged. The database stays gated forever: every ordinary read/write/DDL returns MigrationInProgress, and only a reinstall or a patched library escapes. The same happens in a single-entity migration when a Copy transform doubles a large field: a 600 KiB before row passes validation but becomes a >1 MiB candidate row. FinalValidation can wedge the same way. In Validating the identical bug blocks completion, though abort is still possible there.

Evidence

rewrite_migration_page passes the leftover page budgets to each program: `rewrite_entity_page(store, program, &prepared, cursor..., remaining_rows, remaining_row_bytes, remaining_index_bytes, remaining_effects, remaining_journal_bytes, ...)` (l.198-210). Inside, `page.rows` counts only this entity's rows: `if next_row_bytes > row_byte_budget || next_index_bytes > index_byte_budget { if page.rows == 0 { return Err(InternalError::store_unsupported()); } ... }` (l.396-402), and the same pattern for effects/journal bytes (l.419-424). final_validate_entity_page has the same pattern with the leftover `remaining_bytes` (l.765-769). Validation has it too (migration_validation.rs l.333-337, l.451-455). Phases RewritingRows/RebuildingIndexes/FinalValidation are not `abortable()` (migration_record.rs l.76-82) and all block ordinary operations (l.55-65). Validation also never measures candidate row size against the rewrite budget; it only budgets the before-row `raw_row.len()` and staged unique/relation keys.

Recommendation

Make the fatal oversize condition page-global: pass 'rows already consumed by this page' (or a flag) into the entity page and error only when no row at all has been accepted in the whole page; otherwise Stop with exhausted=false. During Validating, also compute each row's candidate byte size, derived-key bytes and effect count against the fixed rewrite/final-validation budgets. Record any row that can never fit as a typed finding while abort is still permitted, rather than discovering it after the irreversible boundary. Add a multi-program test whose first entity's tail leaves a small leftover budget.

Severity adjusted from critical to high during verification.

Its only guard before calling the next program is `== 0` (l.182-190). Inside rewrite_entity_page, `page.rows` is entity-local, starting at 0 (l.297-305). If entity B's first candidate row exceeds the leftover row or index budget, `if page.rows == 0 { return Err(store_unsupported) }` fires (l.397-400). The same happens for effects/journal bytes (l.420-423). The error propagates out of advance_active_schema_migration RewritingRows (application.rs ~l.1343-1368) before any publish, so every retry recomputes the same page from the same durable cursor. That row passes validation and then fails at page.rows==0 in RewritingRows. Candidate growth, or rewrite budgets that differ from validation's, move the failure past the abort boundary. The escape needs a patched library or a reinstall, which meets the rubric's permanent-wedge criterion.

highverifiedschema-migration-2 · correctness · high confidence
Lineage accepted_head is not re-stamped by SQL DDL, constraint-activation abort, or non-migration builds; every later migration/adoption fails with StaleAcceptedHead
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/migration_planner.rs:431

Failure scenario

Migration-enabled canister creates the DB (lineage at head H1). A controller then runs admin SQL `CREATE INDEX` on a generated entity, and the head becomes H2 while lineage stays at H1. Later a successor with `entity_migration(entity="User", from=1, ...)` is deployed. Startup preflight (preflight_unpublished_schema_migration) returns StaleAcceptedHead instead of MigrationInProgress, so startup fails. `icydb_schema_migrate Advance` with the exact H2 from status fails the same way. Adopt fails with StaleAcceptedHead because the head check comes before the IdentityConflict check. The same happens after the guide-sanctioned 'later deployment may omit the migration capability' step, if that build performs any ordinary schema publication. No operation can re-stamp lineage, so the database can never migrate again.

Evidence

Planner requires lineage head == proposal head: `if lineage.accepted_head() != proposal.expected_head() { return Err(SchemaMigrationPlanningError::StaleAcceptedHead); }` (l.431, also l.495 validate_unchanged_lineage and l.235 adoption, checked before the Unadopted test). Lineage is re-stamped only in application.rs attach_ordinary_lineage_publication (l.1524, migration feature only) and in the migration publish paths. Several head-changing publications carry no lineage op: SQL DDL (`sql_ddl.rs` l.82 `publish_accepted_schema_candidate(...)`), abort_schema_application (application.rs ~l.491, application record only), and the non-migration build (`#[cfg(not(feature = "migration"))] let database_control = vec![DatabaseControlOp::SchemaApplication(operation)];` l.753-754). The pending path pre-stamps lineage with the promoted head (l.689-697, 746-751), so an abort leaves it wrong. The 0.218 design states: "Every later accepted publication updates the relevant entries' accepted_head. SQL DDL therefore changes the recorded head while preserving each entity-source version and digest."

Recommendation

Re-stamp lineage heads inside the shared publication boundary (publish_accepted_schema_candidates_with_database_control or its marker builder) whenever a lineage catalog exists and the head changes, including SQL DDL, activation promotion/abort and non-migration builds (the op codec is already feature-independent). Alternatively, drop the per-entry head binding and bind freshness to the migration command's expected_head only. Add a test: create DB, run SQL DDL, then run a migration successfully.

Generated proposals bind expected_head to the live target head (icydb/src/db/session/catalog.rs:48-54, 80, 109). Heads are re-stamped only by attach_ordinary_lineage_publication (application.rs:1524-1551, migration feature only) and by the migration/adoption publishes. SQL DDL publishes through commit::publish_accepted_schema_candidate(_with_*) (sql_ddl.rs:62-67, 83-88) with no lineage op, and the shared boundary publish_accepted_schema_candidates_with_database_control (schema_publication.rs:223-305) adds none. The 'source-lineage bookkeeping' comment at sql_ddl.rs:152 refers to source bindings, not the entity lineage catalog. abort_schema_application (application.rs:425-515) publishes only an application record. The pending path pre-stamps lineage with the post-promotion head (l.692-697, 746-751), so an abort leaves lineage at a head that never becomes current. The non-migration build uses `vec![SchemaApplication(operation)]` (l.753-754). After any of these, a later generated apply sees prior_head == accepted_head with no candidates and never re-stamps (l.1538-1540). Any later plan therefore fails StaleAcceptedHead, and adoption fails the same way. The 0.218 design (archive/0.218-design.md:498-503) says SQL DDL must update the recorded head. SQL_SUBSET.md permits SQL-owned indexes on generated entities. Migrations are permanently blocked, but ordinary operation continues under the old Wasm, so high is appropriate rather than critical.

Only four places write lineage, all in application.rs: adopt (l.985), metadata advance (l.1139), physical publish (l.1487), and attach_ordinary_lineage_publication (l.1524-1549, migration feature only). The commit layer never adds a lineage op on its own; schema_publication.rs l.223-306 only passes along the database_control it is given. SQL DDL on a generated entity that already has lineage is reachable and tested. The generated `sql_ddl` endpoint (icydb-model build/actor/db/sql.rs l.77, 170) calls execute_admin_sql_ddl_dispatch. The only gate is ensure_schema_migration_ready_for_schema_changes, which checks for a non-terminal migration record and does not look at lineage. The test schema_admission.rs l.153-195 shows DDL succeeding on generated `Target` after a migration reaches Applied. That test never runs a second migration afterwards, so this path has no coverage. Code and design disagree here. The 0.218 design (l.498-503) says SQL DDL must re-stamp the lineage head and that the next migration binds the latest head. The code does not do this, so the code is the side that looks wrong. The finding is valid without the abort path or the non-migration-build path. Both of those also leave lineage stale. In the abort case, apply l.689-697 and l.746-751 pre-stamp the promoted head, but abort l.469 publishes a different head with only an application-record op. In the non-migration build, l.753-754 attaches no lineage op. There is no clean way out. The only op that re-stamps is an ordinary head-changing apply_schema in a migration-enabled build. A generated change of that kind keeps the old digests (lineage_after_planned l.1839-1869), which causes UnexplainedSchemaDifference or MissingMigration later. A new entity gets no lineage entry and later hits Unadopted. Adopt cannot fix it either: it checks the head before IdentityConflict (planner l.235-240), and already-adopted entries make it fail regardless. Severity is high, not critical. No data is lost and the canister is not permanently wedged: redeploying the previous Wasm, whose terminal receipt still exists, restores service. What is lost is every supported migration path from then on, and that breaks a documented contract under ordinary operator use.

highverifiedschema-mutation-1 · durability · high confidence
Aborting a SQL unique-index activation leaves staged candidate index entries behind for good, and they later break index DDL and generated schema removal
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/sql_ddl/constraint.rs:196

Failure scenario

1) Rows alice, bob, and charlie all have rank=7. 2) Run CREATE UNIQUE INDEX r ON SqlTestUser (rank), then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT r twice; the Forward page stages alice's key under (tag, ord k, gen G). 3) DROP INDEX r aborts the activation. 4) Any later CREATE INDEX, DROP INDEX, or expression-index DDL on SqlTestUser fails with a Corruption error forever. Deleting every row does not help, because deletes no longer touch the retired generation. A later wasm whose generated schema removes SqlTestUser or one of its generated indexes fails prove_empty_user_index_domain; the startup driver then records a terminal SchemaReconciliation failure, so the database stays non-Ready until the operator redeploys without that change.

Evidence

Forward pages physically insert candidate keys: schema_publication.rs:857-863 `index_store.insert(key, IndexEntryValue::presence())`. These are User-kind keys under IndexId::new_with_generation(entity_tag, ordinal, epoch), checked at schema_publication.rs:891-903. Abort only edits metadata: execute_admin_sql_ddl_unique_index_activation_abort -> `before.with_aborted_unique_activation(..)` (snapshot.rs:487-519 drops the activation and the candidate_indexes entry) -> publish_sql_ddl_constraint_removal (sql_ddl.rs:41-70, schema + job delete only). Nothing ever purges the candidate generation's keys; there is no range-remove API in index/store.rs. Complete-domain staging then observes every User key for the entity (mutation/user_index_domain.rs:908 `key.key_kind() == IndexKeyKind::User && key.index_id().entity_tag() == entity_tag`) and compares against a projection built only from snapshot.indexes() (lines 765-775): `if observed_before != self.expected_before { return Err(CurrentDomainMismatch) }` (lines 385-392), which maps to InternalError::store_corruption (line 502). prove_empty_user_index_domain (lines 927-940) fails the same way and is used by generated entity and index removal (application.rs:2419-2422, 2576-2579). The integration test sql_canister_unique_validation_retains_same_page_conflicts (sql_canister.rs:2376-2415) runs exactly the stage-then-abort sequence but never tests a follow-up DDL.

Recommendation

Make abort own physical cleanup of the candidate generation. Options: purge (entity_tag, ordinal, epoch) keys in the same marker when the count is small, or add a bounded, resumable purge job that must finish before the abort's catalog publication or before any later domain replacement. Add a regression test for CREATE UNIQUE INDEX, VALIDATE (stage), DROP INDEX, then CREATE INDEX / DROP INDEX / entity removal.

highverifiedschema-store-1 · durability · medium confidence
Schema publication retain/position sweeps delete or overlay every cardinality record in a single message (unbounded work in DDL and in recovery fold)
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/store.rs:3805

Failure scenario

A journaled store holds an entity with ~1M rows and a single-field index with distinct values, so after the builder reaches Ready there are ~1M count records. An admin runs an online DDL (e.g. ADD INDEX or a generated schema upgrade). (a) In the DDL message, prepare_positioned_journal_batch_publication and retain_materialized_candidate_entries do O(N) heap BTree inserts and a full stable-map scan. For large N this exceeds the message instruction limit, so every DDL traps and schema changes become impossible. (b) If the DDL does fit, convergence later folds that batch: retain_canonical_candidate_entries removes ~N stable-BTree entries in one message. Each attempt traps on the instruction limit and rolls back, the fold watermark never advances, the journal backlog stops draining, and write admission eventually refuses writes. Only a code upgrade gets the canister out. As a side effect, positions and tombstones for count keys the builder deletes between publication and fold are never retired, because the Canonical-view key collection only sees keys still present in canonical, so they leak heap until restart.

Evidence

Cardinality header/cursor/count records share the per-store canonical map (RawSchemaKey namespaces 5/6/7, store.rs:253-298). All retain sweeps keep only `keep.contains(key) || key.is_identity_state()`:
- retain_canonical_candidate_entries (3805-3827): `let stale = canonical.iter().filter_map(|entry| (!keep.contains(entry.key()) && !entry.key().is_identity_state()).then_some(*entry.key())).collect(); for key in stale { canonical.remove(&key); }`, called from apply_prepared_accepted_schema_fold (3146, 3199) during journal fold/recovery.
- retain_materialized_candidate_entries (3774-3803) iterates every canonical key and inserts a heap tombstone for each.
- positioned_candidate_effect_keys, Effective view (3624-3635), adds every canonical key (count records included) to the publication position set.
Count records are per entity plus per user-index prefix of every index entry (cardinality_build.rs collect_index_page pushes one digest per component prefix), so their number scales with rows x prefix arity. The builder deliberately clears slots in pages of MAX_CARDINALITY_SLOT_CLEAR_ENTRIES_PER_PAGE = 4096 (cardinality_build.rs:39). Folds of batches containing AcceptedSchemaPublish skip cardinality maintenance (recovery.rs cardinality_batch_invalidates_source), so nothing else bounds this sweep.

Recommendation

Exclude cardinality namespaces (5/6/7) from all schema retain sweeps and from positioned_candidate_effect_keys, as identity-state keys already are (e.g. add `is_cardinality()` and filter on it). Source-identity drift already makes stale evidence unusable, and restart_cardinality_generation plus paged clear_cardinality_count_slot_page own bounded invalidation. More generally, the retain sweeps should iterate only schema-owned namespaces (0-3) with range bounds instead of `canonical.iter()`. Add a test that publishes a schema over a store with a Ready generation holding many count records and asserts bounded work and preserved or rotated cardinality state.

Verifier (confirmed): I traced this myself. Cardinality header, cursor and count records live in the same `canonical` StableBTreeMap as schema records (store.rs:253-298; writes at store.rs:1097, 1221-1235, 1386-1395). None of the retain sweeps exclude namespaces 5/6/7. Each one keeps only `keep.contains(key) || key.is_identity_state()`. (1) Fold: prepare_fold_journaled_accepted_schema_candidate (store.rs:3016) sets `retained = candidate_entry_keys(..)`, which covers only snapshots, bundle, root and validation jobs (3542-3571). apply_prepared_accepted_schema_fold calls retain_canonical_candidate_entries at 3146/3199. That function scans all of canonical and does one stable `remove` per stale key, every count record included, in the single fold message (recovery.rs:1500). (2) Online publication: apply_journaled_accepted_schema_candidate, called from schema_publication.rs:589/759, runs retain_materialized_candidate_entries (3774-3803). It collects every canonical key into a Vec and inserts a heap tombstone for each. positioned_candidate_effect_keys with the Effective view (3622-3635) adds every canonical key to the position set, through prepare_positioned_journal_batch_publication (2005-2025, commit_window.rs:913). Nothing else bounds this work. Count records have no global cap: only per-page limits exist (cardinality_build.rs:36-39). Per the 0.230 design, one count record exists per distinct accepted index prefix of length 1..=k. recovery.rs:1103-1108 only skips maintenance for publish batches; it does not bound the sweep. The test at store/tests.rs:2719-2760 shows the authors know count keys reach the positioned-retirement path ('canonical-only derived metadata'), but nothing covers the O(N) cost. The design wants old generations retired on schema change (0.230-design.md:262), so wiping the counts is semantically acceptable. Doing it unpaged in one message is the defect, and the paged clear_cardinality_count_slot_page (1164-1204) already exists for exactly this job. A few hundred thousand count records push both the DDL message and the fold message past per-message instruction limits. A fold that keeps trapping stalls convergence. crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/application_lowering.rs:2009

Failure scenario

(1) An entity has `level: Nat32` and `index(fields=["name"], predicate="level = 3")`. The persisted text `level = 3` parses to Int64(3). Every insert evaluates Nat64(3) vs Int64(3) under Strict, gets false, and no index entry is written. A query `WHERE name = 'bob' AND level = 3` carries Nat64(3). Planner implication decides Nat64(3) == Int64(3), so the filtered index is eligible and its guard clause is stripped from the residual. If the planner picks it, the scan of the empty index returns no rows although matching rows exist. (2) An entity has `index(fields=["email"], unique, predicate="status = 'Active'")` with an enum `status`. The rendered text is `status = 'Active'`, and Value::Enum vs Value::Text never matches, so no row is ever a member. Two Active users with the same email both commit: the declared filtered uniqueness is silently unenforced. The same applies to Decimal (`price = 10`), Float (`ratio = 1.5`) and enum IN. (3) A field named `count` with `predicate="count > 0"` compiles. At startup, acceptance calls parse_sql_predicate, gets Keyword(Count) where an identifier is required, returns SchemaSnapshotAcceptanceError::Predicate and then store_unsupported. Generated schema publication fails and the database stays unavailable until redeploy. The persisted text also depends on the lexer grammar with no format-version signal: reserving one more keyword later would make existing snapshots, and every per-row index plan during writes and replay, fail as 'store corruption'.

Evidence

Generated index predicates are bound to a typed, field-ID-bound AcceptedCheckExprV1 and then immediately rendered to SQL text; only the text is persisted (application_lowering.rs:2009-2024; the same code is copied at 2055-2068 and 2888-2902). The renderer turns an enum literal into its editable variant-name Text and a Ulid into Text (schema/check/render.rs:109-118). Nat/Int/Decimal values render as bare digits (sql_shared/literal_render.rs:8-35). At runtime the text goes back through parse_sql_predicate (predicate/mod.rs:65-76). There, integers parse to Value::Int64 first (sql_shared/types.rs:511-516), and equality and IN use CoercionId::Strict (predicate/parser/lowering.rs:93-101, 48-53). The program is compiled with no schema-aware literal canonicalization (index/plan/mod.rs:55-61, predicate/runtime/mod.rs:88-100). Write-time membership then compares under Strict: compare_eq requires same_variant (predicate/semantics.rs:39-42), and the scalar fast path decodes Nat only from Value::Nat64 (runtime/compare/scalar/direct/decode.rs:84-91) and otherwise returns false (direct/compare.rs:51-53). The planner's implication check uses compare_numeric_or_strict_order instead (query/plan/planner/index_select.rs:896-900, 940-953), so Nat64(3) and Int64(3) count as equal there. Acceptance checks only that predicate field names bind (schema/integrity/nullable_unique.rs:51-60, 236-240). The SQL DDL path additionally type-checks with validate_predicate (sql/ddl/index.rs:536-548), but the generated path does not. The shared lexer reserves COUNT/ORDER/INDEX/MIN/MAX/SUM/END/DEFAULT/FILTER/LIMIT/… (sql_shared/lexer/keywords.rs:3-89) and rejects quoted identifiers (lexer/scan.rs:48-50). The macro predicate tokenizer reserves only AND/OR/NOT/IN/BETWEEN/IS/NULL/TRUE/FALSE (icydb-model-macros/src/predicate.rs:227-237), and render_value emits raw field names.

Recommendation

Make one authority own index predicates. Persist the bound AcceptedCheckExprV1 (field-ID and typed-literal based, exactly as check constraints do) as the index predicate contract. Compile write-time membership, planner implication, dependency discovery, duplicate detection and fingerprinting from that structure. Derive SQL text only for DESCRIBE/SHOW. Route SQL DDL `CREATE INDEX … WHERE` through the same catalog binder rather than keeping a separate SQL-only validate_predicate gate. This also removes the name relabeling on rename, the placeholder `AcceptedSchemaFingerprint::new([1; 32])` value-catalog handles in application_lowering.rs, the three copies of the lowering code, and the per-row reparse of predicate text in index/plan/mod.rs:224-247. Until then, reject at acceptance any generated predicate whose rendered text does not re-parse to a type-equivalent predicate. Add end-to-end tests for Nat, enum and keyword-named-field filtered indexes; today only Bool/Text/IS NOT NULL predicates are exercised.

Cursor HMAC key is deterministic on wasm32/IC, so continuation tokens can be forged
crates/icydb-core/src/db/integrity.rs:1020

Failure scenario

An attacker calls any public endpoint that follows the READ_ADMISSION guidance (`execute_live_page(continuation)`) and receives one valid continuation. From their own canister they call management `canister_info(target)`, which returns install timestamps in recent_changes. Without it, they can guess a window of days (about 2^28 ms). Offline they compute HMAC-SHA256 for each candidate (ts, seq) until the token verifies, which takes seconds. With the key they forge tokens. Setting progress.rows_emitted=0 bypasses an authored total LIMIT, because dynamic.rs:479-486 computes remaining_limit = row_limit - token.rows_emitted and checks window equality but not progress. Setting last_emitted_logical/last_consumed_physical to any in-envelope value seeks forward or replays arbitrarily, including past rows an app meant to cap with `.limit(n)`. Envelope containment (index/envelope/mod.rs:84-100) and contract equality (dynamic.rs:332-356) still stop rows outside the query predicate from being exposed. The documented tamper-evidence guarantee is nonetheless void on every deployed canister.

Evidence

generate_cursor_authentication_key() builds the 32-byte key from two `Ulid::generate()` calls. On wasm32, crates/icydb-core/src/types/ulid/generator.rs:88-96 computes the random component as `(u128::from(ts & 0xFFFF) << 64) | u128::from(self.sequence)` with the comment "IC canisters cannot synchronously request fresh entropy... deterministic uniqueness". `ts = ic_cdk::api::time()/1_000_000` (runtime now_millis). IC time is constant within one message, so the second call takes the `ts <= last_ts` branch at generator.rs:57-61 and returns `previous.increment()`. The key is therefore key = ULID(ts, (ts&0xFFFF)<<64|seq) || ULID(ts, ...|seq+1): a pure function of the first-boot millisecond and a small counter (seq is typically 1 at fresh boot, convergence.rs:50-53). The getrandom path exists only under cfg(not(wasm32)), and tests (commit/store/tests.rs) check only that the key is nonzero. The key protects every scalar and grouped token (codec.rs encode/decode_authenticated_payload). CURSOR.md says modified tokens 'fail closed before execution', and PERSISTED_FORMAT_INVENTORY says 'Wrong-key or modified bytes ... fail closed'.

Recommendation

Source the key from the management canister's `raw_rand`. For example, fetch it asynchronously in the replicated startup driver (a spawned future from the watchdog), or require it before the database reports Ready. Persist it in the commit control slot as today, and refuse to issue or accept cursors until it exists. Do not derive secrets from the ULID generator. Add a wasm-target test or static guard that the key never comes from `GenerateKey`. If authentication cannot be guaranteed, remove the 'authenticated' claims and stop relying on token-carried progress (rows_emitted) for LIMIT enforcement.

Verifier (confirmed): I traced it end to end and the reasoning holds. integrity.rs:1020-1031 builds the 32-byte HMAC key from two `Ulid::generate()` calls. On wasm32, generator.rs:88-96 sets the random component to `(ts & 0xFFFF) << 64 | sequence`. `ts` is `ic_cdk::api::time()/1_000_000` (runtime.rs:32-36). `seed_from_system()` returns NotInitialized on wasm32 (random.rs:40-42), so no entropy is ever mixed in. The only caller is convergence.rs:53, on the fresh-boot path, and the key is persisted unchanged after that. There is no raw_rand anywhere in the crates. Because IC time is constant within a message, the second call takes the `ts <= last_ts` branch (generator.rs:57-66) and returns `previous.increment()`. The key is therefore a function of the boot millisecond plus a tiny counter (seq=1 on a fresh heap; the incarnation ID does not use this generator). It does not even include the canister id. codec.rs:106-126 and 167-208 use this key as the sole HMAC-SHA256 key for scalar and grouped tokens, so brute-forcing about 2^28 candidate timestamps is cheap. The documented guarantee is thus void: CURSOR.md:14-16 says modified tokens 'fail closed before execution' and CURSOR.md:62 says 'Changing any bound fact rejects the token'. The LIMIT bypass is real: dynamic.rs:479-484 computes remaining_limit from token-carried rows_emitted, and validate_scalar_page_token (dynamic.rs:331-356) checks window, authority, signature and order terms but not progress. The comment at dynamic.rs:489 ('The cursor authenticates that total separately') relies on the broken authentication. Impact is bounded as the finding says: resume_bounds_for_continuation (index/envelope/mod.rs:84-100) enforces envelope containment, and forged unconsumed_lookahead is rejected outright (dynamic.rs:576-578), so no rows outside the query's predicate/envelope are exposed and this is not an authorization bypass (critical). It remains a violation of a normative security contract, reachable on every IC deployment, so high is appropriate.

No IC entropy source exists anywhere in the crate: rg finds no raw_rand, and getrandom is only used under cfg(not(wasm32)). Every token IcyDB issues is the header, payload and HMAC-SHA256 over them in the clear (codec.rs:106-127), so one genuine token gives an attacker a known plaintext and its MAC to brute-force the key offline. The key is minted by the startup watchdog timer, which is scheduled to run immediately after install. The attacker can bound that time from the install timestamp that canister_info returns in recent_changes. So the search space is roughly a few thousand ms times a handful of counter values, and even a blind multi-day window (about 2^28) is only minutes of CPU. Progress is never checked. A forged rows_emitted=0 therefore resets the remaining total LIMIT (dynamic.rs:479-486), and the forged boundaries set where the scan resumes (dynamic.rs:573-590). unconsumed_lookahead is rejected at dynamic.rs:576, so no fabricated rows can be injected, and envelope and contract checks keep results inside the app's query predicate. The concrete security gain is bypassing an authored total LIMIT and seeking or replaying anywhere within the query's key range. Confidence: high. I traced the path statically from init to the forged-token decode. I did not run anything.

crates/icydb-schema/src/decimal/arithmetic.rs:208

`Decimal::from(10u128.pow(21)) + "0.000000000000000001".parse::<Decimal>()?` returns 170141183460469231731.687303715884105727 (≈1.7e20), about 6× smaller than the left operand. `Decimal::from(10u128.pow(30)) + Decimal(1e-28)` returns ≈1.7e10. Typed newtype arithmetic (derived Add/Sub/Sum on Decimal newtypes) persists these wrong values. For division, a real overflow such as 1e37 / 1e-28 gives 1.7e20 rather than the maximum magnitude.

Evidence

checked_add_impl aligns both mantissas to max(scale) via checked_mul by 10^diff; if that multiplication overflows, saturating_add (l.208-227) returns `saturating_extreme(target_scale, ...)` = ±i128::MAX × 10^-target_scale. `impl Div` (l.435-447) likewise saturates at DEFAULT_DIVISION_SCALE 18 (≈1.7e20) instead of the largest representable magnitude. The property test decimal_add_saturation_boundary_property (decimal/tests.rs ~l.330-356) only asserts that the mantissa is i128::MAX/MIN/0, so this behavior is enshrined rather than checked for monotonicity.

Recommendation

On alignment overflow, round the higher-scale operand down to the lower scale (lossy but monotonic), or step the target scale down until both operands fit. When the magnitude really overflows, saturate at scale 0 (the largest magnitude). Strengthen the property test to require |a+b| ≥ max(|a|,|b|) for same-sign operands.

Example: 1.7e30 / 3.0000000001 has a true quotient of about 5.7e29, but the numerator 1.7e30×1e10 overflows, and the result is about 1.7e20. crates/icydb-model/src/base/validator/num.rs:123

Failure scenario

A field has validator `MultipleOf::new(10_000_000_000_000u64)` (target mantissa 1e13, scale 0). A caller submits "5.0000000000000000000000000001" (scale 28, mantissa 5e28, which fits in i128). Aligning the target gives 1e13×1e28 = 1e41, which overflows, so Rem returns ZERO and validation passes. Core admission then rounds to the field scale (e.g. 5.00) and stores a value that is not a multiple. A value with a large mantissa and a lower scale than the target (e.g. 1.7e37 + 0.1 vs target 0.25) bypasses the check the same way.

MultipleOf::validate does `if !(v % self.target).is_zero() { issue }`. `impl Rem for Decimal` (arithmetic.rs l.456-462) is `self.checked_rem_impl(rhs).unwrap_or(Self::ZERO)`, and checked_rem_impl (l.84-97) returns None when aligning either operand to max(scale) overflows i128. An arithmetic failure is therefore reported as 'is a multiple'.

Recommendation

Rewriting a scalar-WHERE CASE into AND/OR drops CASE's lazy evaluation, so a CASE-guarded division errors on the rows it was meant to skip
crates/icydb-core/src/db/query/plan/expr/canonicalize/case.rs:202

Failure scenario

`SELECT id FROM Orders WHERE CASE WHEN qty = 0 THEN FALSE ELSE total / qty > 5 END`. This is the standard SQL idiom for guarding division. After the rewrite, `total / qty > 5` is evaluated for rows with qty = 0, apply_decimal_arithmetic_checked returns NotRepresentable, and the whole query fails with a numeric error. The same CASE in a SELECT projection works, because the projection path keeps lazy CASE. DELETE uses the same scalar-WHERE lowering (select/mod.rs:116-124).

Evidence

lower_searched_case_to_boolean (202-249) rewrites `CASE WHEN c THEN r ELSE e END` into `(COALESCE(c,false) AND r) OR (NOT COALESCE(c,false) AND e)`. The AND/OR children are then flattened and re-sorted by label (normalize.rs:127-148). admit_expansion (budget.rs:224-265) checks only size, not whether the results can fail. At runtime the filter is a CompiledExpr, and Binary AND/OR evaluate both operands eagerly (evaluate.rs:200-205: `let left = left.evaluate(reader)?; let right = right.evaluate(reader)?;`). Division by zero is an error (numeric/mod.rs:77-80 -> ProjectionEvalError::Numeric). truth_admission.rs:76-81 and 112-115 admit arithmetic compare operands inside CASE results in scalar WHERE, and canonicalize/mod.rs claims the rewrite happens only for 'shapes proven equivalent'.

Recommendation

Only expand CASE when every result and ELSE branch is error-free: boolean literals, field or null tests, and comparisons without arithmetic or fallible functions. Otherwise keep the CASE node, which the compiled evaluator already evaluates lazily. Alternatively, give AND/OR short-circuit semantics and do not reorder the guard. Add a regression test for the division-guard idiom in WHERE and DELETE.

Arithmetic compares cannot become a predicate, so the compiled expression is the filter. Binary AND evaluates both operands eagerly (compiled_expr/evaluate.rs:200-205), and division by zero returns NotRepresentable (numeric/mod.rs:77-80). eval_compiled_filter_expr_* turns that into a query error (executor/projection/eval/scalar.rs:383-387, 404-414). An unexpanded CASE is lazy (evaluate.rs:405-419), so the rewrite is not equivalent despite the claim in canonicalize/mod.rs:11-12. I lowered severity to medium: the query fails with a typed error rather than returning wrong rows or corrupting data, and NULLIF-style rewrites avoid it.

The identical CASE works as a SELECT projection (lazy CASE). It also works in WHERE when there is no division, and when the qty=0 row is absent. So the error comes from dividing on the row the guard should skip. DELETE with the same WHERE fails the same way, and no rows were deleted.

.github/workflows/ci.yml:34

Failure scenario

A Cargo.lock refresh (for example a grouped Dependabot minor/patch PR) pulls a dependency with `rust-version = "1.90"`, or icydb uses a language feature newer than 1.88. The MSRV job compiles on 1.98.1 and passes. Users on the advertised 1.88.0 get 'package X requires rustc 1.90' or compile errors. Clippy's incompatible_msrv lint catches only std-API use in crates that declare rust-version, not dependency MSRV or language features.

Evidence

The job uses `dtolnay/rust-toolchain@e97e2d8...` with `toolchain: ${{ env.RUST_MSRV }}` (1.88.0), then runs `cargo check --locked -p icydb ...` in the repo root (ci.yml:42-44). The pinned action's action.yml only runs `rustup toolchain install` and `rustup default <toolchain>`; it never sets RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN. rust-toolchain.toml:2 pins `channel = "1.98.1"`, and rustup gives a toolchain file precedence over `rustup default`. Nothing checks `rustc --version`. README.md:1 and INSTALLING.md:24 advertise a 1.88.0 dependency MSRV.

Recommendation

Set `RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN: ${{ env.RUST_MSRV }}` at job level, or invoke `cargo +1.88.0`. Add a step asserting `rustc --version` starts with `rustc 1.88.0`. Have check-ci-workflow-invariants.sh enforce both.

Verifier (confirmed): Confirmed. I fetched action.yml at the pinned commit e97e2d8. Its steps are `rustup toolchain install <tc>`, `rustup default <tc>`, and `rustc +<tc> --version`, plus GITHUB_ENV writes that set only CARGO_HOME, CARGO_INCREMENTAL, CARGO_TERM_COLOR, CARGO_REGISTRIES_CRATES_IO_PROTOCOL and CARGO_HTTP_MULTIPLEXING. It never sets RUSTUP_TOOLCHAIN. The job's plain `cargo check --locked -p icydb ...` (ci.yml:42-44) runs in the checkout root, where rust-toolchain.toml:2 pins channel 1.98.1, and rustup ranks a toolchain file above `rustup default`. So the job builds with 1.98.1 (auto-installed), or would error, and never with 1.88.0. The version the action prints uses an explicit `+1.88.0`, which hides the problem. check-ci-workflow-invariants.sh checks only that the job exists (:92, :117). Present impact: I found no locked dependency in the local registry that declares rust-version above 1.88. Per-crate `rust-version = "1.88.0"` (crates/*/Cargo.toml:4-5) lets clippy's incompatible_msrv catch std-API drift, but not dependency MSRV or language-feature drift. The advertised MSRV gate (README.md:1, INSTALLING.md:24, and the release job's `needs: dependency_msrv`) is ineffective. Medium is appropriate.

`schema migration run` treats identical status pages as stalled, but core returns identical pages during legitimate multi-page FinalValidation and Idle journal draining
crates/icydb-cli/src/observability/migration.rs:97

Failure scenario

The operator deploys a physical migration touching an entity with 300 rows and runs `icydb schema migration run app` as docs/guides/schema-migrations.md prescribes. Advances go Prepared -> Validating (pages) -> ReadyToRewrite -> RewritingRows (pages) -> RebuildingIndexes -> FinalValidation. The next Advance validates 256 rows, stays in FinalValidation with identical public counters, and the CLI exits 1 with 'deployed migration made no bounded progress'. A 100k-row table needs about 390 re-runs of `run` (or manual `advance`). The misleading 'stuck' message may push the operator toward unsafe actions. The same thing happens at the first Advance of any second physical migration while the prior plan's journal still has pending pages.

Evidence

run_to_terminal: `let next = advance(target, &status)?; ... if next == status { return Err("deployed migration made no bounded progress".into()); }`. Core FinalValidation page: migration_execution.rs:713 `let progress = before_progress.with_rewrite_page(final_cursor, 0)?;` (rows_rewritten += 0, only the private row_cursor moves), and application.rs:1395-1403 keeps phase FinalValidation while !exhausted; MAX_MIGRATION_FINAL_VALIDATION_ROWS_PER_PAGE = 256 (migration_execution.rs:99). active_migration_status (application.rs:1790-1801) publishes the same counters, `next_cursor: None`, `terminal_receipt: None`, so SchemaMigrationStatusPage (PartialEq on all fields) is byte-for-byte equal. Idle drain: application.rs:1105-1116 returns schema_migration_status_for_target unchanged while a prior terminal plan's journal drains, and migration_api.rs:25-26 documents that 'A new plan may remain `Idle` while this step drains a prior terminal plan's journal.' The abort loop in the same file (lines 55-58) already acknowledges that the bounded cursor is not public, but run_to_terminal ignores this.

Recommendation

Stop using full-page equality as the progress signal. Best option: expose an opaque progress token (e.g. a page sequence or cursor digest) in SchemaMigrationStatusPage and compare that. Alternatively, allow unchanged pages in the Idle and FinalValidation phases, as the abort loop does, with a generous iteration cap. Add a unit test that drives run_to_terminal through a fake advance sequence with repeated identical FinalValidation and Idle pages.

It runs in every scan loop, including the bounded order window (scan.rs:484, 514, 392). In the facade, page_entry_limit is Some for every cursor page with a PK-only order (facade.rs:305-316, 556-566). crates/icydb/src/db/sql/table_render.rs:900

Failure scenario

An end user writes display_name = "\x1b]52;c;<base64>\x07" or "x\n| 1 | admin | ..." through an ordinary app endpoint. A controller then runs `icydb sql "SELECT * FROM user"`. The operator's terminal executes the OSC/CSI sequences (clipboard write, hidden or rewritten output), or the embedded newline breaks the ASCII table and forges extra rows. A text value "null" is displayed as SQL NULL.

Evidence

render_table_row does `format!("{value:<width$}")` on raw cell strings (table_render.rs:900-907). Projection cells come from RowProjectionOutput::rendered_rows / render_output_value_text, which ends in PublicValue::render_text, where `Self::Text(value) => value.clone()` (icydb-core value/public.rs:66). Grouped rows are stringified on the canister the same way (sql/convert.rs:117-128). The CLI prints SqlQueryResult::render_text() and render_projection_display_rows_lines output directly (icydb-cli shell/render.rs:14-31). It escapes query_field but not row values. Text("null") and NULL also render identically, and the CLI uppercases both to NULL.

Recommendation

Escape control characters (C0/C1, including \n, \r and ESC) and quote or disambiguate Text in render_text and the table renderers, for example with Rust-style escape_debug for text cells and distinct quoting for strings versus NULL. Alternatively, sanitize every cell centrally in render_table_row and render_grouped_lines.

Verifier (confirmed): I traced the path end to end and nothing sanitizes the text. crates/icydb/src/db/sql/table_render.rs:900-907 pads raw cell strings with format!, and render_table_section (table_render.rs:353-365) is shared by the projection (775-797) and grouped (800-822) renderers. Projection cells come from RowProjectionOutput::rendered_rows (icydb-core db/response/rows.rs:38-43), then render_output_value_text (value/output.rs:222-224), then PublicValue::render_text, which returns Text unmodified (value/public.rs:66). Grouped rows are stringified the same way in crates/icydb/src/db/sql/convert.rs:109-139. The CLI prints this output directly (icydb-cli shell/render.rs:14-38), and uppercase_null_cells (render.rs:51-59) rewrites any cell equal to "null", including Text("null"), to NULL. I found no text sanitization anywhere in core or facade: the only is_control/escape use is constraint.rs:1556 and describe.rs:2059. The CLI does escape control characters for query_field (icydb-cli diagnostic.rs:674-693, tested at 1841), which shows the project treats terminal-control injection as in scope but never applied it to row values. The scenario is realistic: an end user stores ESC/OSC or newline characters through an app endpoint, and a controller later runs icydb sql. Medium fits because it is operator-tooling display integrity and missing output validation, not a durable-state or authorization defect.

Value::Principal is encoded via segments::push_terminated_bytes(v.as_slice()), which gives byte-content order. icydb_schema::Principal derives Ord from ic_principal::Principal, and ic_principal 0.1.5 derives Ord on `struct { len: u8, bytes: [u8;29] }`, so shorter principals always sort first. Value::strict_order_cmp uses that Ord (value/compare.rs:50,80). The Account encoder deliberately mirrors the length-first Account::cmp (segments.rs:17-43), but Principal does not. The ordering tests use only equal-length principals ([1] vs [2]).

Value strict/canonical comparison uses that Ord (value/compare.rs:50, 80). Principal has supports_ordering = true (icydb-schema/src/scalar_macros.rs:148-157), and field_key_contract_supports_operator allows Gt/Gte/Lt/Lte (query/plan/key_support.rs:18-27), so range predicates on an indexed Principal are lowered to raw byte envelopes that disagree with semantic order. The Account encoder deliberately mirrors the length-first order (segments.rs:17-43); Principal does not. Oversized equality/range literal on an indexed column returns InvariantViolation instead of a correct result
crates/icydb-core/src/db/access/lowering.rs:776

Failure scenario

`SELECT * FROM grid WHERE terrain = '<4100-byte string>'` on the demo's indexed unbounded Text column fails with an InvariantViolation instead of returning zero rows (no stored component can exceed 4096 bytes). `terrain > '<5000 x a>'` should return rows like 'b' but errors instead. An IN list with one oversized member fails the whole query. Callers see an internal-invariant class for ordinary user input.

Evidence

encode_index_prefix_values encodes the literal with no component-size check. raw_bounds_for_prefix_with_kind / raw_bounds_for_prefix_component_range_with_kind reject components > MAX_COMPONENT_SIZE (4096) with SegmentTooLarge (codec/mod.rs:150, 200 via validate_component_bound). That error is mapped to IndexRangeBoundEncodeError::RawKey, then LoweredAccessError::IndexPrefix/IndexRange (lowering.rs:776, 489), then InternalError::index_invariant() (lowering.rs:81). The main prepare path propagates it (prepared_execution_plan/core.rs:949-955). SQL input allows literals up to about 2 MiB and the planner has no MAX_COMPONENT_SIZE guard. Deferred multi-lookup bounds fail the same way at execution time.

Recommendation

In lowering or planning, recognize literals whose encoded component exceeds MAX_COMPONENT_SIZE. For equality or IN, prune the branch as provably empty. For range bounds, clamp to a sentinel with the same ordering, or fall back to a non-index route. At minimum, map the error to a user-facing Unsupported class.

Verifier (confirmed): encode_index_prefix_values (access/lowering.rs:833-860) encodes literals through encode_accepted_index_literal_component -> encode_canonical_index_component, and neither checks MAX_COMPONENT_SIZE (key/build.rs:230-268, ordered/mod.rs:106-116). admit_query_index_component only charges budget. raw_bounds_for_prefix_with_kind and raw_bounds_for_prefix_component_range_with_kind reject components over 4096 bytes with SegmentTooLarge (codec/mod.rs:145-152, 195-204). That error becomes LoweredAccessError::IndexPrefix/IndexRange (lowering.rs:489, 776), then InternalError::index_invariant() (lowering.rs:79-82). prepare_execution_plan propagates it (executor/prepared_execution_plan/core.rs:949-955). Stored components are capped at 4096 at write time (build.rs:475 etc.), so equality with an oversized literal should return empty, and a range with an oversized bound should still return rows. Instead the query errors with an internal-invariant class. This is a returned error, not a trap, and the input is an edge case, so medium, at most.
mediumconfirmedindex-access-6 · performance · medium confidence
Stable index B-tree page size is derived from the 16,477-byte maximum key (~133 KiB of stable memory per node)
crates/icydb-core/src/db/index/key/codec/envelope.rs:22

Failure scenario

Each node holds about 6-11 entries, so a journaled index with 1M small entries grows stable memory to roughly 12-23 GB after fold. The same data needs about 50 MB of key bytes. A table with a few indexes and a few million rows pays large ongoing storage-cycle costs, grows stable memory quickly during folds, and can approach subnet storage-reservation limits.

Evidence

RawIndexStoreKey::BOUND = Bounded{max_size: MAX_STORED_SIZE_BYTES}. That is 1+18+1 + 4*(2+4096) + (2+63) = 16,477 bytes, with IndexEntryValue max 1. ic-stable-structures 0.7.2 BTreeMap::new sets PageSize::Value(max_node_size*3/4), where max_node_size = header + 11*(4+16477+1+4) + 12*8 ≈ 181 KB, so the page is about 136 KB. The allocator hands out one chunk of that size per node, whatever the actual key sizes (typically about 50 bytes). IndexStore::memory_bytes reports only key+value bytes, which hides this. The design doc 0.248-uint256/patch-1-measurement.md notes that page size comes from the maximum, but does not quantify per-node stable cost.

Recommendation

Measure stable-memory growth per index entry. Consider an Unbounded key BOUND, which gives DEFAULT_PAGE_SIZE 1 KiB with overflow pages, or a much smaller bounded maximum by moving large components out of line. Report real allocator usage in storage diagnostics.

Verifier (confirmed): RawIndexStoreKey::BOUND is Bounded{max_size: MAX_STORED_SIZE_BYTES} (codec/envelope.rs:24-27). That is prefix + 4*(2+4096) + (2+63), about 16.5 KB (codec/bounds.rs:26-29), and the IndexEntryValue bound is 1 byte (index/entry.rs:20, 254-256). Journaled index stores use StableBTreeMap::init (index/store.rs:171). In ic-stable-structures 0.7.2, BTreeMap::new with two bounded types sets PageSize::Value(max_node_size*3/4) (btreemap.rs:326-347). max_node_size = header + 11*(4+key+value+4) + 12*8 (node/v1.rs:199-209), about 181 KB, so each chunk is about 136 KB. Allocator::allocate writes the next free chunk header one chunk further on (btreemap/allocator.rs:160-191), so stable memory grows by about one full chunk per node whatever the real key sizes are. The archived design note (docs/design/archive/0.248-uint256/patch-1-measurement.md:152-165) acknowledges that page size comes from the maximum but does not quantify the per-node stable cost. This is a real storage-cost and capacity hazard, not a correctness bug, so medium.
mediumconfirmedindex-access-7 · robustness · medium confidence
Heap-resident exact prefix-cardinality metadata grows with every distinct index prefix and is never trimmed while the canister runs
crates/icydb-core/src/db/index/store.rs:172

Failure scenario

A canister whose database started empty and runs for a long time without upgrades keeps O(distinct prefixes) heap state for every journaled index. For a unique email index plus a two-column index on a 10M-row table that is several GB. It reaches the wasm heap or memory limit, allocation traps start failing update calls, and pre_upgrade may also need heap. This is exactly the heap growth a stable-memory store is meant to avoid.

Evidence

init_journaled uses IndexPrefixCardinality::synchronized_empty() when the canonical map is empty. After that, every insert, remove and journal publish updates first_component_counts/counts (cardinality.rs:523-575): one heap BTreeMap entry per distinct prefix of every length, holding owned copies of the component bytes. There is no size cap (cardinality.rs has no limit). Folds do not trim it (only the delta watermark moves). It is dropped only by reset_journaled_live_projection during recovery when canonical is non-empty (store.rs:531-537).

Recommendation

Bound the metadata: cap the entry count or bytes and switch to unavailable when exceeded, or rebuild lazily and bounded from canonical. Account its size in storage diagnostics.

Verifier (confirmed): init_journaled selects IndexPrefixCardinality::synchronized_empty() when canonical is empty (index/store.rs:171-176). From then on, insert, insert_preflighted_absent, remove and publish_preflighted_journal_entry all call apply_insert/apply_remove (store.rs:453, 482, 504, 597-603). counted_prefixes emits one key per prefix length 1..=component_count, each owning copies of the component bytes (cardinality.rs:862-880). These go into heap BTreeMaps with no cap (cardinality.rs:68-73, 523-601; no size limit in the module). Fold only advances the delta watermark (store.rs:555-569). The metadata is dropped only by reset_journaled_live_projection (store.rs:532-537) or by a reopen with a non-empty canonical. So a database that started empty keeps heap usage that grows with the number of distinct prefixes until the next upgrade. The heap is reclaimed on upgrade, so the canister is not bricked; medium fits.
mediumverifiedintegrity-relations-1 · robustness · medium confidence
Durable startup failure receipts are bound only to database state, so a fixed upgrade cannot clear a failure caused by a code bug and the canister stays wedged
crates/icydb-core/src/db/startup/driver.rs:47

Failure scenario

1. A logic bug in replay-time relation preparation (prepare_row_commit_batch_for_replay -> prepare_source_transition) or in fold returns store_invariant() while a marker is retained or journal debt exists after an upgrade. 2. record_recovery_failure classifies it as terminal and publishes a JournalRecovery or DatabaseControl receipt bound to the unchanged journal proof, control proof or memory id. 3. The operator ships a fixed wasm. post_upgrade calls observe; the receipt still matches because no writes can change the journal or control proof while startup is failed. The driver returns Terminal, the watchdog goes inactive, and every query, write and integrity call keeps returning the StartupFailure. For a schema-reconciliation receipt the only escape is to change the generated schema so the submission key changes. For journal or control receipts the only escape is reinstall, which loses data.

Evidence

terminal_code_for_kind treats STORE_INVARIANT_VIOLATION and RUNTIME_INVARIANT_VIOLATION as persisted, terminal failures for every kind (startup/mod.rs:116-124). InternalError::store_invariant() is the generic 'should not happen' error used throughout the recovery and relation code: 16 uses in commit/recovery.rs and several in reverse_index.rs, e.g. :644 and :1219. The receipt binding (receipt.rs:48-64) holds only durable identities: DatabaseControl{commit_memory_id, stable_key, control: Option<(incarnation, proof)>}, JournalRecovery{incarnation, allocation, journal proof} and SchemaReconciliation{incarnation, submission_key (a digest of the schema fragment, model/actor/mod.rs:88-99), accepted_head}. No build or code identity is included. When a marker is present, capture_database_control_binding records control: None, and observe matches that purely on memory id and stable key (observe.rs:55-64). driver.rs:45-48 returns Terminal as soon as observe() returns Err, and the generated watchdog is set Inactive or stopped on Err (store.rs reconcile_startup_watchdog_from_durable_state, startup_watchdog_callback). receipt::clear is reached only through success paths that run after observe returned Ok.

Recommendation

Bind receipts to a code or build identity as well, e.g. a hash of the generated submission plus the crate/runtime version, so any new wasm makes them stale and forces one fresh deterministic attempt. Alternatively, stop classifying *_INVARIANT_VIOLATION as persisted-state terminal and keep only codes that genuinely indicate persisted-byte corruption or format problems. Consider a controller-only 'clear startup failure and retry' control as well.

Severity adjusted from high to medium during verification.
Verifier (confirmed): I reproduced this from the code. startup/mod.rs:116-120 makes STORE_INVARIANT_VIOLATION and RUNTIME_INVARIANT_VIOLATION terminal for every kind. InternalError::store_invariant() is (InvariantViolation, Store) at error/mod.rs:976, and any other origin maps to RUNTIME_INVARIANT_VIOLATION (error/mod.rs:3199-3202). recovery.rs uses these errors for internal code-logic checks: slot already filled at :1716-1737, wrong prepared op at :1494/:1503/:1538, missing replay candidate at :629. driver.rs:224-235 publishes a receipt whose binding comes from capture_database_control_binding (:270-286) or capture_journal_binding. When a marker is present, observe_commit_control returns empty_control_proof=None (commit/store/mod.rs:705-716), so the binding is control: None and observe.rs:55-64 matches it only on memory id and stable key. Nothing in any binding identifies the code or build. The generated post_upgrade reconciles the watchdog from observe (icydb-model build/actor/db/store.rs:237-256), and startup_watchdog_callback stops on Err (:261-268). receipt::clear is reached only from success paths (driver.rs:53, :123, :148) and from the schema handoff. A fixed wasm therefore cannot clear a JournalRecovery or DatabaseControl receipt. The exposure is also wider than the finding states. drive_recovery_page runs continue_recovery_with_failure_authority, which includes online journal convergence after Ready (recovery.rs:229-231, :250-259). So an invariant error while folding an ordinary committed write's batch also publishes a permanent receipt and gates all operations. The 0.225 design (0.225-design.md:266-290) does say a code change cannot clear DB-control or journal receipts. But its rule 1 limits publication to persisted-corruption, format-incompatibility, or generated-schema errors. Classifying code-level invariant violations as persisted failures goes beyond that rule, and no doc lists INVARIANT_VIOLATION as terminal. The trigger needs a latent bug, but this is a fast-moving pre-1.0 recovery and fold path and the only escape is reinstall, which loses data. I keep high.
Skeptic · reachability (upheld, medium): Everything after the trigger checks out. Once a JournalRecovery or DatabaseControl receipt matches, nothing clears it: no upgrade, and no rollback to an older wasm either, because the binding holds only durable identities. The only exit is a new incarnation, which means reinstall. What I could not build is the trigger. I found no concrete inputs that make the recovery or fold path return an InvariantViolation-class error from valid state. The one example I checked, reverse_index.rs:644, cannot fire: decode_relation_target_data_key with RelationTargetMismatchPolicy::Reject never returns Ok(None) (reverse_index.rs:1702-1718). The other store_invariant sites I read (recovery.rs:1494, 1503, 1538, 1718-1737) are internal bookkeeping checks that only a code bug can hit. So this is a latent hazard with no present trigger, not a high-severity defect reachable from caller input. I rate it medium ("latent hazard very likely to cause future bugs") rather than refuting it, because: (a) The exposure is wider than the claim says. The same driver runs online convergence after Ready. Every committed write's journal batch is folded through prepare_recovered_row_transitions -> prepare_row_commit_batch_for_replay (recovery.rs:797, ~957), so any invariant bug in shared row, index or relation preparation turns into a permanent brick in steady state, not only after an upgrade. (b) All InvariantViolation errors map to STORE_INVARIANT_VIOLATION or RUNTIME_INVARIANT_VIOLATION whatever their origin (error/mod.rs:3199-3202), and recovery re-tags database-control errors with ErrorOrigin::Recovery. That means executor, index and planner code invariants are all persisted as terminal (startup/mod.rs:116-124). (c) This contradicts the stated intent. The 0.225 design rule 1 (0.225-design.md:268-274) says to record a receipt only for a returned persisted-corruption, format-incompatibility, or deterministic generated-schema error. PERSISTED_FORMAT_INVENTORY.md:27 describes receipts as authority for "corruption". A runtime invariant violation is not persisted corruption. Design rule 6 (a code change cannot clear a matching receipt) is deliberate, so the bug is the classification, not the binding. The code already traps on apply-time contradictions (recovery.rs:1514-1516 trap_validated_journal_apply_contradiction) so they roll back rather than persist; prepare-time invariants do not get the same treatment. One correction to the claim: for schema-reconciliation receipts there is a non-destructive exit. Changing the fragment or adding a migration plan changes the submission key (icydb-model build/actor/mod.rs:88-99). Only journal and control receipts lead to reinstall.

crates/icydb-core/src/db/relation/validate.rs:138

Group G has `members: IdSet<User>` with 200 members, in the same store as User. One atomic batch updates G to remove 80 members (G' keeps 120) and deletes those 80 User rows. REF_INTEGRITY §4.1 explicitly allows pairing a target delete with an update-away. For each of the 80 deleted users, the reverse scan finds G, projects G', and charges 120 references: 80 x 120 = 9,600 > 5,460.
