mediumconfirmedr2-recursive-bounds-2 · performance · medium confidence
Recursive row decoders re-skip every subtree at each nesting level: decode cost is O(bytes x depth), up to ~63x write cost, while all row/page budgets are byte-based
crates/icydb-core/src/db/data/structural_field/value_storage/canonical.rs:154

Failure scenario

A field of kind List^62<Bool> (by-kind), or a canonical List^60<Newtype(Unit)>, holding a chain of one-element lists that ends in a list of N≈500k one-byte leaves. The row is about 500 KB, within every byte bound, and admission charges about N bytes. Every decode performs about 62·N ≈ 31M leaf-skip steps instead of about N. Row validation (validate_all_declared_slots, structural_slot_reader.rs:538) plus the slot decode repeat that 2-3 times. Estimated at tens of wasm instructions per step, one read of this row costs on the order of 10^9 instructions. A public page query that touches a few such rows (at most 100 rows allowed) exceeds the 5B query instruction limit, so every caller whose scan includes the rows fails. Writes (40B update limit) and recovery replay (prepare + verify decode again, recovery.rs:797-800, :2788-2835) pay the same multiplied cost. Instruction figures are estimates; the mechanism was verified by code reading.

Evidence

decode_canonical_value_storage_bytes first walks the whole value (canonical.rs:109). Then at every list/map level, decode_canonical_list/map calls skip_canonical_value on each child, which walks the child's full subtree (canonical.rs:154, :177, :181, recursion at :213), before decoding that child (:155-158), which repeats the skip one level down. Each node is walked once per list/map ancestor. The by-kind lane has the same shape: decode_accepted_list_bytes / validate_accepted_list_bytes (accepted.rs:236, :289) use walk_binary_list_items, which runs skip_binary_value over each item's full subtree (binary.rs:438, :468-470) before recursing into it. Encoding and admission are single-pass O(n) (canonical.rs:52-100, admission.rs:548-573). The only bounds are bytes/items: MAX_ROW_BYTES=4 MiB (codec/mod.rs:21), MAX_ACCEPTED_VALUE_BYTES=4 MiB (admission.rs:24), and public row/byte caps (RESOURCE_MODEL.md:101-110). None scale with depth.

Recommendation

Make recursive decode single-pass: decode each child with a cursor-returning decoder (as the value-storage walk.rs helpers already do) instead of skip-then-decode, and validate boundaries once at the root. Do the same in walk_binary_list_items/walk_binary_map_entries (yield item ranges from one pass, or recurse with the cursor). Alternatively charge decode work per node × depth against the execution budget, or bound nodes × depth at admission.

Verifier (confirmed): I reproduced the mechanism. decode_canonical_value_storage_bytes first skips the whole value (canonical.rs:109). decode_canonical_list and decode_canonical_map then call skip_canonical_value on each child (canonical.rs:154, :177, :181), which recurses over the child's full subtree (:212-214), and then decode the child (:155-158), which repeats the skip one level down. Each byte is therefore walked once per list/map ancestor. The by-kind lane has the same shape. decode_accepted_list_bytes and validate_accepted_list_bytes (accepted.rs:236, :289) use walk_binary_list_items, which calls skip_binary_value over each item (binary.rs:438; map walker :468-470) before on_item recurses into that item. Admission and encoding are single-pass (enum_catalog/admission.rs:549-574; canonical.rs:52-103). The only bounds are byte-based: MAX_ROW_BYTES=4 MiB (codec/mod.rs:21) and MAX_ACCEPTED_VALUE_BYTES=4 MiB (admission.rs:24). Kind depth is capped at 64 (accepted_field_kind.rs:86-88), so the amplification is a constant of at most about 63x, not unbounded. Validation of every declared slot on eager readers (structural_slot_reader.rs:538-562) adds further passes. The finding's scenarios use unusual schemas (List^62<Bool>, List^60<Newtype(Unit)>). A plain recursive record such as Node{label, children: List<Node>} gets about 62 ancestors per leaf without an odd schema. Under the admission budget that allows roughly 1e5 to 1.4e6 leaves, which is tens of millions of skip steps per decode. That can plausibly approach the query instruction limit per row while writes, under the higher update limit, still succeed. The instruction figures are unmeasured estimates, and exploiting this needs write access plus a deep or recursive schema. I found no design doc accepting this trade-off, and the cursor.rs:41-44 comment shows single-pass decoding is an intended property. Medium fits: a missing depth-scaled cost bound and a latent read-DoS hazard, not a correctness bug.
mediumverifiedr2-replay-cost-1 · durability · medium confidence
Migration journal fold reloads and fully re-decodes the durable migration record twice per journal record, so large migrations produce rewrite pages that can never be folded
crates/icydb-core/src/db/commit/recovery.rs:89

Failure scenario

A coordinated migration covers about 1,000 entities, so the record is about 150-300 KiB. The first rewrite page for an entity with 3 indexes commits 256 rows, about 1,024 journal records. Its fold performs 2,048 record loads, which is about 6 full value copies, 4 parses and 8 full re-encodes of the record per journal record. That is several MB of byte work per journal record and about 30-50B instructions for the page, above the 40B limit. The same page fits easily in the producer message. Every watchdog attempt traps and rolls back, and the 1 s cadence successor retries forever at up to 40B instructions each, with no receipt. The migration is already past the pre-rewrite abort point, so the gated database can never progress. After any upgrade it stays Recovering. Even a single-entity migration adds about 12 extra stable B-tree lookups per journal record, roughly 13B for a 16,384-effect page.

Evidence

validate_schema_migration_journal_plan (recovery.rs:89-98) calls load_schema_migration_record() and is invoked once per SchemaMigrationRowPut/SchemaMigrationIndexPut record during fold validation (recovery.rs:1969, 1986). It is invoked again for the same records during apply (recovery.rs:1625, 1646), and again during Verify (2717, 2738). Each load_schema_migration_record() (live_schema_checkpoint.rs:615-621) does the following. It opens the SchemaControlMap: BTreeMap::load, a header get and two range probes (control_store.rs:83-123). from_map decodes the migration record (live_schema_checkpoint.rs:152-160). checkpoint_count does a full value get of the migration record just to test is_some (258-272). load_migration fetches and decodes it again (274-279). Each decode does a CRC32C pass, a full parse, validate() (which re-encodes the whole record, migration_record.rs:822) and a second canonical re-encode compared against the input (migration_record.rs:1063-1068). The record can be up to 2 MiB and hold 4,096 entities and 4,096 staged indexes (migration_record.rs:23-25). A rewrite page is capped at 256 rows but up to 16,384 journal records (migration_execution.rs:95-98, 168). The producer (publish_migration_rewrite_page / preflight_migration_effects, migration_execution.rs:448-665) never loads the record per effect. The fold's cost is therefore O(records x record_bytes), and nothing bounds that product. DURABILITY.md:162-167 lists the page bounds but not migration-record size.

Recommendation

Load and verify the migration record once per fold. Check permits_private_physical_journal in validate_journal_batch_records and carry the verified digest into apply and verify instead of reloading. Stop decoding the migration record in LiveSchemaCheckpointStore::from_map on every open, and use contains_key in checkpoint_count. Add a PocketIC test that folds a 16,384-effect rewrite page under a maximum-entity migration record and asserts the callback stays under 30B.

Severity adjusted from high to medium during verification.
Verifier (confirmed): I checked the code path myself. validate_schema_migration_journal_plan (recovery.rs:89-97) calls load_schema_migration_record() with no cache, once per SchemaMigrationRowPut/IndexPut record. In a fold it runs twice per record: once in validation (recovery.rs:1969, 1986) and once in apply (recovery.rs:1625, 1646, reached through apply_prepared_journal_batch at 1506 with prepared slot None). Each load does the following (live_schema_checkpoint.rs:615-621): opens the control map (control_store.rs:83-123: BTreeMap::load, a header get, two keys_range probes). from_map then gets and decodes the record (152-160), checkpoint_count does a keys_range walk plus full gets of lineage and migration just to test is_some (258-272), and load_migration gets and decodes it again (274-279). Every decode (migration_record.rs:969-1068) does a byte-wise table CRC32C (database_format/mod.rs:388), a parse, validate() which re-encodes the record (822) with another CRC, and a second canonical encode compared against the input (1066). Per journal record that comes to about 6 value copies, 4 parses, 8 encodes and 12 CRC passes over the record, plus roughly 12 stable B-tree operations. The producer never loads the record per effect (publish_migration_rewrite_page and preflight_migration_effects, migration_execution.rs:449-649). The page bounds (256 rows, 1 MiB index bytes, 16,384 records; migration_execution.rs:95-98, journal/codec.rs:32) do not limit record_bytes, which can reach 2 MiB and 4,096 entities (migration_record.rs:23-25). A fold is one atomic batch (recovery.rs:336-339). Once RewritingRows starts there is no abort (may_transition_to, migration_record.rs:114-131), so a fold that exceeds the instruction limit permanently wedges the gated database. I keep high, not critical, because the trigger needs a large but admitted shape: a record of roughly 100 KiB or more (hundreds of migrated entities; lineage holds only transitioned entities, migration_planner.rs:359-372) on a ~1-1.5K-record page, or a moderate record of about 5-10 KiB combined with a high-fanout page near 16K records. A typical small migration adds only about 1B per page. The cost figures are my estimates and have not been measured.
Skeptic · reachability+intent (upheld, medium): The mechanism is real, and I verified the code path end to end. For every SchemaMigrationRowPut or SchemaMigrationIndexPut record, the fold loads the durable migration record twice: once in validation (recovery.rs:1969/1986) and again in apply. The apply load happens because prepare_recovered_row_transitions only prepares RowPut/RowDelete (recovery.rs:766-781). Migration records therefore have prepared_ops == None, and apply_prepared_journal_batch falls through to apply_journal_record, which calls validate_schema_migration_journal_plan again (recovery.rs:1500-1507, 1625/1646). Each load_schema_migration_record (live_schema_checkpoint.rs:615-621) does the following: - open_existing does a BTreeMap::load, a header get and two keys_range probes (control_store.rs:83-123). - from_map gets the record and decodes it (live_schema_checkpoint.rs:152-156). - checkpoint_count does a family keys_range scan (control_store.rs:166-170), then full-value gets of the lineage and migration entries just to test is_some (live_schema_checkpoint.rs:258-272). - load_migration gets the record and decodes it a second time (274-279). Each decode does a table CRC32C pass (database_format/mod.rs:388-394), a parse, validate() (which re-encodes at migration_record.rs:822) and a canonical re-encode compare (migration_record.rs:1066-1068). The producer does none of this per effect: publish_migration_rewrite_page and preflight_migration_effects (migration_execution.rs:448-545, 626-657) only touch the record once per page. Batch decoding already rejects mixed plan digests (0.228-status.md:45-49), so one check per batch would suffice. The per-record reload is redundant, and it is not a documented intent. The claimed high severity is overstated: - **Record size is only large for very large migrations.** The record's entity and transition lists hold only the migrating lineage (migration_planner.rs:359-372, application.rs:1207-1217). Staged indexes are only indexes whose generation changed or that are new (application.rs:1219-1250, migration_planner.rs:1390-1407). Each migrating entity adds about 120 B, plus 56 B per staged index. - **Break-even estimate.** I estimate about 120-150 instructions per record byte per journal record (2 loads). Against the 40B limit, that puts the break-even at a record of about 260-330 KB for a 1,024-record page, which means roughly 1,000-2,500 entities bumped in one coordinated plan. It is about 65-80 KB (around 500 entities) for 4,096 records per page. For 16,384 records per page it is about 16-20 KB, but that needs about 63 derived keys per row. - **Typical migrations are far below the limit.** A few to tens of entities give a record of at most about 5-10 KB and at most about 2K records per page, which adds only about 1-3B instructions. - **The configuration is legal but not typical.** It sits within MAX_SCHEMA_MIGRATION_RECORD_ENTITIES = 4,096 (migration_record.rs:23-25), the 512 KiB plan limit and the 2 MiB proposal limit (icydb-schema/src/bounds.rs:7,10), but it is not realistic IC usage. - **The docs disclaim a recovery instruction-budget guarantee.** DURABILITY.md:325-331 says the maintained engine has no instruction-budget certification and that recovery that cannot complete fails closed. - **The wedge is not permanent in absolute terms.** Installing a Wasm with a cheaper fold unblocks it. This is a real missing bound: the fold's cost is not bounded by what the producer admitted, and the consequence is a stuck, gated database once the migration is past the abort point. It needs extreme but legal scale to trigger, so I rate it medium rather than high.

Unique-validation page fold re-reads, re-hashes, decodes and re-fingerprints the whole canonical accepted-schema bundle once per staged index key
crates/icydb-core/src/db/commit/recovery.rs:1888

Failure scenario

A store's accepted bundle is about 1-1.5 MiB, for example a dozen wide entities with constraints. That is within the 2 MiB proposal bound. An ADD UNIQUE or generated unique activation on a populated entity commits a Forward page with 256 keys in a cheap producer message. Folding it costs 256 x (2 SHA-256 passes plus a decode and an encode of the bundle), at least 130M instructions per MiB per key, which lands around or above 40B. Every watchdog attempt traps and retries each second with no receipt. Online, the backlog stops draining and writes eventually fail with E284 pressure. After an upgrade the database stays Recovering, and the unique validation job cannot advance.

Evidence

The ConstraintValidationIndexPut arm of validate_journal_batch_record (recovery.rs:1888-1925) runs once per record, and each record carries one key. Per record it decodes the job from the first record and calls store.current_canonical_accepted_schema_bundle() with no cache (schema/store.rs:1754-1776). That call reads the root slots and the full bundle bytes from stable memory. It then runs decode_verified_accepted_schema_revision_bundle: SHA-256 over the bundle, a full decode, and semantic_fingerprint(), which re-encodes every catalog and entity snapshot and hashes them again (enum_catalog/publication.rs:986-998, 362-386). Forward pages stage up to 256 keys, one per row (constraint_activation_runner.rs:54-57, 612-626; schema_publication.rs:813-868). The producer checks all entries against a cached bundle once (schema_publication.rs:398-413, 912-932). The batch-level check already loads the bundle once (recovery.rs:2195).

Recommendation

Resolve and verify the canonical bundle and decode the job once per batch, which validate_journal_batch_constraint_validation_job_change already does. Validate all ConstraintValidationIndexPut keys in one validate_candidate_index_entries call. Add a fold measurement for a 256-key page under a large store bundle.

Verifier (confirmed): The ConstraintValidationIndexPut arm (recovery.rs:1888-1925) re-decodes the job and calls store.current_canonical_accepted_schema_bundle() once per record in Fold mode. That call is uncached (schema/store.rs:1754-1776). It reads the root slots and the full bundle from canonical stable storage, then runs decode_verified_accepted_schema_revision_bundle (enum_catalog/publication.rs:1025-1036): a SHA-256 over the bundle, a full decode with validate_decoded_semantics, and semantic_fingerprint (362-386), which re-encodes every catalog and entity snapshot and hashes them again. The producer validates all entries against one bundle per page (schema_publication.rs:398-413), and that bundle comes from the cached effective path (current_accepted_schema_bundle, store.rs:2220-2238). The batch-level check also loads the bundle only once (recovery.rs:2195). Forward pages stage up to 256 keys, and publish_journaled_constraint_validation_job writes one record per key (schema_publication.rs:826-834; runner limits at constraint_activation_runner.rs:54-57). So fold cost is about 256 x the bundle verify cost, and the batch folds atomically. With a bundle of roughly 1 MiB or more (within the 2 MiB proposal and 16 MiB bundle bounds) this plausibly reaches the 40B limit. The oldest head then blocks convergence (fold_oldest_journal_batch, recovery.rs:843-851) and startup recovery. Medium is right: it needs an unusually large per-store bundle, and for typical bundles of 100-300 KiB the overhead is only a few billion.

DDL user-index replacement batches: the fold re-fingerprints the entity snapshot for every 64-key chunk, and admitted batches can hold 2x the 65,536-effect maximum that the convergence evidence proves and measures
crates/icydb-core/src/db/commit/recovery.rs:2024

Failure scenario

Take CREATE INDEX over 65,536 rows, the measured maximum shape, on an entity whose persisted snapshot is about 256 KiB (256 fields plus check constraints, within the 512 KiB fragment bound). The producer pays one fingerprint and commits at about 33B. The fold adds 1,024 chunk fingerprints of about 18-25M each to the measured 21.1B, reaching about 39-46B. It traps on every watchdog attempt and retries each second forever, so convergence halts and the canister is wedged after the next upgrade. A 128 KiB snapshot already pushes the fold above the 30B design ceiling. Separately, CREATE INDEX on an entity that already has indexes produces up to 131,072 stable B-tree ops per fold. That is 2x the shape any proof or measurement covers, and the replay cost of these batches is unverified.

Evidence

validate_accepted_schema_index_chunk re-encodes and SHA-256s the full accepted-after entity snapshot through accepted_schema_cache_fingerprint_for_persisted_snapshot (schema/fingerprint.rs:52-62). It does this for every AcceptedSchemaIndexDelete and AcceptedSchemaIndexPut record (recovery.rs:2016-2027). The producer computes the fingerprint once (user_index_domain.rs:309-311) and stamps it on each 64-key chunk (schema_publication.rs:620-647). CREATE INDEX (field-path and expression) and DROP INDEX all use complete-domain replacement (sql_ddl.rs:221-233, 268-280, 485-497). That replacement deletes every existing user-index key of the entity and re-puts every accepted-after key, including unchanged indexes (user_index_domain.rs:366-420; schema_publication.rs:1071-1095). The fold applies each key as a stable canonical insert or remove (recovery.rs:1663-1684; index/store.rs:743-780). The staging budget admits up to 65,536 deletions plus before+after projections up to 131,072 (user_index_domain.rs:42; mutation/budget.rs:14-15), so one batch can carry about 131,072 key effects in about 2,048 chunks. The convergence proof's MAX_CALLBACK_POSITIONED_EFFECTS is 65,536 (convergence_candidate.rs:49). The only measured maximum is a 65,536-key fold at 21,089,837,408 instructions, with a 32.6B producer (0.230-status.md:715-717). That fixture is no longer run by any test: publish_promotion_index_fixture and append_promotion_index_fixture_page have no callers (canisters/audit/sql_perf/src/lib.rs:4207-4270).

Recommendation

Check the fingerprint once per (batch, entity_tag) instead of once per chunk. Diff the before and after domains so keys of unchanged indexes are not deleted and reinserted. Either cap per-batch accepted-index effects at the proven 65,536 or re-prove and measure 131,072. Restore a maintained PocketIC test for the largest DDL publication that asserts the fold callback stays under 30B.

Verifier (confirmed): validate_accepted_schema_index_chunk (recovery.rs:2000-2047) calls accepted_schema_cache_fingerprint_for_persisted_snapshot for every AcceptedSchemaIndexDelete/Put chunk. That function is uncached: a full snapshot encode plus SHA-256 (schema/fingerprint.rs:52-62). The producer computes it once (user_index_domain.rs:309-311) and stamps it on every 64-key chunk (schema_publication.rs:616-649). CREATE INDEX (field-path and expression) and DROP INDEX all go through stage_sql_ddl_user_index_domain_replacement (sql_ddl.rs:221-233, 268-280, 485-497). That is a complete-domain replacement: deletion_keys is every observed user key, and final_entries is every accepted-after key (user_index_domain.rs:366-420). Budgets cap deletions at 65,536 (user_index_domain.rs:42, 1028) and before+after projections at 131,072 (mutation/budget.rs:14, user_index_domain.rs:1007). So one batch can carry about 131,072 key effects, for example CREATE INDEX on about 43,690 rows that already have one index. The test-only convergence proof assumes 65,536 (convergence_candidate.rs:49, a #[cfg(test)] module per commit/mod.rs:20-21). The only measurement is the 65,536-key CREATE INDEX fixture at 21.09B fold / 32.57B producer (0.230-status.md:710-722), and rg finds no harness that calls publish_promotion_index_fixture (sql_perf/src/lib.rs:4214-4270). The code facts hold. The wedge magnitude is unmeasured and depends on large shapes. The per-chunk fingerprint costs about 1B at the maximum shape for ordinary snapshots (20 KiB or less) and matters only near the 512 KiB snapshot cap (codec.rs:32). A wide-row entity would also inflate the producer, which might then fail cleanly before any fold. The 2x-effect batch is an unverified replay-cost gap, not a demonstrated trap. Medium stands.

Deterministic registry-reconciliation rejections are non-terminal: the startup watchdog retries every second forever, re-reading the full control slot, while startup_state() reports Recovering
crates/icydb-core/src/db/startup/mod.rs:126

Failure scenario

The documented case from logical_memory.rs:103-107: a store was retired by v2 and the operator redeploys v1. Also: a release changes the registry while a marker is retained. In production the watchdog then fires every second indefinitely, burning cycles (up to about 16 MiB read plus CRC per tick when a marker is retained) and spamming 'retryable failure' logs. Applications following docs/guides/startup-readiness.md see Ok(Recovering), never a StartupFailure, so they keep polling and never surface the rejection. Only another upgrade stops it. This is the DatabaseControl counterpart of xc-security-2, which covers migration-planning codes.

Evidence

reconcile_current_registry rejects with store_unsupported, which is RUNTIME_UNSUPPORTED (error/mod.rs:1730-1732, 3198). Rejection cases: retired quartet reintroduced (convergence.rs:156-157); omitted store with debt (337-339); registry change with a marker (182-184); 17th quartet (171-173); non-fresh new roots (305-306, 317-318). Format admission failures are attributed to DatabaseControl (commit/recovery.rs:218), and for that kind only persisted-corruption codes are terminal (startup/mod.rs:116-126). record_recovery_failure therefore returns Err without a receipt (driver.rs:229-231). The callback logs and returns WatchdogDecision::Continue with a 1 s cadence (build/actor/db/store.rs:196-206, 284-293). ic-timers applies no backoff (ic-timers 0.8.0 snapshot/model.rs:500-515). Each tick re-runs format admission, because the cache is pushed only on success (database_format/mod.rs:160-175). Admission reads and CRC-checks the whole control slot, including up to 16 MiB of retained marker bytes (commit/store/mod.rs:467-497, 552-568). Each tick also runs observe() three times. observe() returns Ok(Recovering) because recovery never completes (observe.rs:98-100).

Recommendation

Classify deterministic registry rejections as a typed, non-persisted startup failure: stop the watchdog and report the failure through startup_state(), but publish no receipt, so reverting still recovers. Alternatively, add bounded exponential backoff for repeated identical retryable failures.

Verifier (confirmed): store_unsupported maps to RUNTIME_UNSUPPORTED (error/mod.rs:1730-1732, 3198). Admission failures are attributed to DatabaseControl (recovery.rs:218), and for that kind only persisted-corruption codes are terminal (startup/mod.rs:116-126). record_recovery_failure therefore returns Err without writing a receipt (driver.rs:223-225). The watchdog returns Continue on a 1 s cadence (build/actor/db/store.rs:197-205, 280-292). ic-timers 0.8.0 WatchdogDecision::Continue keeps the cadence successor with no backoff (snapshot/model.rs:500-515). The admission cache is pushed only on success (database_format/mod.rs:171-172), so every tick re-reads and CRC-checks the full control slot (commit/store/mod.rs:467-500, 555-568). observe() returns Ok(Recovering) because the recovery domain never completes (observe.rs:93-95). Mitigating factor: non-terminality looks deliberate. A DatabaseControl receipt would still match after a revert, and logical_memory.rs:110-123 expects the original actor to recover. Still, the unbounded retry loop and the fact that startup_state() never reports a failure for a permanent rejection (the reintroduced-retired case in logical_memory.rs:103-107) are real. Medium is appropriate.

crates/icydb-core/src/db/commit/schema_publication.rs:690

Failure scenario

A canister with the migration capability renames an entity that lives in a heap store and has no relations from journaled stores. After upgrade the watchdog stops with IN_PROGRESS. The controller runs `icydb schema migration run` and sees Applied. The metadata publication touched only the heap store, so no journal batch exists and nothing reschedules the watchdog. startup_state() stays Recovering, and every db() call returns DATABASE_STARTUP_RECOVERY_PENDING. The migration guide's flow ('continue polling until Ready') never completes. Only another upgrade, even with the same wasm, re-arms the watchdog in post_upgrade.

Evidence

The generated handoff stops the watchdog on SCHEMA_MIGRATION_IN_PROGRESS (build/actor/db/store.rs:342-347). The migrate endpoint calls migrate_generated_schema with no watchdog reconciliation (crates/icydb/src/lib.rs:996-1012; build/actor/mod.rs:192-204). The only wake after a commit is retained journal debt (commit/guard.rs:334-336), measured only over batches with nonzero journal sequence (backlog_admission.rs:104-109). advance_metadata_schema_migration publishes via publish_accepted_schema_candidates_with_database_control (application.rs:1129-1158). For heap stores, publish_candidates_atomically assigns JournalSequence 0 (schema_publication.rs:686-692), so batch_count is 0 and no wake happens. The receipt written uses the migration submission key (application.rs:1904-1920), not the generated key that readiness checks (application.rs:2966-2996). Readiness therefore stays Recovering until the handoff runs again, and that requires the watchdog. The heap metadata path is permitted: only physical migrations require journaled stores (application.rs:1167-1182).

Recommendation

After any migration command that reaches Applied or Aborted, or that changes accepted schema, invoke the installed startup wake-up. Equivalently, have migrate_generated_schema reconcile the watchdog from durable state. Add a heap-store entity-rename migration test that asserts Ready without a second upgrade.

Verifier (confirmed): The handoff stops the watchdog on SCHEMA_MIGRATION_IN_PROGRESS (build/actor/db/store.rs:342-347). A heap-only metadata rename reaches that point through preflight_ordinary_source_application (application.rs:766-782). The migrate endpoint calls migrate_generated_schema directly (build/actor/mod.rs:192-204; crates/icydb/src/lib.rs:996-1012). with_request_execution only installs a scope (request.rs:101-104). The only call sites for the startup wakeup are in the commit guard (guard.rs:282, 318, 331, 335). The no-error wake requires retained_journal_debt, which is `proposed.batch_count() != 0` (guard.rs:287-290). Batches with JournalSequence 0 are skipped in that count (backlog_admission.rs:104-106), and heap stores always get sequence 0 (schema_publication.rs:686-690). The metadata advance publishes with a 'migration/...' submission key (application.rs:1129-1150, 1904-1922). Readiness checks only the generated key (application.rs:2977-2996), which only a rerun of apply_generated_schema writes. Metadata migrations do not require journaled stores (only the physical path calls ensure_physical_migration_stores_are_journaled, 1094-1096). Result: after Applied, the canister stays Recovering until the next upgrade, although a same-wasm upgrade is enough to fix it.
mediumconfirmedschema-application-4 · robustness · high confidence
Pending application needs an exact precomputed final head; any intervening publication leaves the job unfinishable and unabortable, holding a record slot forever
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/application.rs:2815

Failure scenario

Explicit apply_schema adds a check on entity E with 300 rows, giving Pending with candidate head H at revision R+3. Before continue is driven to completion, SQL DDL (say ADD COLUMN on entity F) or another apply_schema touching F publishes, so the head moves. continue then starts validation and promotes, making the new check durable and enforced, but finalize returns conflict. Every later continue returns conflict and abort returns store_corruption, so the receipt stays Pending forever and holds one of 64 slots. Once 64 such records accumulate, every new application, including generated deploys, fails with schema_application_conflict, which is a terminal startup code.

Evidence

At apply time the Pending receipt reserves `candidate_head` from final_candidates_for_pending_row_local_constraint, which assumes exactly two more revisions for that store and unchanged heads for all others (2729-2733, 689-692). finalize_schema_application requires `schema_application_target(db)?.accepted_head() == candidate_head` or returns conflict (2815-2817). valid_record_transition also requires Applied.accepted_head == candidate_head (application_store.rs:176-179). Nothing blocks other publications while a job is Pending: lower_existing_entity only rejects the entity that owns the activation (application_lowering.rs:1624-1629), and SQL DDL has no pending-application check. After promotion, continue takes the `accepted && pending.is_none()` path into finalize, which conflicts (386-393), and abort needs the activation, which is gone, giving store_corruption (531-543). continue/abort also reject when the database identity changed (324-327, 434-437); that identity hashes the whole store registry, so adding a store in an upgrade orphans the job. Pending records are never retired (application_store.rs:343-347).

Recommendation

Either serialize schema publication while any Pending application exists (reject other applications and DDL), or have finalize check that the recorded (store, entity, constraint) activation was promoted and then record the actual resulting head, relaxing valid_record_transition to match. Also give an operator path to retire orphaned Pending records, for example after a registry or identity change.

Verifier (confirmed): Confirmed. final_candidates_for_pending_row_local_constraint assumes exactly two more revisions for that store and unchanged heads for all others (application.rs:2729-2733, feeding 689-692). finalize_schema_application requires the whole-database head to equal candidate_head (2815-2817), and valid_record_transition requires Pending to Applied with candidate_head == accepted_head (application_store.rs:176-179). Nothing serializes other publications while an explicit Pending record exists. The only guard, lower_existing_entity, is per entity; SQL DDL has no pending-application check; and an explicit, non-generated Pending receipt does not affect Ready. start_journaled_validation and promote_row_local_activation build on current_bundle (constraint_activation_runner.rs:786-810), so any intervening publication makes the promoted head differ from candidate_head. After that, continue takes the accepted && pending.is_none() branch into finalize and gets a conflict every time (application.rs:386-393). Abort's prepare_pending_application_abort requires the activation, which is now gone, and returns store_corruption (531-543). A database-identity change, such as adding a store (write_store_authority at 3057-3068), orphans the job through the conflicts at 324-327 and 434-437. terminal_retention_candidate never retires Pending records. The check itself is enforced correctly and only the receipt and slot leak, and exhausting all 64 slots is far-fetched, so medium is right.

mediumconfirmedschema-application-7 · robustness · medium confidence
Nested-leaf expansion during lowering has no budget; a record DAG with wide reuse can trap before any size check
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/application_lowering.rs:2822

Failure scenario

A proposal defines R0 with 256 fields of type R1, R1 with 256 fields of type R2, and R2 with 256 Nat64 fields, plus an entity field of type R0. Lowering tries to build about 16.7M leaves with cloned paths and exceeds the instruction or heap limit. An explicit apply_schema call traps, so it is rolled back but the call is a DoS. If a generated model has such a shape, every startup watchdog tick traps, no failure is ever persisted (the trap rolls it back), and the database stays Recovering.

Evidence

push_nested_leaves pushes one leaf, with a cloned path Vec<String>, for every record member and recurses into each composite record member. `active` only blocks cycles on the current path, so a reused type is expanded again for every sibling (2822-2863), bounded only by depth 64. It runs for every field in initial and existing lowering (2734, 1775) before the snapshot's 512 KiB encoded-size check. The team already guards the same blowup for query projections with an up-front budget (types/query_projection.rs:24-56; composite_catalog/tests.rs:226-240: 'Never construct this expanded tree'), but not here. Proposal bounds allow 256 fields per record and 1024 types (icydb-schema/src/bounds.rs).

Recommendation

Charge a shared budget while building nested leaves, for example capped by MAX_SCHEMA_SNAPSHOT_BYTES / per-leaf cost like validate_query_projections, and reject with Unsupported when it is exceeded.

Verifier (confirmed): Confirmed. push_nested_leaves (application_lowering.rs:2822-2863) pushes a leaf with a fresh path.clone() for every member. It recurses into each composite record member, and `active` only prevents cycles on the current path, so a reused type is expanded once per sibling. The only bound is depth 64. It runs from lower_migration_nested_leaves for every field in initial lowering (2734) and existing lowering (1775). That happens before bundle construction, which is where validate_query_projections (enum_catalog/publication.rs:281) and the 512 KiB snapshot-size check run. Bounds allow 256 fields per record and 1024 types (bounds.rs). A three-level 256-wide DAG therefore yields about 16.8M leaves, each carrying a cloned Vec<String> and a kind clone, which is gigabytes of heap and certain to trap. The projection code already guards the equivalent blowup with a byte budget (types/query_projection.rs:24-56), and the composite_catalog tests warn never to build such trees, but lowering has no guard. An explicit apply traps and rolls back, a self-inflicted DoS by the operator. A generated model of this shape would trap on every watchdog tick without ever persisting a failure. Medium is appropriate.
mediumconfirmedschema-catalogs-2 · robustness · high confidence
DESCRIBE / SHOW COLUMNS expand composite types with no depth limit or cycle check, so recursive (or heavily reused) composite types trap the call
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/describe.rs:2189

Failure scenario

The schema declares `Node { label: Text, children: List<Node> }` (or the accepted Left/Right record cycle), and entity Tree has a field of type Node. Any caller running SQL `DESCRIBE Tree` or `SHOW COLUMNS Tree`, or calling try_describe_entity_by_name("Tree"), recurses without end ('composite(path=Node, ..., shape=record{children:list<composite(path=Node ...') until the wasm stack overflows and the call traps. It fails on every call for as long as the schema exists. An acyclic chain of named tuples T0=(T1,T1), ..., T20=(Nat8,Nat8) is accepted too, because tuples produce no nested leaves and query projection keeps them closed; describing it builds about 2^20 expansions and exhausts the instruction or memory limit.

Evidence

write_persisted_field_kind_summary's Composite arm (describe.rs:2189-2201) calls write_accepted_composite_shape_summary (1887-1923), which calls write_accepted_composite_element_summary (1925-1933), which calls write_persisted_field_kind_summary again for each member. There is no depth counter, visited set or output budget. SqlColumnSummary::new bounds only extras and default text, not field_type. Recursive composites are accepted authority: application_lowering.rs:5724 (mutual Left/Right record cycle) and :5284 (collection named-type cycles) lower and publish successfully. Every other walker has a guard (resolve_newtype_value_kind uses a visited set; nested_leaf_contract_matches uses an `active` set plus depth; query projection uses a byte budget). The same function renders every field and nested leaf (describe.rs:1497, 1515, 1706, 1805).

Recommendation

Render a composite reference by path only (e.g. `composite(path=Node)`), or expand each type at most once per rendering using a visited set, with a hard depth and output-size budget that returns a typed error. Add a DESCRIBE test over the recursive-record fixture.

Severity adjusted from high to medium during verification.
Verifier (confirmed): I confirmed unbounded mutual recursion. write_persisted_field_kind_summary's Composite arm (describe.rs:2189-2201) calls write_accepted_composite_shape_summary (1887-1923) -> write_accepted_composite_element_summary (1925-1933) -> write_persisted_field_kind_summary, with no depth counter, visited set or output budget. Recursive composites are accepted authority. AcceptedCompositeType::validate only checks that referenced ids exist (composite_catalog.rs:290-360, matches_kind_at_depth returns `by_id.contains_key` for Composite). The tests initial_lowering_cuts_mutual_record_leaf_expansion_at_the_resolved_back_edge (application_lowering.rs:5724) and ..._collection_named_type_cycles (5284) lower and round-trip such schemas. Every entity field goes through summarize_persisted_field_kind (describe.rs:1497, 1706), and the callers are SQL DESCRIBE, SHOW COLUMNS and SHOW CONSTRAINTS (session/sql/execute/metadata.rs:48-122). So describing any entity that reaches a recursive composite recurses until the stack or memory runs out and the call traps. I lowered the severity from high because the blast radius is limited to read-only introspection for entities that reach a cyclic type. No state changes, reads and writes are unaffected, and the precondition is a developer-authored schema, not caller input.

An adopted DB has User v1 with digest D1. A deploy without a plan adds a generated CHECK constraint (or changes an insert default) on User. The ordinary lowerer accepts it, and lineage keeps v1/D1. Later a plan migrates only Order v1 to v2. validate_unchanged_lineage sees User's digest D1' != D1 and returns MissingMigration. Adding `entity_migration(entity="User", from=1)` fails UnexplainedSchemaDifference, and bumping User without a transform is a meaningless bump. preflight_ordinary_source_application returns Ok whenever `proposal.migration().is_none()` (l.766-770), so ordinary generated applications never compare the entity version/source digest with lineage. attach_ordinary_lineage_publication (l.1524-1551) re-stamps only heads via lineage_after_planned(before, [], head), keeping the old version and digest. validate_unchanged_lineage then requires `*source_digest == proposal.entity_source_digest(source)` for every non-transitioned entity (migration_planner.rs l.509-516, else MissingMigration). The companion rule rejects any difference beyond entity renames (l.453-465). The source digest includes constraints and defaults (source_digest.rs l.17-20), and the 0.218 design says the declared version advances whenever generated-owned schema changes.

Once lineage exists (in migration and non-migration builds alike), reject ordinary generated applications whose entity source digest or declared version differs from adopted lineage without a plan, with a typed 'requires migration' error. Verifier (confirmed): preflight_ordinary_source_application returns Ok whenever `proposal.migration().is_none()` (application.rs:766-770). No other ordinary-path code compares lineage version or digest: application_lowering only handles field-ID lineage, and ensure_generated_schema_application_admitted only inspects the migration record. attach_ordinary_lineage_publication calls lineage_after_planned(before, [], head) (l.1532-1551), and that function copies each Adopted entry's old version and digest (l.1839-1870). validate_unchanged_lineage then requires digest equality for every non-transitioned entity, returning MissingMigration (migration_planner.rs:509-516). A no-transform companion transition for that entity is rejected with UnexplainedSchemaDifference (l.453-465). The digest covers 'the complete entity contract' (icydb-schema/src/source_digest.rs:17-20). The existing-head lowerer explicitly accepts insert-default changes and generated check additions (application_lowering.rs:522-531), plus the pending row-local activation path. The 0.218 design says same-version lineage 'may reconcile only when its generated-owned source meaning is already exact' (design l.411-412), so the code is the side that is wrong. Recovery requires an artificial transform, so medium is right.

Document the retry path in schema-migrations.md.

Fixing rows does not change the accepted head, so the same successor yields an identical digest and stays Aborted indefinitely. Budget exhaustion maps to SchemaDdlAdmission (error/mod.rs:2991-2993), which is terminal for SchemaReconciliation (startup/mod.rs:130-131), so a generated removal in a large store fails terminally. I lowered severity to medium: every failure is fail-closed on an admin/schema path, with no wrong results and no caller-controlled DoS. Also, the target entity's own complete-domain work is already capped at 65,536 source rows by design. The real defect is that foreign entries in the same store count against the budget, which makes index DDL and generated removals unavailable for every entity once the store holds roughly 262k index entries.

Historical rows with length 50 are valid under the authoritative accepted rule. CompiledAcceptedTargetedRules::compile chains accepted and activating sources (targeted.rs:228-252), so one root holds two rules with the same id. The integrity lane builds TargetedRule{id} entries from accepted constraints (compile.rs:656-664) and evaluates them via `self.targeted_rules.evaluate_constraint(id, values_by_slot)` (compile.rs:461-468). That filters with `root.rules[*ordinal].id != constraint_id` (targeted.rs:440-446), which keeps both the accepted and the candidate rule. InspectionPlan uses CompiledAcceptedRowConstraints::compile (inspection_plan.rs:170), which includes activations. Record in the compiled rule whether it is accepted or activating, and have evaluate_constraint (the integrity path) evaluate only accepted rules. Alternatively, compile the integrity program from accepted constraints only. Add a test with a pending same-ID replacement.

CompiledAcceptedTargetedRules::compile chains accepted and activating sources (targeted.rs:228-252), and compile_sources pushes both into the same root with the same id (282-311). The integrity lane creates TargetedRule{id} entries only from accepted constraints (compile.rs:656-664). It evaluates them via targeted_rules.evaluate_constraint(id) (compile.rs:461-468), which filters with `root.rules[*ordinal].id != constraint_id` (targeted.rs:440-446), so both the accepted rule and the candidate rule are evaluated. A candidate violation is then reported under the shared id. InspectionPlan compiles through CompiledAcceptedRowConstraints::compile (inspection_plan.rs:170), which includes activations. integrity/row.rs:594-620 labels the finding IntegrityFindingClass::Corruption. This contradicts the doc comment at compile.rs:421-425 and the inventory statement that the accepted operation 'stays authoritative until promotion'. The existing test integrity_check_program_excludes_pending_activation_semantics (check/tests.rs:1472) covers only a new-identity check activation, not a same-id replacement. Verify phase restarts on any write to any entity in the store, so activations can starve while unique activations block inserts
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/constraint_activation_runner.rs:1238

Failure scenario

Entity A (10k rows) shares a store with entity B, which gets a write every few seconds. CREATE UNIQUE INDEX on A followed by repeated VALIDATE CONSTRAINT: every Verify attempt (40 pages) sees B's writes bump the store revision and restarts to Forward, so the index never promotes. Meanwhile every INSERT into A fails with constraint_activation_write_blocked until the operator gives up with DROP INDEX. The same starvation hits NOT NULL, CHECK, and generated activations.

Evidence

current_store_revision reads `JournalTailStore::data_mutation_revision` (lines 1234-1239). The journal bumps it on every batch with any affected entity tag (journal/store.rs:805-818). Verify checks it before and after each page, and any mismatch restarts the whole job at Forward with checkpoint None (restart_validation_if_revision_changed, lines 1278-1290; used at 630-635, 716-721, 1041). Forward exhaustion captures the revision in one message and Verify can only run in a later one, so the window always spans messages. An entity-scoped revision already exists (journal/store.rs:649 entity_mutation_revision). While a unique activation is live, all Insert/Replace writes to the entity are blocked (check/compile.rs:476-500).

Recommendation

Fence Verify on the entity-level mutation revision for the activation's entity. For row-local kinds, where new writes are already gated, consider allowing the fence to tolerate writes to other entities. Document the liveness requirement in SQL_SUBSET.md.

Verifier (confirmed): current_store_revision reads JournalTailStore::data_mutation_revision (runner:1234-1239). The journal bumps it for any batch with row-mutation entity tags from any entity (journal/store.rs:774, 805-818). A per-entity revision exists (journal/store.rs:649). Forward captures the revision only when it exhausts (runner:996-1011). Each resume call runs a single phase and page, so Verify always spans later messages. Verify checks the revision before each page (runner:630-635, 716-721) and again at the end (1041). Any mismatch restarts to Forward with no checkpoint (1278-1290, constraint_validation.rs:404-417). With 256 rows per page (runner:54), 10k rows means about 40 sequential Verify calls with zero writes anywhere in the store. unique_activation_write_blocker blocks every Insert and Replace for the entity while the activation is live (compile.rs:476-500). Partly mitigating: the design is intentionally conservative. ATOMICITY.md:222 requires a 'stable participating revision', and DURABILITY.md:340-356 documents store-wide invalidation, including other entities, for application jobs. So this is a liveness and usability problem rather than a correctness bug, and DROP INDEX always recovers. Given that inserts stay blocked while the activation starves in busy multi-entity stores, medium stands.

crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/constraint_validation.rs:570

`ALTER TABLE t ADD CONSTRAINT wide CHECK (c1 IS NOT NULL AND ... AND c33 IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID` on a journaled entity with one violating row. Every `VALIDATE CONSTRAINT wide` re-scans the first page and fails with an InternalError Corruption before publishing. Findings are never returned and validation can never make progress; only DROP CONSTRAINT recovers. activation_dependency_fields returns every distinct dependency of the check expression (constraint_activation_runner.rs:1220-1231), and each finding carries that full list (lines 1102-1107). Receipt validation rejects `finding.field_ids.len() > MAX_CONSTRAINT_VALIDATION_FINDING_FIELDS` (32, lines 44 and 570). record_forward_page ends with `self.validate(None)` (line 373), which returns store_corruption. Check admission only bounds nodes (256), children (64), and depth (32) (check/mod.rs:45-56), so an AND of 33 comparisons over 33 fields is admissible.

Make the bounds consistent. Either cap distinct field dependencies at bind/acceptance time to MAX_CONSTRAINT_VALIDATION_FINDING_FIELDS, or store a bounded or empty field list in findings for wide checks, or raise the receipt bound to match the expression bounds (the job byte ceiling still holds).

Nothing caps the dependency count: check admission bounds only depth 32, nodes 256, children 64, literal bytes and canonical bytes (check/mod.rs:45-56). An AND of 33 IS NOT NULL terms is therefore admissible. Each finding carries the full list (runner:1102-1107), and ConstraintValidationFinding::new does not truncate it (constraint_validation.rs:113-124). record_forward_page ends with self.validate(None) (constraint_validation.rs:373). receipt_is_invalid rejects field_ids.len() > MAX_CONSTRAINT_VALIDATION_FINDING_FIELDS = 32 (lines 44, 570), which returns store_corruption. That happens inside record_forward, before any publication (runner:705-710), so the job never advances and every VALIDATE retry hits the same error. Only DROP CONSTRAINT recovers. For generated checks, the unpublished first-page pass reports a violation there as an ordinary constraint violation (runner:385-406). mediumconfirmedschema-store-3 · durability · medium confidence
SchemaStore::init_journaled uses StableBTreeMap::init, which silently reinitializes a non-empty schema allocation with a bad header
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/store.rs:928

Failure scenario

The first bytes of a journaled store's schema allocation are corrupted, for example by a write through a mis-mapped memory or a bad restore. On the next post_upgrade the thread-local initializer calls init_journaled, sees a magic mismatch, and irreversibly overwrites the header with an empty map. Accepted roots, bundles, identity-state records and validation jobs vanish silently, with no typed error at the boundary. Later stages either fail with a confusing downstream corruption error (e.g. the fold needs a canonical root) or treat the store as having no accepted authority, which invites regenerating authority from the generated model. That contradicts PERSISTED_FORMAT_POLICY's fail-closed rule: no silent wrong logical state and no reconstruction from generated models.

Evidence

`canonical: StableBTreeMap::init(memory)`. In ic-stable-structures 0.7.2, BTreeMap::init does: `if dst != MAGIC { // No BTreeMap found. Create a new instance. BTreeMap::new(memory) }`, which writes a fresh empty header over the existing allocation. control_store.rs:90-99 deliberately guards the same upstream behaviour ('Reject malformed framing before the upstream infallible tree loader'), but the per-store schema allocation (generated via icydb-model journaled_store_cell_tokens, called from a const thread_local initializer) has no such check.

Recommendation

Before init, check `memory.size() > 0` and the BTR magic, and if the memory is non-empty but not a BTreeMap, fail closed. Since the constructor is infallible and called from a const thread_local, record a poisoned state and have registration or startup observation report store_corruption. Alternatively, use `load` after an explicit framing check, mirroring SchemaControlMap::open_existing. The same pattern probably affects the Data/Index/Journal stores and should be reviewed there.

Verifier (confirmed): The code is as described. store.rs:928 calls `StableBTreeMap::init(memory)`. In ic-stable-structures 0.7.2 (btreemap.rs:274-290), init creates a new map when the 3-byte magic doesn't match, and BTreeMap::new calls save_header() plus Allocator::new (btreemap.rs:326-365), overwriting the tree header and allocator header. The generated cell (icydb-model/src/build/actor/db/store.rs:466-489) is a lazy thread_local, not const as the finding says, but that doesn't change the outcome, and it does no framing check. The other guards don't catch this. database_format::admit_or_initialize_database_format (database_format/mod.rs:229-252) checks store allocations only for virginity when the boot record is missing, never their framing when it is present. register_journaled_store (registry.rs:83-106) checks shape only. The project guards exactly this upstream behaviour in control_store.rs:90-99 ('Reject malformed framing before the upstream infallible tree loader') but not here. That is inconsistent with PERSISTED_FORMAT_POLICY.md:136-151 (no silently wrong logical state). One mitigation: preflight_initial_application (application.rs:2257-2273) refuses to re-apply generated authority over a populated data/index store. That limits the 'regenerate from model' consequence, but accepted roots, identity state and validation jobs are still destroyed silently. The trigger needs the magic bytes to be corrupted already, and raw restore is explicitly unsupported (PERSISTED_FORMAT_POLICY.md:115-128), so it is unlikely. That makes it a missing validation / latent hazard: medium.
Also reported as: xc-robustness-4
mediumconfirmedschema-store-4 · performance · high confidence
Heap-store identity allocation fully decodes, re-verifies and rewrites the whole live checkpoint (bundle up to 16 MiB plus identity inventory) on every write
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/live_schema_checkpoint.rs:376

Failure scenario

A heap store with a moderately large accepted bundle (hundreds of entities, a few hundred KB of snapshots) and one entity with an auto-increment Identity field: every insert performs roughly four bundle decode/verify/encode passes and one full stable rewrite, costing hundreds of millions of instructions per insert. Batch inserts or high write rates hit instruction limits and cycle costs. As the schema grows, single-row inserts approach the per-message limit.

Evidence

commit_window.rs:962-996 calls preflight_live_identity_range_checkpoint and apply_live_identity_range_checkpoint for every LiveRebuiltMetadata identity range. Each one runs LiveSchemaCheckpointStore::open, whose from_map (152-161) decodes the migration record (up to 2 MiB) and counts checkpoint keys. It then runs load, whose decode_checkpoint does a CRC over the whole record, CandidateSchemaRevision::from_encoded (full bundle decode, validate_decoded_semantics, semantic fingerprint that re-encodes every entity snapshot), and `encode_checkpoint(store_path, &checkpoint)? != bytes` (a full re-encode) (514-520). apply_identity_range (376-400) then encodes again and writes the full record back: store path + encoded bundle + all identity states. MAX_LIVE_SCHEMA_CHECKPOINT_BYTES allows a 16 MiB bundle plus 65,536 x 104-byte identity records.

Recommendation

Store the heap-store identity high-water records separately from the immutable candidate bundle, e.g. one control record per owner or a small identity-only record. Then a range advance reads and writes only the affected 104-byte state and verifies the bundle only when the schema changes. Also avoid re-verifying the bundle on the preflight/apply hot path, for instance by trusting the root/bundle hash binding once per message.

Verifier (confirmed): The cost is real, but a few details in the finding are overstated. For every LiveRebuiltMetadata identity range, commit_window.rs:962-996 calls preflight_live_identity_range_checkpoint and then apply_live_identity_range_checkpoint. Each call opens LiveSchemaCheckpointStore (live_schema_checkpoint.rs:141-161): a migration-record decode if one exists, map.len plus two gets. Each call then load()s: a full stable read of the record, then decode_checkpoint (470-526), which does a CRC32C over the body, then CandidateSchemaRevision::from_encoded (publication.rs:761-774 -> 986-998). That is SHA-256 over the whole bundle, a full bundle decode, and semantic_fingerprint, which re-encodes the catalogs and every entity snapshot (publication.rs:362-386). It then runs encode_checkpoint and compares the bytes. apply_identity_range (376-400) encodes again and rewrites the whole record: store path, bundle, root and every identity state. Corrections: encode_checkpoint copies `candidate.encoded_bundle()` bytes plus a CRC; it does not re-encode the bundle. So a commit costs two full bundle verify passes plus several copy/CRC passes and one full stable rewrite, not four decode passes. The cost is also per commit, not per row: a batch holds one contiguous range per Identity owner (IDENTITY_CONTRACT.md:190-194), so 'batch inserts hit limits' is overstated. Even so, every committed write that allocates an identity value on a heap store scales with the size of the accepted bundle (up to 16 MiB). With a large schema that is a big per-write instruction and cycle cost, and with multi-MB bundles it could approach the message limit. It is a performance/latent hazard with no correctness defect: medium.
mediumconfirmedsession-sql-2 · robustness · medium confidence
SQL compiled-command cache is bounded by entry count only and keeps full SQL text twice plus literal payloads, so heap can be exhausted
crates/icydb-core/src/db/session/sql/cache.rs:153

Failure scenario

An app stores user uploads with `execute_trusted_sql_mutation("INSERT INTO Asset (id, data) VALUES (..., X'<~1 MiB hex>')")`. Each distinct statement keeps about 2 MiB of key text, another 2 MiB FIFO copy, and about 1 MiB of decoded blob. After roughly 600 uploads the heap passes the default 3 GiB wasm memory limit; 1024 entries would need about 5 GiB, more than wasm32 can address. From then on, any update message that allocates traps. Rollback restores the already-full heap, so the canister stays unusable until an upgrade. Smaller literals still pin hundreds of MiB, and every INSERT evicts useful cached SELECT compilations.

Evidence

`SqlCompiledCommandCache::new(SQL_COMPILED_COMMAND_CACHE_MAX_ENTRIES)` (1024) → `BoundedCache::new` → `new_weighted(max_entries, usize::MAX)` (bounded_cache.rs:106). Entries go in with weight 0: `cache.insert(cache_key, compiled.clone())` (compile_cache.rs:132). The key holds `sql: String` (cache.rs:57), and `insert_weighted` clones the whole key into the FIFO queue (`insertion_order.push_back(key.clone())`, bounded_cache.rs:148). `CompiledSqlCommand::Insert` holds the `SqlInsertStatement` by value, including decoded `Value::Blob` literals (compiled/command.rs:76-78). The trusted mutation surface always goes through this cache (`compile_sql_mutation_with_execution_context` passes empty bindings). MAX_SQL_INPUT_BYTES is 2 MiB + 4 KiB, and a single blob literal can be 1 MiB. By comparison, the shared query-plan cache is weight-bounded at 4 MiB. Compiled SELECT commands also keep strong `Rc`s to prepared plans (`set_cached_select_plan`), which escapes that 4 MiB accounting.

Recommendation

Bound the cache by retained bytes, like the shared query-plan cache: charge the key text, the FIFO copy, and the compiled payload. Alternatively, skip caching statements whose literal payload exceeds a small threshold (and never cache mutation-surface INSERT/UPDATE). Keep the FIFO queue from duplicating the raw SQL text, for example by storing a hash or an Rc<str>.

Severity adjusted from high to medium during verification.
Verifier (confirmed): The mechanism is accurate. SqlCompiledCommandCache::new(1024) calls new_weighted(max, usize::MAX) (session/sql/cache.rs:150-152, bounded_cache.rs:105-107), and compile_cache.rs:131-133 inserts with weight 0. The key owns sql: String (cache.rs:57), and insert_weighted clones the whole key into the FIFO queue (bounded_cache.rs:148), so the SQL text is kept twice. CompiledSqlInsertCommand holds SqlInsertStatement by value (compiled/command.rs:76-78). The trusted mutation path always passes empty bindings and therefore always uses the cache (compile_cache.rs:65-83, session/sql/mod.rs:95-112). Limits allow large entries: MAX_SQL_INPUT_BYTES is about 2 MiB (sql_shared/mod.rs:21), blob literals can be 1 MiB (lexer/token_body.rs:9), and rows can be 4 MiB (codec/mod.rs:21). Compiled SELECTs also keep strong Rc prepared plans outside the plan cache's weight accounting (command.rs:142-155). I lowered the severity because exhausting the heap needs hundreds of distinct statements, each close to 2 MiB, pushed through the trusted surface inside update messages. The public update endpoints do not use this cache (update.rs:393-423 go through the policy path), and cache writes made during query calls are discarded. An upgrade clears the heap, so the canister is not permanently wedged. This is a real missing byte bound, i.e. medium, and only a DoS if the app builds large literal SQL from caller data.
mediumconfirmedsession-sql-3 · durability · medium confidence
Resumable job gets permanently stuck in Active when one matching row deterministically fails write admission (e.g. a row-local CHECK)
crates/icydb-core/src/db/session/sql/resumable_update.rs:1397

Failure scenario

Constraint `CHECK (discount <= price)` exists. Start a job with `UPDATE Product SET discount = 50 WHERE category = 'sale'`. Forward pages 1-3 commit. The scan then reaches a sale row with price = 40. `resumable_row_needs_patch` selects it, the writer rejects the after-image, and advance returns TargetMutationFailed(Other) at the same sequence and checkpoint. Every retry repeats the same result. The job is partially applied, can never become terminal, cannot be acknowledged or cancelled, and permanently holds one of the shared progress-store slots. The error carries no key, so the operator cannot easily find the offending row.

Evidence

`classify_mutation_job_target_execution_failure` (1416-1431) makes only `ExecutionBudgetExceeded` a terminal restart. Every other writer error becomes `MutationJobTargetExecutionFailure::Target`, which `persist_classified_mutation_job_execution_failure` returns as `Err(TargetMutationFailed(reason))` without persisting anything (1388-1401). Eligibility (`prove_resumable_update_fixed_eligibility`, 1718-1765) rejects only relation, unique and global-validation fields; row-local CHECK constraints over assigned fields are still admitted. mutation_job.rs: `acknowledge_mutation_job` rejects Active jobs, and `cancel_unadvanced_mutation_job` works only before the first page. The 0.233 design lists 'No abandon_mutation_job for partially applied jobs'.

Recommendation

Persist deterministic per-row admission failures as a typed terminal `RestartRequired` (e.g. TargetRowRejected) so the job can be acknowledged and its slot reclaimed. Alternatively, reject at start any patch whose assigned fields appear in an accepted row CHECK, or add an explicit abandon surface for advanced jobs.

Verifier (confirmed): classify_mutation_job_target_execution_failure (resumable_update.rs:1416-1431) makes only ExecutionBudgetExceeded a terminal restart. Every other writer error, including a row CHECK violation, becomes Err(TargetMutationFailed(Other)) with nothing persisted (1388-1401). Every retry repeats it at the same sequence and checkpoint. Eligibility (1718-1765) rejects only relation, unique and global-validation fields. AcceptedFixedUpdatePatch::from_update_intent validates only the authored field values (data/persisted_row/patch.rs:152-214), not cross-field row CHECKs such as discount <= price. Row CHECK constraints exist, including NOT VALID ones (SQL_SUBSET.md:409-410). Active jobs cannot be acknowledged, and cancel works only before the first page (session/mutation_job.rs:118-160). The 0.233 design names this class of problem ('a deterministic pre-commit failure can retain one of the 64 shared progress slots indefinitely', 0.233-design.md:104-107) but fixed only the timestamp and staging cases, and explicitly lists 'No abandon_mutation_job' as a non-goal. 'Permanently' overstates it, though. An operator can unblock the job by fixing the offending row, or by any accepted-schema change such as dropping the constraint, which gives an AcceptedSchemaChanged terminal restart in prepare_mutation_job_authority (resumable_update.rs:497-510). The job can then be acknowledged. Medium is appropriate.

crates/icydb-core/src/db/data/persisted_row/patch.rs:866

That function first runs resolve_insert_structural_patch_with_accepted_contract(..., None) (patch.rs:815-824), which calls accepted_insert_generated_value for every omitted generated slot (Ulid::generate() / the operation timestamp). The merge loop then takes baseline values only for `Some(FieldWriteManagement::CreatedAt | UpdatedAt)` and uses `None => candidate.required_cached_value(slot)?` (866) for everything else, generated fields included. preserve_dynamic_replacement_identity (write.rs:521-555) preserves primary-key slots only. Verifier (confirmed): Traced end to end. write.rs:1418-1429 routes (Replace, Some(before)) to resolve_existing_replace_structural_patch_with_accepted_contract. That function first builds a full insert candidate with identity_allocation=None (patch.rs:815-824), so any omitted non-PK generated slot goes through accepted_insert_generated_value (patch.rs:1055-1056: `Ulid::generate()` / operation timestamp). The update path, by contrast, preserves such fields from the baseline (patch.rs:722-731). The logical-change comparison at patch.rs:876-886 then always sees the regenerated value as a change, so UpdatedAt advances on an otherwise identical replace. Caveats: no contract explicitly defines how replace treats non-PK insert-generated fields. The function's doc comment ("Ordinary omitted fields use current insert policy") is consistent with regeneration, so this may be an unexamined gap rather than a deliberate choice. mediumverifiedsql-parser-1 · robustness · high confidence
ORDER BY arithmetic sub-parser recurses on parentheses with no depth guard (stack overflow instead of ExpressionDepthLimit)
crates/icydb-core/src/db/sql/parser/projection/arithmetic.rs:56

Failure scenario

`SELECT id FROM T ORDER BY id + ` followed by ~16,000 '(' then `1` then ~16,000 ')' is about 32,007 tokens (under MAX_SQL_TOKENS) and ~32 KB (under MAX_SQL_INPUT_BYTES). The parser recurses ~16k levels × 2 frames, each holding Result<SqlExpr,_> temporaries. That is well beyond the default 1 MiB wasm32 shadow stack, so the message traps instead of returning the documented typed ExpressionDepthLimit. On native hosts (tests, off-chain tooling) a stack overflow aborts the whole process. It is reachable through `UPDATE ... ORDER BY` / `DELETE ... ORDER BY` / `EXPLAIN` on any SQL surface; generated endpoints are controller-gated by default, but guarded icydb_query and application-forwarded execute_trusted_sql_* expose it to end users.

parse_projection_arithmetic_leaf: `if self.peek_lparen() { self.expect_lparen()?; let expr = self.parse_projection_arithmetic_expr(0)?; ... }` and parse_projection_arithmetic_expr (line 8-15) calls parse_projection_arithmetic_leaf again. Neither function (nor parse_projection_arithmetic_expr_tail / parse_projection_arithmetic_from_left) calls enter_sql_expr_depth, unlike parse_sql_expr/parse_sql_expr_prefix. Entry: clauses.rs:53-57 (`ORDER BY field <+|-|*|/>`) and clauses.rs:43-48 (aggregate followed by an operator), reached from parse_order_limit_offset_clauses for SELECT, DELETE, UPDATE and EXPLAIN. The post-parse validate_sql_statement_input cannot help: parentheses add no AST nodes, and the overflow happens during parsing. No test covers parenthesised ORDER BY arithmetic.

Recommendation

Wrap parse_projection_arithmetic_expr (or the parenthesis branch of the leaf) in enter_sql_expr_depth/leave_sql_expr_depth, and cap its left-associative loop the same way as binary_chain_depth. Better still, route ORDER BY arithmetic through the guarded parse_sql_expr(Projection) so only one guarded grammar remains. Add a regression test with ~200 nested parentheses in an ORDER BY operand.

Severity adjusted from high to medium during verification.
Verifier (confirmed): I re-traced this path and it holds. In arithmetic.rs:8-15 and :56-61, parse_projection_arithmetic_expr and parse_projection_arithmetic_leaf call each other on every '('. Neither calls enter_sql_expr_depth, and that guard is only used in projection/mod.rs:202 and :251. The path is reachable from clauses.rs:43-48 and :53-57 through parse_order_terms, which statement/mod.rs:87 calls for SELECT (select.rs:45), UPDATE (update.rs:27) and DELETE (delete.rs:23). The token cap is MAX_SQL_TOKENS=32,768 and the byte cap is about 2 MiB (sql_shared/mod.rs:21-22), so ~32k '(' tokens are admitted. Closing parens are not needed, because the recursion happens on the way down, before expect_rparen can fail. validate_sql_statement_input only runs after parse_sql returns (parser/mod.rs:77), so it cannot help. On wasm32 (1 MiB stack, laid out stack-first) this traps. On native hosts it aborts the process. The trap only rolls back the attacker's own message and the default endpoints are controller-gated, but the rubric explicitly rates a trap on caller-controlled input as high.
Skeptic · reachability (upheld, medium): The claim holds. The path is real and I found no guard that stops it. The ORDER BY arithmetic sub-parser (arithmetic.rs:8-86) never calls enter_sql_expr_depth. By contrast, parse_sql_expr (projection/mod.rs:202) and parse_sql_expr_prefix (projection/mod.rs:251) do call it, and parse_sql_expr also has a binary-chain check (projection/mod.rs:232). The lexer (sql_shared/lexer/scan.rs:14-30) caps only the token count at 32,768, with no parenthesis-depth check. The input byte cap is 2 MiB + 4 KiB. Parentheses add no AST nodes, so the post-parse validate_sql_statement_input (parser/mod.rs:77, sql/input.rs:203) runs too late and cannot see the nesting. The workspace sets no custom wasm stack size (searched for stack-size/zstack: nothing outside tests), so the default 1 MiB wasm32 shadow stack applies. Value has large variants such as Account and U256, so each Result<SqlExpr, _> sret slot is roughly 64-80 bytes. With at least two such slots per nesting level, about 16k levels needs more than 2 MiB, so a trap is effectively certain. I lower the severity from high to medium for four reasons: (1) No lasting harm. A trap only rolls back the attacker's own message; icydb_query is even a query call. It cannot wedge the canister or corrupt state, and it does not affect other callers. (2) Default gating. Every generated SQL endpoint is controller-gated (require_sql_controller at lib.rs:720/740/779/799). The only non-controller routes are icydb_query when the app installs a permissive ReadAuthorizationGuard (lib.rs:669-672), or app code that forwards input into execute_trusted_sql_*. The docs say the trusted helpers are not public-safe (db/session/sql.rs:33-37). (3) Documented gap. The contracts say parser stack bounds are not yet guaranteed: RESOURCE_MODEL.md:175-177 lists "parser/normalizer scratch" stack bounds as "separately qualified work", and READ_ADMISSION.md:45-47 says the input limits are "not a complete bound on ... SQL parsing". So this is a missing bound and an inconsistency with the typed ExpressionDepthLimit guard used everywhere else in the parser, not a violation of a normative contract. (4) Native hosts. The CLI parses the user's own input locally (icydb-cli/src/shell/route.rs:16), so a crash there is self-inflicted. A related gap follows from the same code (not separately traced to failure). parse_projection_arithmetic_expr_tail (arithmetic.rs:22-35) has no binary-chain limit, so `ORDER BY id + 1 + 1 + ...` builds a left-deep chain about 16k deep without recursing. Validation rejects it at depth 129, but dropping that tree afterwards is recursive and could also overflow.
mediumconfirmedsql-parser-2 · correctness · high confidence
Scope normalization rewrites a record path whose inner segment matches the entity or alias name to a top-level field (wrong column in SELECT/UPDATE/DELETE)
crates/icydb-core/src/db/sql/identifier.rs:67

Failure scenario

Entity `Account` has a record field `owner` containing sub-record `account` with field `id`, plus its own primary key `id`. `DELETE FROM Account WHERE owner.account.id = 5`: the WHERE identifier `owner.account.id` goes through normalize_identifier → fallback qualifier `owner.account`, whose tail `account` matches `Account` → rewritten to `id`. The statement deletes the row whose primary key is 5, not rows whose owner.account.id is 5. The same happens for projection FieldPath (`SELECT owner.account.id` returns the PK) and for GROUP BY/RETURNING through normalize_identifier. Short aliases (`FROM Shape s`) collide with record segments named `s` in the same way.

Evidence

identifiers_tail_match (identifier.rs:67-78) accepts any qualifier whose LAST segment equals the entity/alias case-insensitively. normalize_identifier_to_scope's fallback (identifier.rs:33-45) splits on the last '.' and removes everything up to it when the qualifier's tail matches. lowering/normalize.rs:495-516 (normalize_field_path_to_scope) tries the longest prefix first and truncates the path at any inner segment that tail-matches a scope candidate (`qualifier_tail = &segments[split_at - 2]`). Nothing checks that the removed prefix starts at the root, or that the extra leading segments are a real schema qualifier.

Recommendation

Only strip a qualifier that is a root-anchored prefix exactly equal to a scope candidate: the alias, the authored entity name, or the exact schema-qualified name used in FROM. Stop treating an arbitrary `X.<entity>` in the middle of a path as a schema qualifier. If a path is ambiguous (the root names both a scope and a record field), reject it rather than silently picking the qualifier reading. Add tests for record segments named like the entity and like the alias.

Verifier (confirmed): I reproduced this from the code. SqlExpr::from_field_identifier (model.rs:557-572) turns `owner.account.id` into FieldPath{root:owner, segments:[account,id]}. normalize_field_path_to_scope (lowering/normalize.rs:486-521) first tries split_at=2 with qualifier_tail=segments[0]="account". identifiers_tail_match("Account","account") (identifier.rs:67-78) returns true, so the result is Field("id"). The WHERE surface produces SqlExpr::Field("owner.account.id") instead. That goes through normalize_identifier -> normalize_identifier_to_scope, whose fallback (identifier.rs:33-45) splits on the last '.', matches the tail of the qualifier `owner.account`, and also returns `id`. Scope candidates are the entity, the expected entity, the alias and their last segments (normalize.rs:157-180). Nothing checks that the stripped prefix is root-anchored. The test at identifier.rs:93 (`other.Users.name` -> `name`) shows that ignoring the schema segment is deliberate. Still, NESTED_STORAGE admits dotted record paths in WHERE, so an admitted nested path is silently re-targeted to a top-level column. For DELETE or UPDATE that means wrong rows get written. It needs a record member named like the entity or alias, so it is an edge condition, and medium fits. PostgreSQL would fall back to the composite reading here, so this behaviour is non-standard.
mediumconfirmedsql-parser-3 · correctness · high confidence
Numbers in scientific or hex notation are silently split into a number plus an implicit projection alias
crates/icydb-core/src/db/sql_shared/lexer/token_body.rs:76

Failure scenario

`SELECT price * 1e3 FROM Product` parses as `SELECT price * 1 AS e3` and returns the price unchanged under the label `e3`. Likewise `SELECT flags + 0x1F FROM T` gives `flags + 0 AS x1F`, and `SELECT n * 1.5e2 FROM T` gives `n * 1.5 AS e2`. The same inputs are rejected in WHERE, ORDER BY, VALUES and function arguments, so only projections silently compute the wrong value.

Evidence

lex_number (token_body.rs:76-94) consumes only `[0-9]+(\.[0-9]+)?` and stops before `e`, `E`, `x` or `_`; the rest lexes as a new Identifier token. In projection, parse_projection_alias_if_present (projection/mod.rs:167-177) treats any following Identifier as a bare alias. Decimal::from_str explicitly rejects exponent notation ('intentionally unsupported'), so the design intends to fail closed, but the lexer/alias interaction bypasses that.

Recommendation

In lex_number, reject a digit run immediately followed by an identifier-continue byte (`[A-Za-z_]`) with InvalidNumericLiteral, as PostgreSQL 15+ does ('trailing junk after numeric literal'). Alternatively, lex exponent/hex forms and reject them explicitly. Add parser tests for `1e3`, `0x1F` and `1_000` in projection position.

Verifier (confirmed): lex_number (token_body.rs:76-94) consumes only digits with an optional .digits part. For `1e3` the next byte is 'e', which is an identifier start, so scan.rs:54 lexes Identifier("e3"). For `0x1F`, scan.rs:45 only treats x as a blob prefix when followed by a quote, so `x1F` becomes an identifier. In a projection, parse_sql_expr_at_current_depth (projection/mod.rs:209-245) stops at the Identifier because it is not a binary op, and the Projection surface has no postfix handling. parse_projection_alias_if_present (:167-177) then takes the identifier as a bare alias. The result is `price * 1 AS e3`. In WHERE, SET, VALUES and ORDER BY the stray identifier produces a parse error, so only projections silently compute a wrong value. A form like `amount * 1e8` is plausible in the IC domain (e8s). Adding an explicit `AS x` after it makes the query fail instead, so the silent case is the bare form only. Medium is appropriate.
