DDL accepts dotted multi-segment column names in ADD COLUMN / RENAME COLUMN, persisting top-level fields that SQL cannot address consistently
crates/icydb-core/src/db/sql/parser/statement/ddl.rs:376

Failure scenario

`ALTER TABLE Player ADD COLUMN profile.rank int64 EXPECT SCHEMA VERSION 3 SET SCHEMA VERSION 4` publishes a top-level DDL field literally named `profile.rank`. After that: `SELECT profile.rank` / `WHERE profile.rank = 1` lower to the nested path (root `profile`, segment `rank`), which either errors or, if a record field `profile` exists, silently reads the nested field. `INSERT INTO Player (profile.rank) ...` (columns used verbatim, session/sql/execute/write/insert.rs:152) writes the dotted top-level field. CREATE INDEX on it fails, and dependency checks such as sql_predicate_references_field_root misattribute it to `profile`. The persisted schema ends up with a column that reads and writes resolve differently.

Evidence

parse_alter_table_add_column_statement uses `let column_name = self.expect_identifier()?;` (ddl.rs:376), and RENAME uses expect_identifier for both names (ddl.rs:519, 525). SqlTokenCursor::expect_identifier joins `a.b.c` into one dotted string. Neither bind_alter_table_add_column_statement / bind_alter_table_rename_column_statement (ddl/field.rs) nor the schema resolvers (mutation/field_allocation.rs:22-36, mutation/field.rs:440-469) nor validate_schema_snapshot_acceptance (schema/integrity.rs) validates field-name shape; they only check exact-duplicate names. Constraint names (validate_constraint_name) likewise allow '.'.

Parse DDL column, rename-target and index/constraint names with a single-segment identifier helper (reject when a Dot follows), and make schema-side DDL candidate resolution reject names containing '.' (ideally the same identifier charset the SQL lexer accepts), so the catalog enforces this regardless of frontend.

Verifier (confirmed): ddl.rs:376, :519 and :525 use expect_identifier, and cursor.rs:141-153 joins dotted segments into one string. bind_alter_table_add_column_statement (ddl/field.rs:200-248) and bind_alter_table_rename_column_statement (:419-460) pass the name straight to resolve_sql_ddl_field_addition_name_candidate (field_allocation.rs:22-36) and resolve_sql_ddl_field_rename_candidate (mutation/field.rs:440-469). Those only reject exact duplicates. validate_schema_snapshot_acceptance (integrity.rs:79-131) has no check on name shape. On the read side, the WHERE Field("profile.rank") is split into a FieldPath by normalize_field_identifier_expr_to_scope (normalize.rs:470-481), and CREATE INDEX splits on '.' (ddl/index.rs:386). INSERT column lists are used verbatim (insert.rs:147-152). So reads and writes address the field differently. This is mitigated because DDL is admin- or controller-only and the mistake can be undone with an exact-match RENAME COLUMN or DROP COLUMN. It remains a real catalog-level validation gap, so I keep medium.

Numeric-widening compare/eq sends floats (and Nat128 values ≥ 2^127) through a lossy i128 Decimal; out-of-range values compare as None and rows silently drop out of WHERE filters
crates/icydb-core/src/value/ops/numeric.rs:119

Failure scenario

Take entity M with a Float64 field `v` holding rows v=1e-30, v=0.25 and v=3e40. `SELECT * FROM M WHERE v < 0.5` returns only the 0.25 row; the 1e-30 row is silently missing. `WHERE v > 1` misses the 3e40 row. With two Float64 fields a=b=1e-30, the row matches neither `a = b` nor `a <> b`. Two Nat128 fields holding values ≥ 2^127 never satisfy `a < b` or `a >= b`. In compiled expressions (evaluate.rs:581-606), `f < 0.5` or `f * 2` over such values returns invalid_binary_operands, so the whole query errors. The existing tests only cover values inside the decimal range.

Evidence

compare_decimal_order and to_decimal (numeric.rs:48-63,119-127) require `to_decimal(x)?` on both sides. Float64 → Decimal::from_f64_lossy → from_float_text (icydb-schema decimal/text.rs:19-27) formats into a 69-byte buffer and parses with scale ≤ 28 and an i128 mantissa. It returns None for |x| ≥ ~1.7e38 (buffer or mantissa overflow) and for values needing more than 28 fractional digits (e.g. 1e-30, 6.62607015e-34, 1.2345678901234567e-13). Decimal::from_u128 returns None above i128::MAX. db/numeric::compare_numeric_order/compare_numeric_eq use the same conversion. The SQL compile path chooses NumericWiden for any Float/Decimal/numeric literal with an ordering op (db/query/plan/expr/predicate/compile.rs:1010-1017), and for every field-to-field ordering compare and numeric field-to-field equality (compile.rs:1022-1031, normalize.rs:273-297). The runtime direct compare returns None for NumericWiden, so evaluation falls to eval_compare_values → compare_order(...).is_some_and(..) = false. Value::cmp_numeric's F64 fallback returns None for mixed (F64, Decimal) representations, so Float64(1e300) vs Float64(1.0) is also None.

Recommendation

Do not require exact Decimal conversion for comparison. Compare same-family floats directly (total_cmp on the finite wrappers), and compare float vs integer/decimal with an exact mixed algorithm (e.g. decompose the f64 exactly into mantissa·2^exp and compare as rationals), falling back to Decimal only for decimal vs integer. Compare Nat128 vs Nat128 natively. Add tests with 1e-30, 1e300 and u128::MAX on both predicate and expression paths, and check index-range and residual paths agree.

FromStr fails on i128 mantissa overflow (text.rs:108-120), and checked_from_mantissa_scale (decimal/mod.rs:387-414) returns None when scale > 28 and the mantissa is not divisible by 10. So 1e-30, 3e40 and 1e300 all give None. compare_numeric_order (db/numeric/mod.rs:341-345) requires both Decimals. compare_literal_coercion (compile.rs:1005-1020) picks NumericWiden for Float/Decimal/Int literals under ordering ops. normalize.rs:497-504 leaves ordered NumericWiden literals untouched. The direct scalar compare returns None for NumericWiden (direct/compare.rs:36), so evaluation falls back to eval_compare_values, where compare_order(...).is_some_and(..) is false (runtime/compare/value.rs:23-25). Field-to-field ordering stays NumericWiden (normalize.rs:273-297). Numeric equality between fields is also widened, so a=b=1e-30 matches neither = nor <>. Projection eq/order (value/ops/ordering.rs:31-57) use compare_decimal_order, and evaluate.rs:581-606 turns None into invalid_binary_operands. Nat128 values of 2^127 or more fail through from_u128. One claim is weak: Value::cmp_numeric (the F64 vs Decimal mixed case) is only used in tests. I lowered the severity because it only affects extreme magnitudes: floats below roughly 1e-11 carrying full precision, floats of 1.7e38 or more, and Nat128 values of 2^127 or more. Rows silently drop out, but only under those edge conditions.

Persisted LOWER/UPPER index expression keys depend on the Rust toolchain's Unicode tables, with no version pinning
crates/icydb-core/src/value/ops/text.rs:57

Failure scenario

A canister built with toolchain N stores a row whose name contains 'ɤ' under an UPPER(name) index. The canister is upgraded with a toolchain carrying newer Unicode tables. Now lookups compute a different key and miss the row, unique checks see no conflict and admit duplicates, and update/delete compute the new key and cannot remove the stale entry. The result is orphaned index entries and index/row divergence (integrity findings) without any schema change.

Evidence

lower_text/upper_text call std `str::to_lowercase`/`to_uppercase` (text.rs:49-63). db/scalar_expr.rs:88-110 uses them to derive persisted index-expression keys (PersistedIndexExpressionOp::Lower/Upper/LowerTrim). The only safeguard is the comment 'pinned Rust 1.98.1' and a test bounding output growth. No Unicode version is recorded in accepted schema or index metadata (grep finds none). Case mappings of long-assigned characters do change across Unicode versions: Unicode 16 added capitals U+A7CB and U+A7DC, changing UPPER(ɤ U+0264) and UPPER(ƛ U+019B).

Recommendation

Freeze the mapping: vendor a fixed case-mapping table, or record a text-transform/Unicode version in the persisted index expression and force a rebuild on mismatch. Add a golden test that pins outputs for characters whose mappings changed across recent Unicode versions.

Verifier (confirmed): lower_text and upper_text (value/ops/text.rs:22-24, 49-63) use std to_lowercase and to_uppercase. db/scalar_expr.rs:88-110 applies them for the persisted index expression ops Lower, Upper and LowerTrim; Trim also depends on Unicode White_Space. I found no Unicode version recorded anywhere (a grep for unicode_version, UNICODE_VERSION and char::UNICODE returns nothing), and no rebuild trigger. rust-toolchain.toml pins 1.98.1 only for this repo. Downstream canisters compile icydb with their own toolchain (Cargo.toml rust-version = 1.96.0 is a minimum, not a pin), so a routine toolchain bump can change case tables. The only tests are a growth-bound loop and a few ASCII and ß vectors (text.rs:157-189). Neither pins mappings for characters that change between Unicode versions. For example, Unicode 16 added capital pairs for ɤ and ƛ. Code points that were unassigned when stored also become mappable later. After such a bump, lookups, unique checks and delete/update key derivation diverge from the stored index entries. The trigger needs uncommon characters plus a toolchain upgrade, so medium is appropriate.

crates/icydb-core/src/db/numeric/mod.rs:365

Failure scenario

Take `ORDER BY created_at` (Timestamp, not indexed) over 30k rows: about 450k comparisons. Each unequal pair expands two 13-digit mantissas, roughly 26 u128 div/mod library calls per operand, i.e. thousands of instructions per comparison where a native i64 compare costs a few. Total: billions of instructions, close to the 4.5B read instruction ceiling (budget.rs:51). The query fails with InstructionUnits exhaustion, or burns most of the message, for a sort that native comparisons finish in a few million instructions. ORDER BY on a Float64 column is worse because of the float formatting and parsing. MIN/MAX over 100k rows pays the same per-row cost. These are estimates; nothing was measured.

`canonical_value_compare` = `compare_numeric_or_strict_order(left, right).unwrap_or_else(..)`, and `compare_numeric_order` (line 341) does `coerce_numeric_decimal(left)?` / `coerce_numeric_decimal(right)?` then `left.partial_cmp(&right)`. This happens even when both values are `Int64`, `Nat64` or `Timestamp` (the numeric check runs before `strict_order_cmp`, value/compare.rs:36). `Decimal::cmp_decimal` (icydb-schema/src/decimal/compare.rs:8-66): after the equality and sign checks it always calls `write_u128_decimal_digits` for both mantissas (lines 98-126: `value % 10` and `value /= 10` on u128 per digit, which are software library calls on wasm32), then compares the digit strings, even when both scales are 0. `Float64::try_to_decimal` (icydb-schema/src/numeric_value.rs:115) calls `Decimal::from_f64_lossy` (decimal/mod.rs:237), which calls `from_float_text(format_args!("{n}"))` (decimal/text.rs:19): the float is formatted to text and parsed back, for each operand on every comparison. Callers: executor/order.rs:958-965 (sort, bounded top-K, cursor-boundary compare at 969-981), aggregate/value_reducer.rs:241/251 (MIN/MAX per row), grouped page_finalize.rs:739.

Recommendation

Add a same-variant fast path before decimal coercion in `canonical_value_compare` / `compare_numeric_or_strict_order`: if both values have the same discriminant, return `strict_order_cmp`. This gives the same ordering for exact numeric types, and for finite Float64 the lossy text conversion preserves order, so the native compare matches. Separately, make `Decimal::cmp_decimal` compare mantissas directly when scales are equal, and otherwise align scales with a checked pow10 multiply, instead of building digit strings. Measure before/after with the sql_perf canister on a sorted Timestamp/Float64 query.

Severity adjusted from high to medium during verification.
Verifier (confirmed): The mechanism is real. `canonical_value_compare` (numeric/mod.rs:365) calls `compare_numeric_order` (341-345) before `strict_order_cmp` (value/compare.rs:36). Timestamp, Int64 and Nat64 all pass `supports_numeric_coercion` (value/semantics.rs:29-41), so every same-variant pair is converted to Decimal on every comparison. `cmp_decimal` (icydb-schema/src/decimal/compare.rs:40-44) always runs `write_u128_decimal_digits` on both mantissas once they are unequal and have the same sign, even when both scales are 0. The fast path the reviewer proposes gives the same ordering: exact for integer and time types, and it also holds for floats because a failed conversion already falls back to strict compare. I lowered the severity for two reasons. (1) Reach: under READ_ADMISSION.md:18-23 PublicRead rejects full scans and materialized ordering. Non-indexed ORDER BY therefore only runs on trusted/admin lanes, and it fails with a typed budget error rather than a trap. (2) Magnitude is overstated. LLVM usually lowers u128 division by the constant 10 inline, or compiler-builtins takes a fast u64 path, so the cost is likely around 1-3k instructions per unequal compare. A 30k-row sort (~450k comparisons) then costs roughly 0.5-1.5B instructions, not "close to 4.5B". This is a large avoidable cost, not a failure at realistic sizes.
mediumconfirmedxc-performance-2 · performance · high confidence
Bounded top-K window is O(N·K) and charges K+1 SortComparisons per row, so moderately large LIMIT/OFFSET without an index-backed order fails deterministically
crates/icydb-core/src/db/executor/order.rs:575

Failure scenario

`SELECT * FROM T ORDER BY name LIMIT 1000` on a 40k-row table with no index on `name`: the charge is (40,000−1,000)×1,001 ≈ 39M > 32M, so the query fails with ExecutionBudgetExceeded(SortComparisons) regardless of data order. A full sort (≈640k comparisons) or a heap top-K (≈400k) would pass easily. OFFSET makes it worse: `LIMIT 50 OFFSET 5000` (K=5050) fails after about 11.4k rows. When scan order runs opposite to the ORDER BY (e.g. ascending ULID primary key with `ORDER BY created_at DESC`), every row replaces the worst, so the real work is also N×K comparisons; multiplied by the Decimal comparison cost above, that is billions of instructions.

Evidence

`BoundedOrderRows::push`: once the window is full and a candidate replaces the worst row, it runs `self.worst_index = Some(self.worst_row_index(&compare));` and `worst_row_index` (605-617) scans all K kept rows. The charge is made per push in `BoundedOrderWindow::push` (487-500) and `DataRowOrderWindow::push` (400-415): `comparisons = retained_count.saturating_add(1)` once the window is full, charged before insertion whether or not a replacement happens (`charge_order_candidate_work`, 620-633), against the SortComparisons ceiling of 32,000,000 (budget.rs:43). The unit test at order.rs:1090-1093 confirms the formula (4 pushes, K=2 → 7). K = offset + limit (+1 lookahead) (window.rs:12-18). The window is used for any cursorless load whose ORDER BY the access route does not satisfy (terminal/page/plan.rs:128-161 and the direct `MaterializedOrder` lane, direct_path.rs:133-145).

Recommendation

Replace the linear worst-row scan with a binary max-heap keyed by the resolved order (O(log K) per push) and charge ceil(log2 K)+1 per push, i.e. the real bound. Alternatively, switch to collect-then-full-sort when K is large relative to the scanned rows. Add a regression test with N ≫ K under the production budget.

Severity adjusted from high to medium during verification.
Verifier (confirmed): Verified. `BoundedOrderRows::push` (order.rs:575-596) rescans all K retained rows through `worst_row_index` (605-617) on every replacement. `BoundedOrderWindow::push` (487-500) and `DataRowOrderWindow::push` (400-414) charge `retained_count + 1` SortComparisons per push once the window is full, whether or not a replacement happens. The test at order.rs:1090-1093 pins this formula (pushes 4,1,5,0 with K=2 give 0+1+3+3=7). K is offset + limit (+ lookahead) (window.rs:12-18), and the SortComparisons ceiling is 32,000,000 (budget.rs:43). A full sort instead charges n·ceil(log2 n) (budget.rs:962-968). So `ORDER BY name LIMIT 1000` over 40k unindexed rows charges about 39M and fails, while the same query without LIMIT charges about 640k and passes. That inversion is a real defect. I lowered the severity from high because public reads cannot reach it: they reject materialized ordering (SortRequiresMaterialization) and cannot supply OFFSET (READ_ADMISSION.md:18-23, 90-92). For public ByKeys candidates, ≤1024 keys × ≤101 comparisons is far below the cap. It affects trusted/admin SQL, fails with a typed error, and workarounds exist.

crates/icydb-core/src/db/commit/prepare.rs:430

For an update: `validated_existing_row` (write.rs:627-640) validates the before-row. `resolve_update_structural_patch_with_accepted_contract` validates it again (patch.rs:635-636). `canonical_before` (write.rs:1471 → patch.rs:351-359) validates, materializes and re-encodes it. The after-row is encoded in resolve and then validated at write.rs:1435, and again in constraint_scheduler.rs:67-68. Commit window: `PreflightStoreOverlay::from_row_ops` clones every after image (commit_window.rs:290-303); `CommitRowImages::from_bytes` copies before and after again (prepare.rs:221-241); `decode_commit_marker_structural_slots` validates both images (prepare.rs:499-517); then `new_slots.map(canonical_row_from_structural_slot_reader_with_accepted_contract)` (prepare.rs:430-432 → patch.rs:340-346) materializes every slot and re-encodes a row the canonical encoder produced in the same message; `stage_prepared_row_op` clones the row once more (commit_window.rs:316-322). The key is decoded twice as well (commit_window.rs:517 and prepare.rs:718-719).

Recommendation

In NormalWrite mode, carry the `CanonicalRow` token (and its validated reader) from session resolution into commit prepare. Reuse it instead of re-validating and re-canonicalizing; keep full validation plus canonicalization for RecoveryReplay and DerivedRebuild, where the bytes come from persisted markers. Share row bytes between overlay and marker (e.g. `Rc<[u8]>`) instead of cloning. If the NormalWrite re-canonicalization is intentional defense in depth, document it and measure what it costs.

Verifier (confirmed): I traced the chain and it holds. For the before-row: `validated_existing_row` validates it (write.rs:627-640), resolve validates it again (patch.rs:635-636), and `canonical_before` validates, materializes and re-encodes it (write.rs:1471 → patch.rs:351-359). For the after-row: it is validated at write.rs:1435, again in constraint_scheduler.rs:67-68 (only when the entity has constraints), and again in commit prepare (prepare.rs:499-517). Prepare then materializes every slot and re-encodes the row (prepare.rs:430-432 → patch.rs:340-346). The bytes are copied repeatedly: overlay (commit_window.rs:290-303), `CommitRowImages::from_bytes` (prepare.rs:221-241), staging (commit_window.rs:316-322) and `to_vec` at write.rs:1506-1508. The key is decoded twice (commit_window.rs:517, prepare.rs:718-719). Some of this is intentional defense in depth: commit prepare treats marker bytes as untrusted (`RawRow::from_untrusted_bytes`) and is shared with RecoveryReplay. Even so, re-canonicalizing a row that the same message just produced canonically, plus about four validations per image, is redundant in NormalWrite. There is no correctness defect; it is a several-fold CPU multiplier on the write path. Keeping medium is appropriate for a performance unit.
mediumconfirmedxc-robustness-2 · robustness · medium confidence
Scalar page kernel preallocates Vec::with_capacity(OFFSET+LIMIT+1) unclamped, so large OFFSET/LIMIT traps before any budget check
crates/icydb-core/src/db/executor/terminal/page/scan.rs:481

Failure scenario

On wasm32 (usize = 32 bits), an authorized caller of the generated `icydb_query` SQL endpoint (trusted lane, gated by controller or the app's read guard) issues `SELECT * FROM users WHERE id >= 0 ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 OFFSET 4000000000`. row_keep_cap saturates to about 4e9 and Vec::<KernelRow>::with_capacity(4e9) exceeds isize::MAX, so it panics with 'capacity overflow' and traps. With OFFSET or LIMIT around 10,000,000 it instead allocates hundreds of MB of heap up front, even though the page envelope then scans at most a page of rows; in an update context the wasm heap growth persists. Canister code on a trusted typed lane that forwards a user page size into `.limit(n)` hits the same trap.

Evidence

scan_rows_with: `let staged_capacity = staged_row_capacity(key_stream, row_keep_cap, row_skip_count); let mut rows = Vec::with_capacity(staged_capacity);` (480-481). staged_row_capacity = `row_keep_cap.saturating_sub(row_skip_count)` (589-601). execute_scalar_page_kernel_dyn hard-codes `row_skip_count: 0` (line 290) while row_keep_cap comes from plan.rs:114-121 streaming_page_scan_keep_cap = continuation.keep_count_for_limit_window(plan, limit) = offset.saturating_add(limit) (cursor/continuation.rs:89-99) + 1 for cursor emission. That path is taken for every ordered load whose order the route satisfies, which is exactly the shape public/typed reads require because materialized sorts are disallowed. Admission bounds only LIMIT (query/admission/policy.rs:291-303, plan_summary.rs:241-247). OFFSET is a raw u32 (PageSpec, sql/parser/mod.rs:154-169) and is never bounded. Execution budget charges are per page unit, after this allocation. Contrast: stream/access/scan.rs:585 clamps with LIMITED_SCAN_PREALLOC_CAP=32, order.rs:569 clamps with BOUNDED_ORDER_INITIAL_CAPACITY, covering.rs uses limit.min(32), and traversal.rs:496-505 charges TemporaryBytes before its allocation. The same unclamped pattern exists in covering/pure.rs:467 via pure_covering_output_capacity_hint = raw LIMIT (484-494).

Recommendation

Clamp preallocation like the sibling paths (`staged_capacity.min(LIMITED_SCAN_PREALLOC_CAP)`, or the page envelope's ResultRows limit) and let Vec grow. Apply the same to pure_covering_output_capacity_hint. Optionally bound OFFSET in admission or at the planner so hidden-offset scans fail with a typed error, consistent with READ_ADMISSION.md's 'do not emulate continuation with hidden offsets'.

Verifier (confirmed): The core defect holds, but the example scenario is wrong. scan_rows_with (terminal/page/scan.rs:480-481) preallocates Vec::with_capacity(row_keep_cap - row_skip_count) with no clamp. pure_covering_output_capacity_hint (covering/pure.rs:484-494 -> 467) likewise preallocates the raw LIMIT. The cited trusted SQL `SELECT * ... ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 OFFSET 4000000000` does not hit the row_skip_count=0 kernel. execute_sql_projection_rows_for_canister (session/sql/projection/runtime/mod.rs:34-37) never enables cursor emission. An identity projection with route order therefore takes DirectDataRowPath::Plain (plan.rs:468-480), whose skip count is the OFFSET (direct_path.rs:43, 152-157). A non-identity projection takes the retained-slot short path (plan.rs:299-327, 569-601), also with skip=offset. In both cases capacity = LIMIT. The OFFSET-dominated capacity from execute_scalar_page_kernel_dyn (scan.rs:290, plan.rs:95-122) applies only to cursor-emitting pages or to shapes with a retained_slot_layout but no retained slot rows, such as field-path projections (entrypoints/scalar/runtime.rs:211-219). A LIMIT-driven variant is solid on every path. SQL LIMIT is a raw u32 (sql/parser/mod.rs:154-174), and neither the SQL lane nor with_read_execution_budget (executor/budget.rs:636-651) checks it before execution. `SELECT * FROM users ORDER BY id LIMIT 4000000000` gives with_capacity(4e9) on the direct path, and `SELECT id ... LIMIT 4000000000` does the same on pure covering. On wasm32 either one panics with 'capacity overflow' or aborts on allocation failure. That contradicts RESOURCE_MODEL.md:116 ('Trusted reads bypass public shape policy, not ... execution limits'). Public lanes are capped at 100 rows and cannot supply offsets (READ_ADMISSION.md:91-93), so only trusted or controller callers can reach this. Medium is right. The claim that heap growth persists after a trap is inaccurate: a trapped message's memory changes roll back. Growth persists only when the large allocation succeeds and the message commits.

mediumconfirmedxc-security-2 · robustness · medium confidence
Startup watchdog replans deterministic migration-planning failures every round with no backoff, log or receipt
crates/icydb-model/src/build/actor/db/store.rs:338

Failure scenario

A developer upgrades with a source migration plan that bumps an entity version by 2 (the guide requires exactly 1), or deploys a successor to a database whose lineage is unadopted. Every watchdog tick then re-runs memory bootstrap, a recovery page, fragment decode and full migration planning, fails with SCHEMA_MIGRATION_VERSION_GAP or UNADOPTED, records nothing, logs nothing (the Ok(false) branch has no println), and reschedules immediately. Cycles drain continuously while every ordinary request gets the 'retryable' DatabaseStartupRecoveryPending. This lasts until an operator redeploys, and gives no diagnostic explaining why. It contradicts docs/guides/schema-migrations.md ('The watchdog does not keep retrying that pending plan') and the in-code intent for IN_PROGRESS ('stop this watchdog without persisting a failure or repeatedly replanning while idle').

Evidence

complete_generated_schema_handoff: if apply fails and `error.code() != SCHEMA_MIGRATION_IN_PROGRESS`, it returns `__record_generated_schema_startup_failure(...)`. That call reaches driver::record_schema_failure, which returns `Ok(false)` when classify_terminal_failure_parts rejects the code. terminal_code_for_kind (crates/icydb-core/src/db/startup/mod.rs:110-139) treats only STORE_*/RUNTIME_CORRUPTION/... and SCHEMA_DDL_ADMISSION, RUNTIME_CONFLICT, RUNTIME_UNSUPPORTED, etc. as terminal for SchemaReconciliation. Per-reason codes such as SCHEMA_MIGRATION_VERSION_GAP (registry.rs:605, a distinct code), DOWNGRADE, UNADOPTED and UNEXPLAINED_SCHEMA_DIFFERENCE are not terminal. Those codes come from preflight_unpublished_schema_migration -> plan_schema_migration -> schema_migration_planning_error (application.rs:2119, 1878-1891). The watchdog callback maps `Ok(false)` to `WatchdogDecision::ContinueImmediately` (store.rs:280), which in ic-timers 0.8 means a zero-delay reschedule. observe.rs:104-108 reports Recovering while the schema is unreconciled.

Recommendation

Treat deterministic migration-planning codes like IN_PROGRESS (stop the watchdog and leave readiness gated for operator commands), or classify them as terminal SchemaReconciliation failures so a receipt surfaces through startup_state(). Separately, never map a failed attempt to ContinueImmediately: return Err so it uses the cadence-based retryable path, and add a bounded retry/backoff policy.

Verifier (confirmed): I reproduced the mechanism. With a migration plan present, preflight_ordinary_source_application (application.rs:760-787) runs preflight_unpublished_schema_migration. schema_migration_planning_error (application.rs:1875-1901) maps planner rejections to InternalError::schema_migration(reason). Diagnostic::error_code() uses ErrorCode::from_parts (registry.rs:48-63, lib.rs:972-974), which gives each reason its own leaf code: UNADOPTED=229, VERSION_GAP=231, DOWNGRADE=232, UNEXPLAINED=240, and even PROGRESS_CORRUPT=245 and CANDIDATE_MISMATCH=246. terminal_code_for_kind (startup/mod.rs:110-139) matches only the broad codes (RUNTIME_UNSUPPORTED=22, RUNTIME_CONFLICT=20, RUNTIME_CORRUPTION=17, etc.), so none of these reasons is terminal. record_schema_failure then returns Ok(false) (driver.rs:279-290). complete_generated_schema_handoff returns that Ok(false) (store.rs:338-346). The watchdog callback maps Ok(false) to WatchdogDecision::ContinueImmediately with no log line (store.rs:276-280). In ic-timers 0.8.0, ContinueImmediately resolves to deadline=now, delay 0 (schedule.rs:92-95; registry/mod.rs:1617-1630). drive_recovery_page keeps returning ApplyGeneratedSchema because no receipt exists (driver.rs:113-116), and observe reports Recovering (observe.rs:104-108). The result is a zero-delay replanning loop: it burns cycles every round and ordinary requests stay gated until a redeploy. No test covers it; VERSION_GAP appears only in the CLI, application.rs and the registry. Two parts of the finding are overstated. First, the guide sentence at schema-migrations.md:286-289 is about a *valid* pending plan, so this is not a direct contradiction of the doc. It does contradict the in-code intent at store.rs:333-336. Second, controllers probably still have `icydb schema migration status` for diagnostics. The canister is not bricked (a redeploy fixes it) and the input is operator-controlled, not caller-controlled, so medium stands.

It is applied to every line (input.rs:84), before append_shell_statement_line and without checking whether a quote is still open. The quote tracking in drain_complete_shell_statements (input.rs:173-216) runs only afterwards. The lexer (icydb-core/src/db/sql_shared/lexer/token_body.rs:37-72) scans to the next quote and keeps raw newlines, so the trimmed whitespace, or a ';;' at the end of a line inside a literal, silently changes the stored value. The trigger is narrow: interactive, multi-line string literals with significant edge whitespace or ';;' at a line break. A readback shows the difference, so this is a minor bug rather than medium.

In most mismatched setups the result is a loud error ('expected wasm not found after build'), not silent misbehavior. The stale-wasm rollback needs a leftover file at exactly that repo-specific path, which is unlikely downstream. The command family is described as local (cli/mod.rs:82, canister.rs:28), `--wasm` is an override, and the only documented use is `icydb canister upgrade demo_rpg` (INSTALLING.md:363). lowconfirmedexecutor-core-1 · robustness · medium confidence
Instruction ceilings count from each tracker's own start, so every mutation-job advance or maintenance allowance gets a fresh 30B regardless of work already done in the message
crates/icydb-core/src/db/executor/budget.rs:489

Failure scenario

An application update method calls advance_trusted_mutation_job for job A, which uses about 25B instructions, then for job B in the same message (or first does about 6B of its own work). B's tracker starts at a delta of 0, so B only raises typed exhaustion after another 30B plus up to 5B of reserve work. The IC limit of about 40B is hit first and the message traps. The trap rolls back the whole message, including job A's already-committed page, and the 'deterministic exhaustion persists a progress-only terminal transition from the reserve' design never runs. If the caller repeats the same pattern, the jobs never advance. Multi-candidate schema proposals have the same problem: each candidate gets its own 30B.

Evidence

check_instruction_watermark computes `delta = last_instruction_counter.map_or(0, |previous| current.saturating_sub(previous))` (lines 492-498). The first sample always charges 0. `with_mutation_execution_budget` (658-669) creates `HardExecutionBudgetTracker::new(&MUTATION_HARD_BUDGET, ..)` and baselines on entry. `MaintenanceConstructionBudget::new()` (725-737) creates another fresh MUTATION_HARD_BUDGET tracker. MUTATION_EXECUTION_INSTRUCTION_LIMIT is 30B and the failure reserve is 5B (lines 26-29), sized against the 40B update ceiling on the assumption that nothing else runs in the message. `CandidateSchemaRevision::new` calls `Self::prepare(bundle, &MaintenanceConstructionBudget::new())` once per candidate, including inside loops (schema/application.rs:2364, 2742). The public guide says page execution has 'a fixed 30-billion-instruction allocation and a 5-billion failure reserve below the IC update-message ceiling', but nothing enforces one advance per message.

Recommendation

Bound instructions against the message rather than the tracker's creation time. Seed the tracker with the absolute counter read when the budget is created (ic0.performance_counter(0) since message start) and set the ceiling to IC_UPDATE_LIMIT − reserve − already_consumed. Alternatively reject a second mutation-job advance within one message. Pass one MaintenanceConstructionBudget through a whole multi-candidate operation instead of creating one per candidate. Add a wasm or PocketIC test, since the native counter is always 0.

Verifier (confirmed): The mechanism is real, and the line references are correct. At budget.rs:489-498, check_instruction_watermark charges `map_or(0, ...)` on its first sample, and runtime.rs:13 reads performance_counter(1), the call-context counter. Every tracker therefore baselines at whatever the counter shows when it is created. Nothing charges the instructions the message used before that point. with_mutation_execution_budget (budget.rs:658-669) builds a fresh MUTATION_HARD_BUDGET tracker with no request scope. MaintenanceConstructionBudget::new() (budget.rs:725-737) does the same. Nothing limits a message to one advance. charge_mutation_job_operation (session/mutation_job.rs:176-189) charges only QueryExecutions against the request scope, and REQUEST_HARD_BUDGET allows 256 of those (session/request.rs:21). Mutation instructions are never charged to the request scope. CandidateSchemaRevision::new (enum_catalog/publication.rs:663-667) creates a fresh budget on every call, even though its doc comment says 'one operation-wide allowance'. application.rs:2364 calls it inside a loop over candidates. application.rs:2742 is a single call, not a loop. The severity is inflated, though. The 30B instruction ceiling is a backstop, not the main bound. Page work is limited by count and byte policy: at most 4,096 keys and a batch-row cap derived from max index fanout (the docs say 240 rows), plus 16 MiB scan and staging caps (session/sql/resumable_update.rs:91-120). The 0.233 design (0.233-design.md:640-655) calibrates those limits so every admitted page fits well inside the allocation. The 30B check only fires when 'policy and executor authority diverged'. The measured worst case is about 4.95B for a 240-row page at 64 indexes (changelog 0.233.md:104). The scenario of 'job A uses about 25B' contradicts that calibration. Two maximal advances in one message cost about 10B, far below the 40B IC ceiling. To actually hit the IC trap, the application itself must burn about 35B before calling. A trap then rolls the message back atomically. That causes no durable inconsistency and does not wedge anything: the next message without that extra work advances normally. The only real loss is that the typed-exhaustion terminal backstop can't be reached when an already-diverged policy coincides with heavy prior work in the same message. Maintenance pages have the same shape. Migration steps run one page per public call (application.rs:1270-1400, reached only from :1025), and each page has its own row and byte soft limits. Schema candidate preparation is small and bounded. So this is an undocumented, unenforced assumption (roughly 'advance near the start of a message') plus a misleading doc comment. That is a low-severity robustness gap, not a medium one.
lowunverifiedexecutor-core-2 · robustness · high confidence
Read executions never set an instruction baseline at start, so work before the 64th charge (or the first charge of 1MiB or more) is counted by neither the execution nor the request scope
crates/icydb-core/src/db/executor/budget.rs:636

Failure scenario

A query reads about 31 rows just under 1 MiB each (MAX_ROW_BYTES is 4 MiB). Each row costs two sub-1MiB charges (stored and materialized bytes), so there are 62 charges before the first sample. All stable-memory reads and decoding of about 31 MiB before that point are charged to no instruction counter. Separately, an execution that performs fewer than 64 small charges records zero instruction units even if uncharged computation between those charges is heavy. The 4.5B read ceiling plus 500M headroom no longer bounds the real cost, so a query near the 5B query-call limit traps instead of returning ExecutionBudgetExceeded.

Evidence

with_read_execution_budget (636-651) passes a tracker with last_instruction_counter = None straight to with_execution_budget, which calls only precharge (charge_raw, no sampling). charge() samples only once charges_since_instruction_watermark reaches 64 or amount >= 1 MiB (590-601), and that first sample charges a delta of 0. finish_instruction_watermark (502-510) returns Ok without sampling if no baseline was ever set. By contrast, with_mutation_execution_budget calls tracker.check_instruction_watermark() before installing (664-667), and PreparationWork::run captures a baseline when it is constructed (query/preparation.rs:96).

Recommendation

Call tracker.check_instruction_watermark() (or set last_instruction_counter to the current counter) in with_read_execution_budget before installing, the same way the mutation path does, so the whole execution interval is measured.

lowunverifiedexecutor-core-3 · durability · medium confidence
Checks inside the commit window that can fail after marker publication return Err to the caller while the marker is kept, so the reported-failed write is later committed by recovery
crates/icydb-core/src/db/executor/mutation/commit_window.rs:625

Failure scenario

If a generation drift or a journal-append error ever happens (for example a future refactor that bumps the index generation in begin_commit, or a journal-store error on the second store of a multi-tail marker), the typed insert or update returns an error. Ordinary operations then return startup-pending until the watchdog replays the marker, and the write that was reported as failed becomes durable. A client retrying the 'failed' insert then gets a key-exists conflict, and non-idempotent application logic built on the error result diverges.

Evidence

Inside finish_commit(commit, |guard| { ... }), `index_store_guard.verify()?` (624-626) and `append_prepared_journal_batches(guard, &effects)?` (632) return errors normally; they are not wrapped in enforce_preflighted_apply, which traps. commit/guard.rs:313-324 keeps the marker and arms the recovery wake-up on any returned error. The generation guard is a pure preflight comparison: nothing between capture during preflight and begin_commit (lines 574-592) touches index stores, so it could run before the marker is published. ATOMICITY.md §1 states 'either all intended durable mutations are committed as a unit, or the operation returns an error and no partial durable mutation is made visible', which conflicts with the later rule that a normally returned commit-apply error keeps its marker.

Recommendation

Move the IndexStoreGenerationGuard check before begin_commit_window_payload. There it is a clean pre-marker rejection. Decide whether steps that can still fail after the marker, such as the journal append, should trap (atomic rollback) or return a distinct 'committed-pending-recovery' outcome rather than an ordinary error. Reconcile ATOMICITY.md §1 with the retained-marker rule.

Also reported as: xc-contracts-4, commit-5
lowunverifiedexecutor-core-4 · correctness · medium confidence
The commit path marks every touched store's index Ready after each write, which is a latent visibility hazard and an Err that can follow a durable commit
crates/icydb-core/src/db/executor/mutation/commit_window.rs:691

Failure scenario

Today, admission blocks ordinary writes while recovery is running, so this is effectively a no-op. But if any path ever lets an ordinary write reach a store whose index is still Building (for example a future online rebuild, or a heap store left in Building), one row write would mark the partly rebuilt index query-visible. Planners would then choose that index and return incomplete results. Independently, if advance_access_state_revision fails, the caller gets Err for a write that is already fully committed and has its marker cleared.

Evidence

After finish_commit succeeds and clears the marker, apply_prepared_row_ops calls `mark_store_handles_index_ready(&synchronized_store_handles)` (691, 1061-1066). That function runs handle.mark_index_ready() for any store where a single row op touched both the data store and the index store. set_index_state (registry/handle.rs:1092-1106) flips Building to Ready and can fail through JournalTailStore::advance_access_state_revision. Building is set by recovery's reset_journaled_live_projections (commit/recovery.rs:686) and by user-index domain replacement (commit/schema_publication.rs:1076). Only full rebuild or validation should restore Ready (db/mod.rs:311-321, 'Recovery restores visibility only after rebuild and post-recovery integrity validation').

Recommendation

Remove the post-commit Ready promotion from the mutation path, since a single synchronized row does not prove a whole store is synchronized. Leave readiness to the recovery or rebuild owners. If it must stay, make it infallible or debug-assert that the state is already Ready.

plan.rs:121 adds one lookahead row to the scan keep cap for cursor emission (`keep_count.saturating_add(usize::from(self.cursor_emission.enabled()))`). apply_load_cursor_and_pagination_window then truncates to `logical.page.limit`, which the session sets to the page size (dynamic.rs execution_limit), so the lookahead row is dropped. lowunverifiedexecutor-stream-7 · performance · medium confidence
Residual-retry stop condition `post_access_rows > keep_count` is unreachable, so full pages trigger redundant widened re-scans
crates/icydb-core/src/db/executor/kernel/mod.rs:208

Failure scenario

An initial cursor page over an index-range LIMIT pushdown with a residual filter, LIMIT 10: fetch is 11 and the keep cap is 11. If all 11 scanned rows match, rows_scanned is 11 and post_access_rows is 10 ≤ 10, so the fetch widens to 12 and the whole attempt reruns. Work and budget are roughly doubled on every such page, and selective predicates can climb to the unbounded fallback even when the first attempt already filled the page.

Evidence

retry_decision stops only when `post_access_rows > keep_count`. post_access_rows is measured after the page window: kernel rows are truncated to `limit` (terminal/page/mod.rs:219-226, post_access.rs:75-82), the direct path uses rows_matched capped by keep_cap = offset+limit, and the ordered direct path uses a window of keep_count. So post_access_rows is always ≤ keep_count and the check never fires. Every attempt with `rows_scanned >= fetch` widens the fetch (and falls back to an unbounded scan once the fetch reaches 256), and each retry re-materializes from the start.

Recommendation

Carry the pre-window matched count, including the lookahead, in the attempt metrics and compare that count against keep_count. Or stop when the window is full and the lookahead row was observed.

lowunverifiedexecutor-stream-8 · correctness · high confidence

crates/icydb-core/src/db/executor/stream/access/physical.rs:1179

Update crates/icydb/README.md to describe the icydb::model re-export and the single-dependency guidance.

TrustedTypedWriteBatch::push calls W::Entity::typed_binding(self.session) for every item (write.rs:936), which reissues and revalidates the binding against accepted schema. execute_trusted_typed_write_batch then does `Arc::unwrap_or_clone(write.binding.inner)` (write.rs:1390) while the builder still holds a second Arc in `self.bindings` (write.rs:943). lowconfirmedintegrity-relations-2 · durability · high confidence
Abandoned or expired Deep integrity jobs are never retired and permanently use per-owner and global progress capacity, including the slots that gate SQL mutation and resumable jobs
crates/icydb-core/src/db/integrity/deep.rs:262

Failure scenario

A controller or CI principal starts Deep jobs with unique submission keys, and its client crashes or the principal is rotated out. Each job expires to TerminalPending(Expired) and stays forever. After 8 such jobs that principal gets CapacityExceeded on every DeepStart permanently. If the principal no longer exists, nobody can ever acknowledge its jobs. Across several principals, abandoned integrity records reach 56, and then start_trusted_sql_mutation_job and resumable job creation fail with CapacityExceeded for everyone, with no automatic recovery.

Evidence

Retention (deep.rs:262-280) only moves InProgress past its lease to TerminalPending(Expired), and deletes only `Terminal { receipt_acknowledged: true }` after the retention deadline. TerminalPending and unacknowledged Terminal fall through `_ => {}`. Only continue_deep_integrity_job run by the exact owner can move TerminalPending to Terminal and then to acknowledged (deep.rs:147-163; authorize_job checks owner at 343-351). There is no admin override. insert_new rejects at 64 global or 8 per owner (progress_store.rs:369-372). Non-integrity inserts stop at total >= 56 (progress_store.rs:408, 467), and that total includes integrity records. Corrupt records are skipped by scan_after and owner_job_count (progress_store.rs:732, 764-769) but still count toward the global total. corrupt_jobs is collected in retention (deep.rs:257) and then discarded. A DeepStart replay for an advanced job returns SubmissionAlreadyAdvanced without the job id (deep.rs:335-339). The owner is the caller principal (model/actor/db/sql.rs:222-223).

Recommendation

Have retention terminalize TerminalPending jobs after a bounded grace period. Hard-delete terminal records (acknowledged or not) after a maximum retention time, and do the same for corrupt integrity records. Consider a controller-authorized purge. Also surface the job id on SubmissionAlreadyAdvanced so the owner can finish the protocol.

Verifier (confirmed): The mechanics are accurate. Retention (deep.rs:262-280) only expires InProgress jobs and deletes acknowledged Terminal jobs. TerminalPending and unacknowledged Terminal jobs are kept. insert_new enforces 64 global and 8 per owner (progress_store.rs:369-372). Non-integrity inserts stop at total >= 56 (:408, :467), and job_count counts every record, corrupt ones included (:747-752). However, this is documented, intentional design. 0.212-design.md:1100-1104 says unacknowledged terminal and TerminalPending records 'are never deleted by time-based retention; they count against frozen per-owner/global capacity, so abandoned clients can exhaust only that bounded capacity'. 0.233-design.md:519-534 deliberately lets integrity fill the store to 64 while non-integrity stops at 56, and says 'Existing retained records are never evicted'. operations/DURABILITY_GUIDE.md:249-251 documents it for operators. The owner can always finish the protocol with abort and acknowledgement (deep.rs:187-207, :147-163). What remains is a design gap, not a code defect: there is no controller purge for jobs whose owner principal no longer exists, and roughly 7 or more authorized owners abandoning jobs can permanently block SQL mutation and resumable job admission. Integrity endpoints are application-authorized, so untrusted callers cannot trigger it. I downgrade to low.

For a heap source row, preflight_positioned_rows finds no journal append, so apply uses the unpositioned row_op.apply() (commit_window.rs:655-659). lowunverifiedintegrity-relations-8 · robustness · medium confidence
A retention-page failure turns an already-persisted integrity result into an error; a key/payload job-id mismatch makes every integrity request fail permanently
crates/icydb-core/src/db/session/integrity.rs:77

Failure scenario

A record whose CRC-valid payload carries a job id different from its map key (for example after partial stable-memory corruption) makes every icydb_integrity call perform its work (a Deep page is persisted, a Quick check runs) and then return Err, so Quick results are lost. Deep continuations can be replayed but always error. Integrity tooling stays unusable until the record is removed, and nothing removes it.

Evidence

`run_next_integrity_retention_page::<C>()?; result`: retention runs after the operation, and its error replaces the result. scan_after takes job ids from the decoded payload rather than the stable key (progress_store.rs:732-739). load(job.id) then looks up by payload id, and any error other than Corrupt or Incompatible propagates (deep.rs:260), e.g. JobNotFound when payload id != key. The heap cursor is not advanced on error, so every later call hits the same record again.

Recommendation

Make retention best-effort: log or count its failure and still return the operation result. Have scan_after return key-derived ids, and treat decode or id mismatches as corrupt records to be retired.

lowunverifiedjournal-jobs-5 · durability · high confidence
append_batch_bytes has fallible steps after its first stable write; any Err leaves the tail in a state that identical replay cannot fix
crates/icydb-core/src/db/journal/store.rs:811

Failure scenario

Today the post-write errors look unreachable, because prepare validated the same authority. If a future change or a subtle bug makes one of them fail, the chunks are persisted but control is not updated. Recovery's append_batch then sees identical bytes. With an empty control, validate_current_tail_authority returns (true, Some(_)) and reports corruption. With a non-empty control, it 'succeeds' without counting the batch, and later fold or retirement accounting fails. Either way startup recovery can never complete.

Evidence

The order is: insert all batch chunks (811-814), then the data-mutation revision (815-820), then `self.apply_prepared_entity_mutation_revision_update(entity_revision_update)?` (821). That call re-decodes chunks and calls encode_entity_mutation_revision_chunk(..)? / entity_mutation_revision_data_chunk(..)? / encode_entity_mutation_revision_control(..)?, all fallible. Only after that is the tail-convergence control written (822-825). The caller's append error returns normally with the marker kept (commit_window.rs:632, guard.rs:313-324). On replay, existing bytes == new bytes takes the identical_replay branch, whose validate_replayed_batch_against_control (1581-1594) requires control to already account for the batch.

Recommendation

Make the apply half infallible by construction: build all encoded entity-revision chunk bytes and keys during prepare (PreparedEntityMutationRevisionUpdate carries the final Vec<(key, bytes)>), and make the apply step return (). Alternatively, trap on any post-write error in the append apply, as enforce_preflighted_apply does elsewhere.

Each recovery or online convergence step already validates, applies and folds one batch of up to 16 MiB. lowconfirmedmodel-macros-3 · correctness · high confidence
Redundant-prefix index rejection is backwards for unique indexes and ignores filter predicates
crates/icydb-model-macros/src/node/entity.rs:273

Failure scenario

(a) `index(field = "email", unique)` plus `index(fields = ["email", "tenant_id"], unique)` fails with "index [\"email\"] is redundant". The shorter unique index is the stronger constraint; the longer one is the redundant one. An author who follows the message and deletes unique(email) loses email uniqueness, and duplicate emails are then admitted. (b) WRITE_ADMISSION requires nullable unique keys to carry an `IS NOT NULL` predicate, so predicates on unique indexes are common. `index(field = "email", unique, predicate = "email IS NOT NULL")` next to an unfiltered unique (email, tenant_id) is also rejected. Non-unique partial indexes (e.g. idx(status) WHERE archived = false next to idx(status, created_at)) are rejected even though they do different jobs.

Evidence

validate_redundant_prefix_indexes: `if left_index.unique != right_index.unique { continue; } if is_prefix_of(left_terms, right_terms) { return Err("index {left_terms:?} is redundant (prefix of {right_terms:?})") }`. Terms come from `validated_key_item_terms()` (fields only); `index.predicate` is never compared. No test covers this rule, and the SQL DDL frontend has no equivalent restriction.

Recommendation

For unique pairs, flag the longer index, or better, drop the uniqueness redundancy rule entirely. Skip the check when either index has a predicate, or when predicates differ. Add unit tests for both directions.

Verifier (confirmed): The code does what is claimed. node/entity.rs:273 skips only mixed-uniqueness pairs. For two unique indexes, is_prefix_of (entity.rs:397-404, strict prefix) flags the SHORTER one: `index ["email"] is redundant (prefix of ["email", "tenant_id"])`. For uniqueness it is the longer index that is implied and redundant. Terms come from validated_key_item_terms() (entity.rs:195), and index.predicate is never considered. So a partial index and a full index over prefix-related keys are rejected even though their membership differs (e.g. non-unique idx(status) WHERE archived=false next to idx(status, created_at)). No unit test covers the rule; the only reference is a comment in schema/audit/sql_perf/src/sql_perf.rs:83. I lowered severity to low. The defect only shows up at build time: a misleading diagnostic plus a false rejection that blocks a legitimate schema and forces a workaround. It never produces wrong runtime results by itself. The data-loss chain (author deletes unique(email) because of the message) depends on a human acting on bad advice. Keeping both unique indexes is also genuinely redundant as constraints, so rejecting the pair is reasonable. Only the choice of which index to name, and ignoring predicates, are wrong.

Schema normalization converts the literal back only for Int64/Int128/IntBig/Nat64/Nat128/NatBig kinds (predicate/normalize.rs:469-477). Int8-32, Nat8-32, Float, Timestamp and Duration keep the Decimal. Verifier (confirmed): rewrite_affine_field_compare always emits Value::Decimal (rewrite/affine_numeric.rs:92). It runs only in normalize_where_bool_expr (sql/lowering/predicate/normalize.rs:7-16), which serves grouped WHERE, UPDATE and predicate-required lanes (select/mod.rs:89-137). compare_literal_coercion maps a Decimal literal under Eq/Ne to Strict (compile.rs:1010-1015). Neither SQL canonicalization nor schema normalization turns a Decimal back into the field's type for Int8-32, Nat8-32, Float or Timestamp kinds. canonicalize_int/nat_persisted_literal accept only Int64/Nat64 inputs (schema/types.rs:759-778), and normalize_numeric_value_for_accepted_kind has targets only for 64/128/Big kinds (predicate/normalize.rs:463-477). validate_predicate then rejects the Strict literal type mismatch (query/predicate/validate.rs:469-475; semantic_gates.rs:88-92). So `... WHERE level+1 = 3 GROUP BY level` on an Int32 field is rejected, while the scalar path accepts it. Only the fail-closed rejection is reachable; the 'matches no rows' branch is not, because validation runs first. I lowered severity to low: a narrow spurious rejection with a trivial workaround.

lowunverifiedquery-intent-5 · correctness · medium confidence

Failure scenario

A live page ordered by `div("score", 2_i64)` issues a cursor. A redeploy (schema root unchanged) or a caller-built DynamicQuery then orders by `div("score", Decimal::from(2))`. Filter, access and projection hashes match and the order label is "score / 2" in both cases, so the token is accepted. Its boundary values, computed with integer arithmetic, are compared against decimal order values, which can skip or duplicate rows at the page boundary. This contradicts CURSOR.md's 'Changing any bound fact rejects the token'.

Evidence

`hash_order_spec` feeds `write_expr_label(hasher, term.expr(), budget)`, the rendered label, into the continuation signature. The scalar token's order contract also uses labels: `ScalarOrderTermContract::new(term.rendered_label(), ...)` (session/query/dynamic.rs:318). `write_scalar_projection_literal` renders Int64/Nat64/U256/Decimal/Float64 values by Display, so Float64(2.0), Int64(2) and Decimal(2) all render as "2". The plan cache key deliberately avoids this: 'Typed expression identity, rather than its display label, keeps cache hits from crossing different operand domains' (cache_key.rs:75) and 'Decimal(1) and U256(1) both render as "1" but have different query semantics' (cache_key.rs:473). Grouped aggregate input and filter expressions are also hashed by label (aggregate_hash.rs:56-63), though the structural projection hash usually still separates those.

Recommendation

Hash order terms (and aggregate input/filter expressions) structurally with typed literals, reusing `hash_expr` from projection_hash.rs. Bind a structural digest of the order terms in the scalar token instead of their labels.

lowunverifiedr2-candid-stability-3 · robustness · medium confidence
Recursive public input DTOs (FilterExpr, PublicValue/InputValue) have no decode-time depth bound on the IC, and FilterExpr's error wrapper re-formats the whole message at every level
crates/icydb-core/src/db/query/expr/filter.rs:668

Failure scenario

An app follows the 'frontend-facing filter' design and exports `#[ic_cdk::query] fn search(filter: FilterExpr)`. Any caller sends Not(Not(...)) nested 10^4-10^5 levels deep, at about one byte per level, well within the 2 MiB ingress limit. Decoding recurses until the 1 MiB wasm stack overflows, and the call traps instead of returning the documented InputDepthExceeded. If the innermost node is invalid, the error path also copies about 46*N^2/2 bytes first. The impact is per call and state is rolled back, but over-deep input gets a trap instead of the typed rejection, and each malicious update call burns instructions up to the trap.

Evidence

candid 0.10.37 `check_recursion_depth` is a no-op on wasm (/Users/henk/.cargo/registry/src/index.crates.io-1949cf8c6b5b557f/candid-0.10.37/src/utils.rs:11-31). ic-cdk-macros 0.20.3 decodes arguments with only skipping_quota(10000), no decoding quota, and unwraps (ic-cdk-macros-0.20.3/src/export.rs:255-261). The recursive types are FilterExpr (Junction{filters: Vec<Self>}, Not(Box<Self>)), FilterValue::List, PublicValue::List/Map and PublicEnumValue.payload (filter.rs:27-32, 256-318; value/public.rs:14-42, 170-174). IcyDB's 128-level admission runs only after decoding (query/admission/input.rs:36-40). The FilterExpr Deserialize wrapper (filter.rs:668-680) maps each nested failure to `invalid filter expression: {error}`, and candid's de::Error::custom prepends `Deserialize error: ` (candid-0.10.37/src/error.rs:119-125). The full inner message is re-allocated at each level, which is O(depth^2). READ_ADMISSION.md:46-48 delegates decoder limits to the application, but candid has no depth setting on wasm, decoding_quota bounds work rather than stack, and no guide or template shows a bounded `decode_with` decoder.

Recommendation

Ship a bounded decoder for use with `decode_with` that sets a decoding_quota and tracks depth, rejecting nesting above MAX_QUERY_INPUT_DEPTH. Reference it where READ_ADMISSION delegates decoder limits. Change the FilterExpr wrapper to add its context once (for example only at the root, through a depth-tracking seed) instead of at every level.

lowconfirmedr2-persisted-sql-text-2 · durability · medium confidence
Stored filtered-index semantics depend on current parser code, not on the stored text, so parser fixes silently invalidate already-built index contents
crates/icydb-core/src/db/predicate/mod.rs:65

Failure scenario

Under the current release, a generated unique filtered index `status = 'Active'` on an enum field, or `level = 3` on a Nat32 field, admits no rows, per xc-architecture-1, so its physical index is empty. A later release fixes the parser or normalizer so the literal matches the field type, for example by applying normalize_enum_literals or typed numeric admission in normalized_accepted_index_predicate. The persisted text and fingerprint are unchanged, so the index is neither rebuilt nor re-validated. New writes start inserting entries, and the planner now treats the index as complete. `WHERE status = 'Active' AND email = ?` then returns only rows written after the upgrade, and uniqueness is enforced only among post-upgrade rows. Any other semantic change to coercion, normalization or canonicalization has the same effect. A grammar change, such as a new reserved keyword that collides with a stored field name, instead turns healthy snapshots into decode-time store_corruption (codec.rs:234-235).

Evidence

Only the SQL text is persisted (schema/codec/index.rs:37-43, 59-63). Membership is recompiled from that text by current code on every write: parse, then normalize, then PredicateProgram (index/plan/mod.rs:55-61, 224-247). The meaning therefore depends on parser policy that is not persisted. That policy includes the coercion selection in predicate_compare (Strict for =/IN, NumericWiden for ordering; parser/lowering.rs:93-107), number typing in parse_number_literal (Int64, then Nat64, then Decimal; sql_shared/types.rs:504-520), symmetric operand canonicalization (predicate/model.rs:433-443), normalize(), and the keyword table (lexer/keywords.rs). The accepted fingerprint hashes only the text (schema/store.rs:4314-4318), and the physical generation does not change, so no rebuild is triggered when the code's interpretation changes. PERSISTED_FORMAT_INVENTORY.md:43 lists 'bounded canonical accepted check expressions' but not the index predicate grammar. There is no golden corpus that pins persisted predicate texts to expected trees; parser tests (predicate/parser/tests/mod.rs) exercise the current behavior only. The inspection plan (index/plan/integrity.rs:131-160) runs on demand and does not rebuild.

Recommendation

Treat the predicate grammar and semantics as a versioned persisted format. Add it to PERSISTED_FORMAT_INVENTORY and add a golden corpus of stored predicate texts mapped to expected normalized trees, including keyword-named fields, typed literals and symmetric compares, so any parser change fails CI. Any fix to xc-architecture-1 must ship with an explicit rebuild or re-validation of existing filtered indexes, for example by bumping the physical generation of affected indexes. The durable fix is to persist the bound AcceptedCheckExprV1 so that meaning is stored data, not code.

Severity adjusted from medium to low during verification.
Verifier (confirmed): The code facts check out. Only the SQL text is persisted (schema/codec/index.rs:37-43, 59-63). Membership is recompiled from that text by the current parser and normalize() on every write (index/plan/mod.rs:55-61, 224-247; predicate/mod.rs:65-75). Planning uses the same path (access/path.rs:160, 186). The accepted fingerprint hashes only the text (schema/store.rs:4314-4318). Decode-time acceptance parses the text (schema/codec.rs:234-235 via integrity/nullable_unique.rs:51-59), so a grammar or keyword change would surface as store_corruption. The shared lexer lives in sql_shared. PERSISTED_FORMAT_INVENTORY.md:43 covers accepted check expressions but does not list the index-predicate grammar or the parser modules as owner modules, so the Review Rule would not fire on a parser change. There is no golden corpus pinning persisted predicate texts. Why I lowered it: this is a latent design hazard, not a present defect. Every failure scenario requires a future semantic change to the parser or normalizer, and today's code behaves consistently with itself. The pre-1.0 posture of one current form with recreation on hard cuts (PERSISTED_FORMAT_INVENTORY.md:17-19) is the intended mitigation. What remains actionable is (a) the gap in the inventory and review rule, and (b) a remediation caveat: fixing xc-architecture-1 inside the parser or normalizer, instead of forcing a rebuild or a new generation, would leave existing filtered indexes silently incomplete.

Planning fails with UnexplainedSchemaDifference, although variant names are documented as non-identity metadata. The only way through is to add a physical transform to the entity, which forces a full row rewrite, or to drop and re-add the index across two releases.

An EnumVariant rename rekeys the binding and renames the variant in store.enums (migration_planner.rs:621-648). The target index is lowered with the renamed catalog (lower_migration_index with &store.enums, :1201-1211), and the check renderer writes an enum literal as its current variant name (schema/check/render.rs:109-118). So target reads `status = 'Enabled'`. The expected text comes from relabel_index_for_fields, which rewrites only field names (:1285-1310), so it still reads `status = 'Active'`. index_contract_matches_ignoring_name compares predicate_sql as text (:1323). A non-physical transition then fails with UnexplainedSchemaDifference (:1213-1216). If the index-owning entity has no transition, reconcile_rekeyed_view goes through lower_existing_indexes, which renders the old text with the renamed exact_bundle catalog, and `before != *accepted` rejects it too (application_lowering.rs:1913-1923, migration_planner.rs:1691-1713).

Compare predicates semantically, after binding literals through the accepted enum catalog, rather than as text. Alternatively, extend relabeling to map renamed enum variant literals using the rename set. The structural fix is the field-ID and variant-ID bound predicate tree already proposed in xc-architecture-1. Add a planner test for a variant rename that a filtered predicate references.

lowunverifiedr2-query-call-caches-3 · performance · high confidence
Heap-store schema publications never wake the watchdog, so the database-wide runtime root stays cold for all query traffic until an unrelated update call
crates/icydb-core/src/db/session/sql/ddl.rs:248

Failure scenario

A mixed canister has a journaled Orders store and a heap Session store. A controller runs ALTER TABLE Session ADD COLUMN ... or CREATE INDEX on Session. No journal debt is created, so no watchdog tick runs, and C1 stays dropped. Every following #[query], for any entity including Orders, recompiles the full runtime root and re-decodes the Session bundle. SQL and plans are also recompiled under the new root identity. That is roughly 17x the warm cost in the fixture, and it scales with entity count. It lasts until some update call happens to touch the database. For journaled-store DDL the same cold window lasts until the watchdog has folded the whole backlog. For very large schemas, queries in this window trap at the 5B query limit instead of returning a typed error, even though update calls would succeed.

Evidence

SQL DDL invalidates C1 after publishing and does not rebuild it (ddl.rs:248; also 326, 362, 393, 424, 479, 535). The only replicated re-preparation owner is the watchdog Ready branch (startup/driver.rs:52-58). That branch runs only when the watchdog is woken, which requires retained journal debt (commit/guard.rs:290, 334-335). A heap store (no journal tail) gets JournalSequence 0 for its publication batch (commit/schema_publication.rs:685-691) and is published through the live checkpoint (schema_publication.rs:734-744). Batches with sequence 0 are excluded from batch_count (commit/backlog_admission.rs:104-109), so no wake-up is scheduled. Typed apply_schema, migrate_schema and continue_schema_application on heap stores reach the same publish_candidates_atomically, and their stale C1 misses on the root comparison instead. The C1 rebuild compiles every accepted entity in every store (accepted_schema.rs:125-163). The measured cold cost is about 34.6M instructions versus about 2.0M warm for the ~80-entity SQL fixture (docs/design/0.261-entity-rename/i1-read-investigation.md:26-27). The cold compile is charged to per-entity 30B MaintenanceConstructionBudgets (schema/inspection_plan.rs:158, executor/budget.rs:26, 725-736), not to the request's 4.5B instruction units. C37 explicitly excludes later DDL invalidation from its qualification (c37-runtime-preparation.md:21), and startup-readiness.md:120-122 only says Ready is not a warm-cache promise. The difference between heap and journaled stores is not stated anywhere.

Recommendation

Rebuild the runtime root in the publishing update message instead of only invalidating it: call current_accepted_runtime_root_identity() after publication in the DDL and schema-API paths, as the watchdog does. Alternatively, invoke the startup wake-up for publications on stores without a journal. Document the heap/journaled difference, or remove it.

lowunverifiedr2-recursive-bounds-3 · robustness · medium confidence
Source check expressions reach bind_expression with nesting up to ~1020 levels; the binder recurses (and clones) before the 32-level check-tree bound is applied
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/check/bind.rs:588

Failure scenario

A schema proposal whose check or partial-index predicate is [Field(a), Literal(1), Equal, Not × 1021] passes proposal decoding and validation. Applying it recurses about 1021 frames each in clone, bind_expression and drop. With a large bind_expression frame (it inlines bind_compare and literal admission) this can overflow the 1 MiB wasm stack and trap instead of returning DepthExceeded. Proposals come from a trusted caller and the update rolls back, so the impact is an opaque trap rather than a typed rejection.

Evidence

SourceCheckExpr::validate bounds only instruction count (1024) and stack balance, not nesting (icydb-schema/src/expression.rs:181-224). bind_source_check_expr builds a CheckExprV1Input tree iteratively (bind.rs:94-176), clones it recursively (`source_node_boolean(result.clone())`, bind.rs:176), and passes it to bind_check_expr_v1. That runs bind_expression, which recurses per Not/And/Or with no depth guard (bind.rs:588-612), before validate() rejects depth>=32 (bind.rs:86, check/mod.rs:342). The resulting 1000-deep Box chains are then dropped recursively.

Recommendation

Track tree depth in the postfix stack machine (store depth per stack node, reject when >= MAX_CHECK_EXPR_V1_DEPTH) or bound nesting in SourceCheckExpr::validate, so deep inputs are rejected before any recursive clone, bind or drop.

lowunverifiedr2-recursive-bounds-4 · api · high confidence
Generated-predicate depth bound in the model macros is looser than the accepted check-tree bound, so macro-accepted predicates are rejected at runtime schema acceptance
crates/icydb-model-macros/src/predicate.rs:546

Failure scenario

A generated check or partial-index predicate `NOT NOT ... NOT a = 1` with 32 NOTs, or 31 NOTs around `a IS NOT TRUE`, compiles: the macro accepts depth 32. It lowers to Not^32(Compare) with the Compare at tree depth 32, which bind_check_expr_v1 rejects with DepthExceeded during generated-schema acceptance at runtime. The developer sees a startup/schema-application failure instead of a compile-time error.

Evidence

The macro parser descends only on NOT and parentheses and allows depth up to 32 (predicate.rs:357-371, descend at :546-553). Leaf predicates add no level, and `IS NOT TRUE` wraps a Compare in Not without descending (:422-431). NOT IN lowers to Not(Or(...)) (node/index.rs:632-647) with the Not uncounted. The core tree bound counts every node and rejects any node at depth>=32 (schema/check/mod.rs:342, codec/constraint.rs:296).

Recommendation

Count depth in the macro the way the accepted tree does (every boolean node including the leaf, plus the implicit Not for IS NOT TRUE / NOT IN / NOT BETWEEN), with the same bound as MAX_CHECK_EXPR_V1_DEPTH, or share the constant and the counting rule.

lowunverifiedr2-recursive-bounds-5 · correctness · medium confidence
Rendered partial-index predicate SQL can exceed the SQL predicate parser's source-depth budget even though the bound check tree is within its own limits
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/check/render.rs:64

Failure scenario

A generated partial index with predicate `NOT NOT ((a IN (1,...,64)) AND b = 1 AND b = 2 ... AND b = 63)` binds to Not(Not(And[Or[64 compares], 63 compares])): depth 4, 131 nodes, 64 children, all valid. The rendered SQL parses to source depth 64 (Or) + 63 (And chain) + 2 (NOTs) = 129 > 128. The schema is rejected at acceptance with an opaque predicate error, although both the macro and the check-tree limits admitted it. The failure is closed, so nothing is persisted.

Evidence

Generated/proposal index predicates are bound to an AcceptedCheckExprV1 (depth<32, nodes<=256, children<=64), rendered to SQL and persisted as predicate_sql (application_lowering.rs:2009-2023, :2888-2902). The renderer parenthesizes every And/Or child and joins them flat (render.rs:64-77), and emits NOT (...) (:36-39). The predicate parser adds +1 source depth for every extra chain term (predicate/parser/expression/chain.rs:24, :48) and +1 per NOT (:67), and rejects source depth > 128 (expression/mod.rs:43-50). Snapshot integrity re-parses predicate_sql (integrity/nullable_unique.rs:51-61) and rejects with SchemaSnapshotAcceptanceError::Predicate.

Recommendation

Reject at bind time any index predicate whose rendered SQL would exceed the parser's source depth (compute the same max(prefix,right)+1 measure over the bound tree), or persist index predicates in the accepted-tree form rather than re-rendered SQL, so one set of bounds applies.

lowunverifiedschema-catalogs-4 · robustness · high confidence

Failure scenario

A corrupted or hand-crafted persisted bundle whose enum has zero variants, or whose enum payload is Decimal{scale: u32::MAX} or IntBig{max_bytes: 0}, decodes and passes validate_decoded_semantics, then becomes accepted authority. Every value of that type is then rejected at admission (ScalarConstraint / UnknownEnumVariant) instead of the bundle being classified as corruption at load time.

Evidence

decode_enum_type reads `variant_count = reader.read_count()?` and accepts 0 (codec.rs:162-194); AcceptedEnumCatalog::validate() does not check for empty variants. from_initial_definitions rejects `variants.is_empty()` (enum_catalog/mod.rs:301-305). AcceptedFieldKind::has_valid_local_shape (Decimal scale <= max, IntBig/NatBig max_bytes != 0) is enforced only for entity fields and nested leaves (integrity.rs:218, 339). Enum payload kinds (codec.rs:204-205) and tuple/newtype element kinds (composite_catalog/codec.rs:183-195) are never checked, and a newtype element decoded with nullable=true is accepted although lowering always writes false.

Recommendation

In AcceptedEnumCatalog::validate and AcceptedCompositeType::validate, reject empty variant sets and require has_valid_local_shape() on every payload and element kind (and nullable==false for newtype elements), so decoders and constructors accept exactly the same states.

ON t(email) WHERE deleted = false` makes SHOW COLUMNS report email as UNI although duplicate emails exist among deleted rows.

describe_persisted_nested_leaves shows only `leaf.path().last()` with a flat tree prefix (describe.rs:1803), so profile.address.city and profile.city both appear as 'city'. persisted_relation_cardinality returns Single for every Nested source (describe.rs:1864-1869), even when the path passes through ListItems/SetItems/MapValues. classify_compact_column_key (describe.rs:1652-1669) reports SqlColumnKey::Unique for any single-key unique index and ignores index.predicate_sql(), so a unique index restricted by a predicate on another column is shown as column-level uniqueness.

Recommendation

lowunverifiedschema-catalogs-6 · robustness · medium confidence

Mis-wired or hand-written registration: stores A=(D1,I1,S1) and B=(D2,I2,S1) share one SchemaStore. A schema application for B overwrites the single accepted root, whose store_path is then B. validate_register_store_shape rejects a new registration only if its data, index AND schema pointers all equal an existing handle's (registry.rs:134-140, `ptr::eq(data) && ptr::eq(index) && ptr::eq(schema)`). derive_sql_ddl_field_default_persisted_after (lines 602-613) and derive_sql_ddl_field_rename_persisted_after (lines 844-857) rebuild through new_with_primary_key_fields_and_indexes without with_constraint_candidates, yet copy the constraint catalog including its activations. During pending check or not-null activations it is rejected only at publish by validate_activation_transition_from with InternalError::store_invariant (store.rs:2589-2591). Index DDL and ADD COLUMN are rejected via reject_live_activation (constraint.rs:1382-1388). The SQL contract does not document that a pending (possibly long-lived NOT VALID) activation freezes the entity's DDL.

Check for live activations up front in the rename and default derivations (or carry candidates over and allow metadata-only edits), return a typed LiveActivation DDL diagnostic, and document the restriction in SQL_SUBSET.md.

lowunverifiedschema-store-5 · performance · high confidence

crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/store.rs:3990

Failure scenario

A long-lived database accumulates many retired identity owners, e.g. repeated drop and re-create of entities with identity keys, or many entities with identity fields. Latency and cycle cost grow without bound, and large batches get closer to instruction limits.

accepted_schema_authority_ref_for_selection runs `self.validate_identity_state_closure(&bundle)?` even on a cache hit (3990). That calls identity_state_inventory(Effective) (1663-1723): a stable range plus overlay merge, CRC32C and decode of every 104-byte record, then identity_declarations over every field of every entity. current_accepted_schema_bundle_ref is on hot paths: current_accepted_catalog_selection (commit-context prep for writes), pending_relation_activation_for_target (called per store on every delete via relation/validate.rs:94-99), current_accepted_runtime_entity_for_tag, and others. Retired records are retained forever, up to MAX_IDENTITY_STATE_RECORDS_PER_DATABASE = 65,536.

Recommendation

Validate identity closure once when the bundle cache is (re)built and whenever an identity record is written (all writes go through SchemaStore), instead of on every borrow. Alternatively, cache a closure-valid flag invalidated by identity-state writes.

I lowered the severity for three reasons. First, the practical effects are mostly errors or false rejections, cases (a) and (c). Second, the wrong-row case (b) needs an alias that exactly matches a record field with a nested PK-named field, and PublicPrimaryKeyOnly is capped at one staged row (write_policy/model.rs:90-93). That row could already be deleted by PK through the same surface, so there is no real authorization bypass. Third, both entry points are #[doc(hidden)], not wired into any generated endpoint (the generated surface has only update_primary_key/update_bounded, icydb-model/src/build/actor/db/sql.rs:116-210), and untested. lowconfirmedsession-write-1 · correctness · high confidence
Resumable update stamps UpdatedAt with a fresh clock reading on every forward advance, not the frozen continuation timestamp
crates/icydb-core/src/db/session/sql/resumable_update.rs:658

Failure scenario

An operator starts a resumable UPDATE at T0 over 200 matching rows (64-row pages). Page 1 commits in a message at T1 and stamps UpdatedAt=T1. Page 2 at T2 stamps T2, and so on. If a page's response is lost, the retried page is stamped with yet another time T3. One logical operation leaves rows with several distinct audit timestamps, none equal to the frozen T0, which is the inconsistency the 0.213 design explicitly lists as a hazard. The ManagedTimestampRegression gate (line 1037) is also evaluated against the per-advance clock rather than the operation timestamp.
