Job start freezes `let operation_timestamp = Timestamp::now();` (line 445) into both the canonical intent and the continuation (MutationJobEngineContinuation::initial(..., operation_timestamp)). prepare_mutation_job_execution only checks that it is unchanged: `|| continuation.operation_timestamp != intent.operation_timestamp()` (line 568). The forward advance then ignores it: `let advance_timestamp = Timestamp::now();` (658). That value goes to `execute_accepted_structural_update_bounded_prefix(..., advance_timestamp, ...)` (667-674) → `dynamic_write_context(operation_timestamp)` (write.rs:1143) → resolve_update_structural_patch_with_accepted_contract, which writes it into UpdatedAt. WRITE_ADMISSION.md:164-166 says: "Resumable updates store the timestamp in their continuation before the first row commit and reuse it on every retry or resume." The 0.223 design says "one operation timestamp retained across the whole operation".

Recommendation

Use `continuation.operation_timestamp` (already validated equal to the intent's) as the advance timestamp for the scanner's regression check and the bounded-prefix write. If per-advance stamping is intended, change WRITE_ADMISSION.md and remove the dead frozen field so the contract and the continuation stop implying reuse. Either way, add a multi-page test that asserts UpdatedAt values across pages.

Verifier (confirmed): The code does what the finding says: resumable_update.rs:658 reads `Timestamp::now()` on each forward advance and passes that value to the scanner's regression check (line 1040) and to the bounded-prefix writer (lines 667-674). The frozen `operation_timestamp` is only compared at line 568. That contradicts WRITE_ADMISSION.md:164-166. The contract is the stale side, not the code. The 0.233 design deliberately split statement time from managed-write time. It defines a per-advance timestamp and gives the reasons in 0.233-design.md:314-340 ("Every non-replay mutating Forward advance captures exactly one advance_timestamp = Timestamp::now()", "The advance timestamp is not added to canonical intent or the progress record"). The concern table maps "Managed updated_at time" to "One non-replay Forward advance message". 0.233-status.md marks Patch 1 ("Separate frozen statement time from per-advance managed-write time") Complete, and changelog 0.233:232 records it. The frozen field is not dead: it is the statement timestamp that stays part of canonical intent identity (mutation_job.rs:44). The lost-response scenario is also wrong. A retry of a committed page is answered by exact replay (mutation_job.rs:95 `exact_replay`) and does not re-execute or re-stamp. Only a failed pre-commit attempt gets a later timestamp, which the design says is correct. What remains is a stale-contract mismatch: WRITE_ADMISSION.md should be updated to describe statement time vs per-advance managed time.

lowunverifiedvalue-types-error-8 · correctness · low confidence

Failure scenario

a = Float64(-1e40), b = Decimal(5), c = Float64(2.0) give b < a (rank fallback), a < c (strict total_cmp) and c < b (decimal), which is a cycle. Similarly Int64(5) == Nat64(5) by numeric compare, while Text sorts after Int64 and before Nat64. If an ORDER BY expression mixes such variants (e.g. CASE/COALESCE mixing a float field and a decimal literal), sort_by gets an inconsistent comparator: rows are misordered, and Rust ≥1.81 sort may panic (trap) on detected violations.

Evidence

`compare_numeric_or_strict_order(l, r).unwrap_or_else(|| Value::canonical_cmp(l, r))`: first decimal-widened compare, then strict same-variant compare, then cross-variant rank. Used by the executor ORDER BY sorts (db/executor/order.rs:963,978) and grouped page ordering. Decimal conversion fails for out-of-range floats (see the numeric-widening finding), and numerically equal Int64/Nat64 values have ranks 10/20 with non-numeric variants such as Text (18) in between.

Recommendation

Make the fallback consistent with the numeric compare: order all numeric-coercible variants in one numeric class using an exact comparison that never returns None for finite values, with a deterministic tie-break, before falling back to rank. Or reject mixed-variant ordering keys at planning time.

lowconfirmedxc-architecture-2 · correctness · medium confidence
Migration planner relabels filtered-index predicates one rename at a time, so chained or swapped field renames compute a wrong expected predicate
crates/icydb-core/src/db/schema/migration_planner.rs:1285

Failure scenario

One migration renames `nickname` to `name` and `name` to `display_name`, with `before.fields()` ordered [nickname, name]. The index predicate is `(name IS NOT NULL) AND (nickname = 'x')`. The first step turns it into `(name IS NOT NULL) AND (name = 'x')`; the second turns both occurrences into `display_name`. The correct target is `(display_name IS NOT NULL) AND (name = 'x')`, so the texts differ. A valid metadata-only migration is rejected as UnexplainedSchemaDifference, or, when physical, forces an unnecessary full index rebuild under a new generation. A name swap (a<->b) fails the same way regardless of field order.

Evidence

relabel_index_for_fields iterates `before.fields()` in order and calls `clone_with_renamed_field_path_root(old, new)` once per renamed field (migration_planner.rs:1285-1310). Each call re-parses and rewrites the text predicate (predicate/render.rs:19-30). The result is compared by exact text equality to the freshly lowered target (index_contract_matches_ignoring_name, :1312-1324). A mismatch sets semantics_changed, which fails a non-physical transition with UnexplainedSchemaDifference (:1212-1216) or makes infer_and_rekey_index miss the binding (:1261-1263).

Recommendation

Short term: apply all renames at once, parsing once and mapping every field operand through a single old-to-new name map in one rewrite_field_identifiers pass. Structural fix: resolved by the field-ID-bound persisted predicate from the previous finding, after which rename needs no predicate rewrite at all. Add a migration test with a chained rename and a swapped rename.

Verifier (confirmed): The relabeling logic is as described. relabel_index_for_fields walks before.fields() and applies one clone_with_renamed_field_path_root per renamed field (migration_planner.rs:1285-1310). Each call re-parses and rewrites every occurrence of old_name (predicate/render.rs:19-30, 55-67). The index key is relabeled by FieldId, so only the name-based predicate text is affected. For a swap (net id1 a->b, id2 b->a) the result always collapses to a single name, and for a chain it collapses whenever the head rename is visited first. The comparison is exact text equality (:1312-1324). These migrations can actually be reached. Field rekeys are applied in sort_key order by `from` (icydb-schema/src/migration.rs:256-258). rekey_scoped_exact only rejects a target that is still bound (source_binding.rs:140). So nickname->name plus name->display_name succeeds (name sorts first), and a swap through a temporary name (a->tmp, b->a, tmp->b) also passes binding. The consequences are overstated, though. In the binding-found path, semantics_changed matters only when the migration is not physical (:1212-1216). When physical, every index is re-stamped with the new generation anyway (:1220-1224), so there is no 'unnecessary rebuild'. In the non-physical case the valid migration fails closed with UnexplainedSchemaDifference, or infer_and_rekey_index misses the binding (:1261-1263). No state is corrupted, and splitting the renames across separate migration versions works around it. It is a fail-closed spurious rejection that needs chained or swapped renames of predicate-referenced fields, so I rate it low rather than medium.

The wasm32 `next_component` returns `(u128::from(ts & 0xFFFF) << 64) | u128::from(self.sequence)`, where `sequence` is a heap counter that resets on upgrade. Recommendation

Document that generated ULIDs on IC are unique but not unpredictable. Optionally seed the wasm generator from `raw_rand` during startup (same async step as the cursor key) and use a CSPRNG for the random component.

On every miss, insert_shared_query_artifact walks the whole key and plan graph with artifact_retained_bytes under a charged PreparationWork interval, then inserts and attaches lazy-retention handles (cache.rs:94-112, 243-273). scripts/ci/check-executor-no-production-panics.sh:95

Failure scenario

No present defect. A future `.expect()` added in commit/recovery.rs, journal/codec.rs or the startup driver, where a trap in a timer or post_upgrade recovery page can wedge startup, would pass CI because only executor/ is gated.

Evidence

The find root is `crates/icydb-core/src/db/executor` (script lines 95-103). A crate-wide scan with the same awk logic currently finds only const asserts (schema/migration_validation.rs:42-46, migration_execution.rs:104-109, database_format/convergence.rs:32, startup/receipt.rs:45), two infallible expects (access/plan.rs:337, query/builder/scalar_projection.rs:77) and one misuse assert in the facade future (crates/icydb/src/db/session/request.rs:87).

Recommendation

Widen the gate's root to crates/icydb-core/src/db and crates/icydb/src, keeping an explicit allowlist for const-context asserts. The codebase already satisfies this, so widening costs nothing today.

infounverifiedxc-contracts-10 · docs · high confidence

crates/icydb-core/src/db/relation/reverse_index.rs:429

Failure scenario

Tooling written against REF_INTEGRITY looks for a constraint name in relation write errors and finds none, so it must resolve the name from the accepted schema by constraint ID. There is no functional defect, but the two contracts disagree.

Evidence

`write_violation` builds `mutation_constraint_violation(AcceptedConstraintFactContext::write_admission(method, fingerprint, entity_tag, constraint_id, DiagnosticConstraintKind::Relation, mutation, None))`, which carries numeric facts only (error/mod.rs:651-657). REF_INTEGRITY.md:310-311: 'Accepted and pending relations retain their stable constraint ID and name in typed runtime or validation diagnostics.' WRITE_ADMISSION separately says no runtime schema strings are included in diagnostics.

Recommendation

Change REF_INTEGRITY §7 to 'stable constraint ID (name resolvable via accepted-schema introspection)', consistent with WRITE_ADMISSION's numeric-only diagnostic rule.

crates/icydb-core/src/db/index/store.rs:962

Failure scenario

Each new call site with its own closure adds a full copy of the traversal and merge code to the canister wasm. This is the kind of retained-size growth the wasm-footprint audit tracks, but I measured nothing here.

Evidence

`visit_journaled_entries_in_range<E>(.., mut visit: impl FnMut(..))` contains six traversal loops (live asc/desc, canonical asc/desc, and a merged `ordered_overlay_entries` asc/desc). The inline `|entry| entry.key()` closures inherit the parent's generics, so `OrderedOverlay` and the inlined StableBTreeMap iterator bodies are instantiated again for every caller. `DataStore::visit_keys_in_bounds` / `visit_journaled_entries_in_bounds` / `try_visit_range_with_row_preflight` (data/store.rs:734-1065) follow the same pattern. There are about 45 production call sites of these generic visitors.

Recommendation

Measure with the existing Twiggy `monos` capture. If significant, make the traversal cores non-generic over the visitor (`&mut dyn FnMut(&K, &V) -> Result<bool, InternalError>`), as the executor already does in `execute_kernel_row_scan_with_readers`.

crates/icydb-core/src/db/executor/terminal/page/coordinator.rs:802

Failure scenario

Cursor-paged scans add several hundred to about a thousand instructions of pure accounting per row. That is small next to decode, but it is paid on every row of every production page. The figure is an estimate; the compiler may constant-fold part of it.

Evidence

`begin_production_scalar_page_unit` recomputes `scalar_candidate_inspection_reservation` (11 `PageWork::one(..).merge(..)` over `[u64; 20]`, 872-927) plus the output reservation for every candidate, copies the whole observed array via `current_execution_budget_usage()` before and after, and then runs the preflight, `from_execution_delta` and `commit_observed` loops over all 20 resources (526-567). Each scanned row also makes 6-10 separate thread-local `RefCell` budget charges (row_runtime.rs:55-57, 83-91, 310-327; physical.rs:1090), each of which also charges the request-scope counter.

Compute the reservation once per stream (it depends only on `access_entry_bound`), and batch per-row charges into one bundle call (a pair helper, `charge_current_execution_budget_pair`, already exists).

infounverifiedxc-security-8 · api · high confidence

crates/icydb/src/guards.rs:21

Failure scenario

An app allowlists an analytics principal with guard(allowlist-based fn) to read one reporting entity via `icydb_query`. That principal can read every entity through the trusted SQL lane (full scans allowed), and with `introspection = true` also SHOW MEMORY/STORES and EXPLAIN with literal values. This matches the documentation ('complete admitted generated SQL query lane') but is easy to misuse.

Evidence

ReadAuthorizationContext has only `caller` and `surface`. authorize_sql_read runs before parsing, so a guard cannot tell `SELECT * FROM Payments` from `SELECT * FROM PublicPosts`. The provided `allowlist` helper also ignores `surface`, so one allowlist guard reused for both `icydb_schema` and `icydb_query` grants SQL read to schema readers.

Recommendation

Consider passing the parsed statement's entity name and statement family to the guard (parse first, since parsing is already bounded), or add a prominent warning and a surface-aware allowlist helper.

Area summaries

Commit protocol, recovery, rollback, schema publication

commit1 high4 low1 info

The commit unit is carefully built. Markers sit in a framed, CRC-checked, strictly canonical control slot. Publication is compare-and-swap style: prepare, then backlog admission (Gate 2), then publish only if the control proof is unchanged. The database commit sequence only increases and is bound into every journal batch. Recovery runs in three stages (Replay, Fold, Verify). Its progress cursor is volatile and tied to the marker's identity. Re-appending a batch is idempotent (identical-bytes detection plus a fold-watermark skip). The fold step validates everything before it changes anything, and the marker is cleared only after its own effects are verified. Persisted decoding is bounded and fallible, and production commit code has no unwrap/expect/panic apart from deliberate traps. The main defect: journal batches are routed to their store through the live (overlay) accepted catalog, while rows are prepared against the canonical one. So after a metadata-only entity rename published while writes are still waiting to be folded (routine, because background folding lags writes), background folding can never fold the older batches. The startup driver records a terminal failure and writes eventually back up, until an upgrade forces full startup recovery. The second concern: Replay applies some fallible steps without the preflight its comment claims, and any failure traps. A trap inside the recurring watchdog retries forever and leaves no startup failure receipt. The rest are latent hazards or doc/code mismatches: a tautological schema-fingerprint check, no post-encode length check on the marker, no Drop safety net on CommitGuard, an ambiguous error when a commit fails after its marker is written, and production-only admission paths the unit tests don't exercise. Overall risk is moderate: the core atomicity protocol looks sound for internally produced states, and the problems cluster around background folding and diagnosability of recovery.

Strengths
  • Control-slot framing (magic/version/length/CRC32C), strict canonical re-parse (encoded_len must equal byte length), trailing-byte rejection, u32 length bounds, try_reserve on decoded vectors, and a 16 MiB cap on every persisted marker path (store/mod.rs, control_slot.rs, marker_envelope.rs, marker.rs).
  • Marker publication is compare-and-swap style: prepare_set_if_empty encodes once and captures a control-proof digest; Gate-2 backlog admission measures the exact envelopes it will append; publish_prepared_marker re-reads the slot and refuses if the marker is non-empty or the proof changed (store/mod.rs:318-367, guard.rs:273-291).
  • The database commit sequence is only incremented at publication, checked against every batch, and kept in the permanent prefix across clears, so the global fold order (database seq, allocation, journal seq) is well defined (store/mod.rs:327-335, recovery.rs:717-722).
  • Recovery is staged (Replay/Fold/Verify) with a volatile continuation tied to the marker id. Losing the heap state safely restarts at Replay: re-publishing skips batches whose fold watermark has already passed them, and identical-byte re-append is idempotent (recovery.rs:111-124, 652-663, 2383-2401; journal/store.rs:753-781).
  • Fold does all preparation and validation before any stable write (row transitions, overlay retirement, tail retirement, cardinality maintenance, delta watermark), then applies mechanically. The canonical-predecessor reader overlays batch-final rows, so same-batch unique swaps get correct release proofs (recovery.rs:936-1026, runtime_entity_catalog.rs:35-108).
  • Before clearing the marker, recovery verifies the effects the marker owns: exact row bytes, rebuilt derived index entries for row puts, schema/job/identity publication, database-control ops, fold coverage and empty tails. It walks records in reverse, keeping the last writer per target (recovery.rs:2529-2594).
  • A normally returned apply error keeps the marker and registers the watchdog wake-up in the same message. Missing lifecycle wiring fails before any marker is published (guard.rs:269-341, 359-385).
  • The commit control region is kept apart from the schema-control BTreeMap: the control slot ends before page 257, where CONTROL_START_PAGE begins (store/mod.rs:167-175, schema/control_store.rs:23).
Not covered

I did not check instruction or allocation limits numerically; that needs the IC measurements the contract itself says are missing. What I found: one fold per message handles up to 16,384 records / 16 MiB, and Verify re-derives index entries for every row put in the marker, all in one message. Journal store internals were covered only for append idempotency (chunking, retirement, raw_batch_prefix repair path). The schema store's publication and checkpoint internals (identity transitions, activation transition rules, live_schema_checkpoint.rs) I only read enough to confirm idempotency on replay. I read the executor's commit_window.rs only where it touches the guard, not its preflight logic. I did not read the integration suites (testing/integration/recovery_closeout.rs etc.) or the prepare/tests/images.rs fixtures. rollback.rs and CommitApplyGuard are test-only (cfg(test)), so I treated them as non-production. Two things I noticed outside this unit and did not pursue: (a) database_format/convergence.rs refuses registry changes while a marker is retained (reconcile_current_registry returns store_unsupported), and require_retirable_tail refuses to retire a store whose tail still has retained debt. So adding or removing a journaled store in an upgrade while a marker or debt remains can wedge startup until the code is reverted. (b) Physical migration drains convergence from inside a request (application.rs:1106-1115), which is a documented control-lane exception to 'only the startup driver folds'.

Journal store/codec, mutation & resumable jobs, overlays, write context

journal-jobs4 medium3 low3 info

The persisted-format layer in this unit is strong. The journal codec rejects bad input safely: every length is bounded, the SHA-256 envelope fingerprint is checked before any record is materialized, only version 1 is accepted, and batch shape is checked strictly (duplicate targets, publication-family ordering, sorted index chunks, exact Identity-range proofs). The mutation-job and resumable-job record codecs are equally strict. The real risks sit in the lifecycle code around those codecs, not in the byte formats. (1) Mutation-job preparation treats every catalog-lookup failure as a terminal AcceptedSchemaChanged restart and saves it. That includes the MigrationInProgress gate and recovery-pending admission errors, so healthy jobs are ended during migrations. (2) Direct writes to the progress store (cancel, terminal restart) skip recovery admission. If a commit marker with a MutationProgress effect is still pending in the same message, they can change the record that recovery expects as its exact `before`, and recovery then fails permanently. (3) The durable access-state revision goes up twice on every startup, so no resumable job or exhaustive cursor over a journaled store survives an upgrade. That contradicts DURABILITY.md, which says journaled sources are what cross-upgrade jobs rely on. (4) Heap-store proofs can match again after an upgrade (ABA): the heap generation resets, while the cursor key and database incarnation persist. Journal append and retirement are careful overall, but append still has fallible steps after its first stable write, and there is a prefix-repair path that current code cannot reach in production. Overall risk: medium. No reachable data corruption was found in normal operation. The worst case, a permanently stuck recovery, needs an unexpected error after the marker is written.

Strengths
  • Journal codec (journal/codec.rs) rejects bad input safely at every step: bounded u32 lengths, total length checked against the header, domain-separated SHA-256 fingerprint checked before record decode, record count capped at 16k, exact trailing-byte check, version 1 only with no fallback decoder.
  • Batch-shape validation is thorough and canonical: duplicate row targets, the AcceptedSchemaPublish-at-position-0 rule, strictly sorted per-entity index chunks with deletes before puts, validation-index sets tied to their job, and exact contiguous Identity-range allocation proofs.
  • JournalTailStore separates preflight from apply for retirement (prepare_batch_retirement / apply_prepared_batch_retirement), keeps exact aggregate tail accounting with overflow/underflow checks, and treats re-appending identical bytes as idempotent.
  • Journal integrity inspection runs in bounded pages and can resume; its duplicate batch-ID checkpoint (CheckingBatchIdentity) finds duplicates without keeping an unbounded ID set.
  • MutationJobRecord / ResumableJobRecord check the full state/receipt closure on construction, transition and decode. Exact replay is checked before budget charging. Marker-bound progress uses exact before/after byte compare-and-replace, and recovery applies it idempotently.
  • Entity mutation revisions come from monotonic journal sequences, so Verify's revision check cannot be fooled by ABA on journaled stores. New entities are conservatively initialized to the store-wide data revision.
  • compare_proof_and_advance checks the proof before and after the page and re-validates the current record inside replace_resumable_job_if_current, so nested or stale advances fail safely.
  • The ordered overlay merge is small and well tested, and live and tombstone sets are kept disjoint by every writer, so shadowing semantics are consistent.
Not covered

I did not trace end to end: ResumableForwardScanner::next_mutation/finish and how the bounded-prefix writer advances the checkpoint when the packer rejects a candidate (Verify's full clean scan should catch any rows Forward skipped, but I did not prove the checkpoint logic itself); the full convergence/fold engine in commit/recovery.rs and commit/convergence_candidate.rs beyond the journal-store API they call; how the positioned-overlay publication/retirement callers in data/index/schema stores use it; MutationProgressRecordOp encoding in integrity/progress_store.rs and marker.rs; the typed-binding code in session/write that consumes dynamic_write types. I only skimmed journal/tests.rs. I did not run cargo test or clippy (per ground rules), so the findings come from reading the code, not from runs.

Persisted rows, structural fields, data store, row codec, database format

data4 high7 low1 info

The byte-level codecs in this unit are careful. The row envelope, ByteReader, Structural Binary walkers, canonical value storage and database boot record all use checked arithmetic, depth limits, exact-length and trailing-byte checks, and version-1-only gates. Nothing allocates from a declared count until a skip pass has proved it fits in the bytes. Production code in scope has no panics. The real defects are at seams between the codecs and the rest of the system, not in the primitive parsers. (1) Several lazy or byte-level readers treat legitimately absent historical slots as corruption. This covers the scalar fast path, resumable-update patch checks and nested-path reads. After a routine `ALTER TABLE ADD COLUMN ... DEFAULT`, WHERE filters, OCTET_LENGTH and resumable UPDATEs fail with Corruption errors on rows written before the ALTER. (2) The value-storage walker used for nested record paths still has an old grammar for tag 0x84, while the canonical encoder writes enums as 0x84 plus a 13-byte header. As a result, any projection, filter or grouping on `record.member` fails whenever the record contains an enum member. (3) Record composites store member names as map keys, but the migration planner offers record-member rename as a metadata-only change, which likely makes populated rows unreadable. Everything else is lower risk: by-kind decode paths that skip admission-level checks on corrupt bytes, error-class misclassification, a non-atomic fresh-boot probe, and dead retired-slot machinery. The biggest gap in the tests is historical-layout rows: the data-layer tests contain no rows stamped with an older layout version.

Strengths
  • Row envelope decode (codec/mod.rs) enforces MAX_ROW_BYTES before parsing, exact magic, format version == 1 only (no fallback), non-zero layout stamp, and an exact payload length that must end at the end of the buffer. serialize_row_payload checks the total size before calling the payload writer and verifies the exact written length.
  • ByteReader advances only after checked_add and a bounds check both pass, so a failed read never moves the cursor.
  • Structural Binary / value-storage walkers are depth-bounded (64 / MAX_ACCEPTED_RECURSIVE_DEPTH), use checked arithmetic throughout, enforce trailing bytes, and never allocate from a declared count before skip traversal proves the items exist (try_reserve only after skip; reserve_one per item in the single-pass walkers).
  • Canonical-wire (enum/composite/CatalogValue) fields are decoded and then fully re-admitted (sorted/unique sets and maps, enum type/variant IDs, composite shape, decimal scale), which makes the persisted form canonical in practice.
  • Big-integer minimal-magnitude and sign canonicality, Decimal scale domain 0..=28, Date domain, and float finiteness are all checked at decode.
  • Exact physical slot count is validated against the admitted layout window (history_floor..=current) before any slot traversal. Historical fill semantics live in one place (StructuralRowContract::historical_slot_value), and the direct/dense/sparse readers use it correctly.
  • Database boot record: magic plus CRC32C plus strict version, and virgin-memory checks covering every registered durable role. The commit-control replacement grows memory before the boot record is written, so publication cannot write out of bounds.
  • DataStore journaled overlay cardinality delta stays consistent across live publish, fold put/delete and exact retirement; the live and tombstone sets are kept disjoint.
  • No unwrap/expect/panic/assert in non-test code anywhere in scope (only a compile-time const assert).
Not covered

I did not read key_taxonomy.rs (EncodedPrimaryKey / RawDataStoreKey codec internals); I only traced the parts data/key.rs relies on. I skimmed but did not fully read the unit-test files (store/tests.rs, key/tests.rs, binary/tests.rs, accepted/tests.rs, primary_key_component/tests.rs, reader tests), apart from checking coverage for historical layouts and for enums inside value-storage views. I did not verify the migration-feature publication path end to end for record-member renames, so that finding has medium confidence. I also did not check how mutation jobs classify the Corruption errors from the resumable-update finding. No cargo build or test runs were done, per the ground rules; every finding is from static tracing. Out of scope and only touched: the commit/journal/recovery internals beyond the data-store fold/publish calls, and cursor token codecs.

Index keys/store/scan/range envelopes, access paths, key taxonomy

index-access1 critical2 high4 medium4 low

I read the index-access unit statically and did not run cargo. Most of the machinery is carefully built: index-key framing and decoding are strict, bounded and fallible, and no production code in scope uses unwrap/expect/panic. The low/high sentinels provably enclose every valid component and primary key, because value tags are 1..25 and primary-key tags are at least 0x01. The main scan paths check for an empty envelope before calling range(). The canonical/live/tombstone overlay merge is correct. The integer, float, decimal, bigint and text encoders preserve value order. The serious problems are at the edges between modules. 1. Critical: unique validation rebuilds the conflicting row's key without applying the filtered-index predicate. A batch that moves unique membership across a partial unique index passes at write time but fails deterministically when the journal is folded or replayed. That can stall convergence and block all work after the next upgrade. 2. High: Timestamp is signed (i64) but its index component is written as raw big-endian bytes. Negative timestamps sort after positive ones, so range scans and ordered traversal silently return wrong results. 3. High: index keys cap the primary-key suffix at 63 bytes, but composite primary keys can be up to 254 bytes. For example, an entity keyed by two 29-byte user principals cannot insert rows once it has any secondary index. Medium issues: Principal index order does not match Principal::cmp. Oversized query literals surface as InvariantViolation errors instead of results. The stable B-tree page size (~133 KiB per node) and the heap-resident prefix-cardinality metadata both scale badly. Overall risk is high because of items 1 to 3.

Strengths
  • Raw index-key decode (decode_index_key_frame / decode_raw_index_store_key_segments) is fully bounded and fallible: size window, per-segment zero/overlong checks, component-count cap, trailing-byte rejection; persisted PK decode likewise validates tags, lengths, principal length and composite count.
  • Range sentinel construction is sound: Low=[0x00]/High=[0xFF;4096] components and [0x00]/[0xFF;63] PK suffix strictly enclose all real components (value tags 1..25) and PKs (tags >=0x01), and inclusive/exclusive lowering matches the BOUNDARY contract table (>, >=, <, <=).
  • visit_raw_entries_in_range / visit_canonical_raw_entries_in_range guard with envelope_is_empty before std/stable BTreeMap::range, avoiding inverted-range panics; continuation anchors are checked for envelope containment and strict directional advancement.
  • Ordered overlay (canonical + live + tombstones) merge is correct in both directions, and insert/remove keep live and tombstones disjoint.
  • Order-preserving encoders for Int64/Int128 (biased), f32/f64 (finite, -0 normalized), Decimal (sign bucket + exponent + digits + terminator), IntBig/NatBig (length-prefixed magnitude, inverted for negatives), and escaped/terminated Text are correct and have pairwise property tests.
  • Query-side encoding admits capacity against the construction budget before allocating; unique validation caps its probe at 2 and has explicit batch-override release logic for moved/deleted conflicting rows.
Not covered

I skimmed access/shape_facts.rs and read only parts of access/path.rs and access/plan.rs. Most test modules I did not read in full: key_taxonomy/tests.rs, the store.rs and cardinality.rs test modules, envelope/range/scan tests, and the predicate compile tests. I did not run any tests or builds. Items owned by other reviewers I did not review in depth: executor consumption of index streams (stream/access/scan.rs, physical.rs, covering decode), cursor token decode, the relation reverse-index module, schema-side admission of indexable field kinds, and the planner's range extraction beyond what the traces needed. Findings 1, 6 and 7 come from static tracing only and have not been reproduced.

Accepted schema store, codec, snapshot, wire/format, runtime roots

schema-store1 high2 medium4 low1 info

I found no decoding bugs in the schema-store codec layer. The snapshot codec (codec.rs, codec/*, wire.rs) is a direct, bounded, fallible v1-only mapping: it enforces the 512 KiB ceiling, caps every count by both the remaining bytes and a per-collection maximum before allocating, limits recursion depth and check-expression node counts, rejects trailing bytes, and runs full acceptance validation after decoding. Production code in scope has no unwrap/expect/panic apart from one index guarded by an invariant. Root publication is sound: two checksummed slots, a CAS re-read before the inactive-slot write, and a bundle hash-bound to its root, with the inactive slot and bundle removed afterwards. The real risks are in how SchemaStore shares its stable map. (1) Cardinality-generation records (namespaces 5/6/7) live in the same map as the schema entries. The publication retain/position sweeps treat them as stale schema entries and iterate or delete them all in one message. Their number grows with rows times index prefixes, so online DDL on a large store can run out of instructions, and the schema fold during recovery can trap again on every retry. (2) Identity-state owners are keyed by (entity_tag, FieldId), but FieldIds are dense and reused. Dropping an identity field (or a field before one) and later adding an identity field is rejected as Identity corruption. (3) init_journaled uses the upstream BTreeMap::init, which silently re-initializes a non-empty schema allocation whose header magic is bad. The control store guards against exactly this; the schema store does not. There are also performance hazards on hot paths: heap-store identity allocation fully re-decodes and rewrites the live checkpoint on every write, and every bundle borrow re-scans the identity inventory. Finally, the persisted-format inventory has gaps and there are some dead durable surfaces. Overall risk: moderate. Findings 1 and 2 are reachable through normal schema evolution, not only through corruption.

Strengths
  • Snapshot codec is a direct numeric-tag mapping with no reflected DTO layer. It rejects version != 1 with a typed incompatibility error, rejects bad magic and trailing bytes, caps every count by both remaining bytes and a collection maximum before Vec::with_capacity, and bounds recursion (MAX_ACCEPTED_RECURSIVE_DEPTH, MAX_CHECK_EXPR_V1_DEPTH/NODES).
  • Decode always ends in validate_schema_snapshot_acceptance (dense field IDs and slots, layout window, PK closure, index/relation/constraint integrity), and encode validates first, so invalid authority cannot be persisted or loaded.
  • Accepted-root publication uses two CRC-checked slots, with a re-read CAS immediately before the inactive-slot write. The bundle is bound to its root by bundle_hash and semantic fingerprint, and retain removes the inactive slot and bundle, which prevents silent rollback to an older root.
  • Fold is split into prepare (fallible) and apply (mechanical). Apply contradictions trap, keeping canonical mutation atomic per message.
  • The shared control tree defends against the infallible upstream loader: it checks BTR/BTA magic, verifies a CRC header, enforces a namespace closure and a record cap, and reloads the tree for every operation so interleaved namespace writers cannot use stale roots.
  • The live checkpoint is CRC-protected, bound to its store key, re-encoded canonically on decode, and reserved keys are checked for hash collisions.
  • No unwrap/expect/panic in production code across the reviewed files (one invariant-guarded index noted).
  • Strong tests: a canonical byte fixture with round-trip, truncation and deceptive-length tests, exact depth-boundary tests, and a malformed persisted-format corpus.
Not covered

I did not run any tests, builds or benchmarks, so the instruction-cost estimates in finding 1 are estimates, not measurements. Only skimmed: types.rs and types/query_projection.rs (query-literal canonicalization), and the snapshot.rs activation-transition helpers (with_promoted_*, with_aborted_*). Not reviewed in depth, since they are owned by other units: the identity_state.rs codec internals, the cardinality_generation.rs codecs, the enum/composite catalog codecs, source_binding encode/decode, constraint_validation job codec, and application_store. I did not trace the offline-migration path (migration_* modules) to check whether FieldId renumbering can happen on non-empty entities that carry identity state. That could turn finding 2 from a rejection into a data hazard. I also did not confirm the exact ErrorCode that Corruption/Identity maps to in the startup terminal classifier.

Schema migration planner/execution/records/transforms/lineage

schema-migration2 high3 medium4 low

The migration subsystem is carefully built. It has one singleton durable record with a closed phase machine and exact compare-and-replace marker ops. Persisted codecs (ICYSMIG1/ICYSLIN1/ICYIDST!) are bounded, CRC-checked, canonical and re-encoded before use. Every Advance re-plans against accepted authority and checks the candidate head, and index/relation candidate generations stay isolated. Transforms, casts and findings are typed, and the planner rejects most destructive or unexplained shapes, because the existing lowerer requires exact field/index counts and unchanged kinds. The main risks are liveness and lineage-maintenance defects, not decoding bugs. (1) The per-entity "first row too large" check (`page.rows == 0`) is applied against a page-global leftover budget. A multi-entity physical migration can therefore fail deterministically with store_unsupported inside RewritingRows or FinalValidation. Those phases cannot be aborted, and the database-wide gate is already closed, so the database is permanently gated. (2) Lineage accepted_head/digest is only maintained by migration-aware generated applications. SQL DDL, constraint-activation abort, non-migration builds and plan-less generated changes leave lineage stale, which contradicts the 0.218 design. After that, every future migration and adoption fails with StaleAcceptedHead/MissingMigration, and nothing recovers it. (3) Dangling lineage entries (removed or omitted entities) make `current_proposal_lineage_is_applied` permanently false. Status then never reports Applied, and the plan-carrying successor fails startup with Downgrade. (4) A Rejected migration cannot be retried after a data fix. A generated canister's submission identity is a pure function of its source, and findings beyond the first page cannot be seen. Several smaller transform/finding issues are listed as low.

Strengths
  • Persisted migration record and lineage codecs are bounded before allocation (count caps, 2 MiB caps, try_reserve_exact), CRC-checked, magic/version-1 only, and re-encoded for canonical equality; no legacy fallbacks.
  • SchemaMigrationRecordOp::validate enforces immutable identity (database, heads, submission/plan digests, transitions, entities, staged indexes), a closed may_transition_to matrix and monotonic progress at both apply and recovery time.
  • Each Advance recompiles the plan from accepted authority and checks the recorded candidate_head (CandidateMismatch/PublicationRaceLost), so a changed Wasm, library or proposal fails closed instead of guessing.
  • Candidate index/reverse-relation keys are generation-scoped IndexIds; abort cleanup deletes only candidate generations and advances a durable cursor over every visited entry.
  • Each rewrite page binds candidate row bytes, derived keys and the next cursor into one commit marker whose journal records carry the plan digest; recovery replays them only under a record that permits that digest.
  • Planner resolution fails closed on swaps, occupied targets, wrong stores, version gaps/downgrades, meaningless bumps and companion transitions with unexplained changes; reconcile via the ordinary lowerer rejects field/index count and kind/nullability changes.
  • Checked-cast matrix is exact (sign, overflow, precision, null typed reasons); unique/relation/constraint validation runs on the transient candidate row before any accepted row is rewritten.
  • No panic!/unwrap/expect in production code of the reviewed files; errors are typed and never string-matched.

Schema proposal application, lowering, source binding, field kinds

schema-application3 high4 medium

The schema-application unit is carefully built and fails closed. Existing-head lowering only accepts changes that resolve through immutable source bindings and match accepted authority exactly. Kind, nullability, write policy, codec, index shape, relations and named-type definitions must be identical. Only defaults, display metadata, generated check/targeted-rule additions or edits, and explicit removals proven over empty domains get through. There is no runtime fallback to generated EntityModel/IndexModel. Persisted records (application records, source bindings) are version-1 only, bounded, checksummed and canonical-re-encode checked. I found no panics in production paths. The main risks sit where this unit meets lifecycle and durable state, not in the compatibility decisions themselves. (1) A missing maintained cardinality is treated as store corruption. Every accepted-schema publication makes it transiently missing, and the startup driver persists that as a terminal failure. Cardinality is only rebuilt once startup is Ready, so a quick upgrade that adds a generated check can wedge startup. (2) The 64-slot application-record store evicts terminal receipts by hash order, including the deployed generated submission's receipt that readiness depends on. (3) A Pending application's precomputed exact candidate head makes the job impossible to finish or abort after any other publication. (4) Generated reconciliation rejects every entity with any live activation, including SQL-owned ones, and persists that as terminal while the only way to finish the SQL activation needs Ready. Smaller issues: migration lineage left stamped with a head that was never reached after an abort; entity names admitted that the runtime root then rejects; unbounded nested-leaf expansion during lowering.

Strengths
  • Compatibility decisions are exact and identity-based: lower_existing_fields rejects any kind, nullability, write-policy, storage-decode or leaf-codec change (application_lowering.rs:1806-1813). Indexes must re-lower byte-identically against the current snapshot (1913-1924). Relations must match exactly (2130), and enums/composites must equal accepted definitions (1478, 1512). Additions are fail-closed, not guessed.
  • No runtime fallback to generated EntityModel/IndexModel anywhere in the unit; the generated lane is sealed against removals (application.rs:650, application_lowering.rs:596).
  • Explicit removals require one unambiguous source-bound owner, no live activations or candidates, and proven-empty row, user-index and reverse-relation domains before publication (application.rs:2375-2618).
  • Durable application records are version-1 only, magic + CRC32C + canonical re-encode checked, with bounded counts and strict Pending/terminal state closure (application_store.rs:372-408, application_receipt.rs:272-313, 399-419). Record replacement is compare-and-swap with legal transitions only (application_store.rs:151-186).
  • Source-binding catalog decode is bounded (2 MiB), canonical, and proves one-to-one identities and closure over the bundle before use (source_binding.rs:1273-1348).
  • Targeted-rule semantic edits keep the constraint ID. Abort keeps the prior operation and source binding, as WRITE_ADMISSION.md requires (application.rs:587-633).
  • Generated check proofs use a bounded single-page scan. Findings reject before publication, and incomplete proofs become a durable journaled pending job only on journaled stores (application.rs:2282-2367).
  • No panic!/unwrap/expect/assert in production code of the reviewed files; indexing is by positions derived from the same collections.

Catalog-native schema mutation, SQL DDL bridge, constraints, cardinality, checks

schema-mutation1 high4 medium4 low1 info

The schema-mutation unit is carefully built. The activation lifecycle is a closed, fingerprinted state machine, and publication only accepts exact one-step lifecycle transitions. The persisted codecs (validation jobs, cardinality header/cursor/count records) are bounded, checksummed or fingerprinted, and version-1 only, and no production panics turned up. The main risk is at the edge between activations and physical index state. First, aborting a SQL unique-index activation (DROP INDEX while pending) leaves the entries it already staged in the index store with no owner. Every later complete-domain index DDL on that entity then fails as 'store corruption', and a generated schema that removes the entity or one of its indexes becomes a terminal startup failure. Second, complete-domain staging charges its projection work budget, and walks rows, across the whole store rather than just the target entity, so index DDL and empty-domain proofs stop working once a multi-entity store grows past about 262k index entries. There are also several semantic defects: the integrity check evaluates pending targeted-rule replacements as if they were accepted (false corruption findings); the Verify revision fence is store-wide, so a busy store can stop an activation from ever promoting while unique activations block inserts; and check activations that depend on more than 32 fields can never persist findings. Cardinality generation construction looks correct and conservative.

Strengths
  • Persisted formats in scope (ConstraintValidationJob, cardinality header/cursor/count records) are strictly bounded before allocation (bounded counts, try_reserve_exact, max byte sizes), checksummed or fingerprinted, accept exactly version 1, and return typed IncompatiblePersistedFormat or Corruption errors; tests cover truncation, trailing bytes, and future-version rejection.
  • Activation lifecycle is a closed state machine (EnforcingNewWrites -> Validating -> promote/abort). Every activation is fingerprinted over identity, semantics, state, base schema fingerprint, and epoch. permits_live_activation_transition_to plus SchemaStore::validate_activation_transition_from only accept exact single-step transitions, and all other schema changes fail closed while an activation is live.
  • Constraint IDs use a non-reusing allocator: abort and removal retire the ID, and targeted-rule semantic edits keep the ID on purpose.
  • The unique-activation write barrier is conservative: it blocks Insert/Replace and key-dependent Updates, deletes remove candidate entries, and candidate keys are isolated by physical generation (the activation epoch), so staged keys never collide with accepted or future generations.
  • Every runner step (start, page, restart, promote) publishes the job together with the schema candidate through one commit marker, so a trap mid-message rolls back cleanly without partial activation state.
  • Check evaluation implements SQL three-valued logic correctly with bounded work (node, depth, and literal-byte caps). Targeted-rule traversal is iterative, with depth, node, operation, and path budgets. Floats are finite by construction, so NaN ordering cannot come up.
  • Cardinality build reads only the canonical (folded) view and binds to incarnation, allocation, accepted root, accepted index set, and fold watermark. It restarts into the alternate slot on any drift, and it ignores candidate or unknown user-index keys instead of miscounting them.
  • Dense field and index removal remaps constraints, relations, and index layouts by exact lineage and fails closed on any dangling reference. Field-ID density is enforced by snapshot acceptance, so the DDL field-ID allocator is safe.

Enum/composite catalogs, identity, fingerprint, describe/info, schema integrity, registries

schema-catalogs1 critical2 medium4 low1 info

I found no panics, unwraps or generated-model fallbacks in production code in this unit. Two of the eight findings are serious. First, a record-member rename in a versioned migration is treated as metadata-only, but stored record values use member names as map keys. After such a migration, every existing row that holds the renamed record fails to decode and is reported as corruption. This contradicts PERSISTED_FORMAT_INVENTORY, which says editable member names are never identity authority. Second, DESCRIBE / SHOW COLUMNS renders composite types with no depth limit and no cycle check. Recursive composites, which the lowering pipeline accepts and tests, recurse until the stack overflows and the call traps; acyclic tuple chains that reuse a type grow exponentially. Third, SchemaProposal checks entity names more loosely than the runtime root does (up to 128 bytes, and uniqueness is case-sensitive), so a hand-built proposal can make every session operation in the database fail with a corruption error. The rest is low-severity: decoders accept states that construction rejects, a few DESCRIBE misreports, the registry accepting partially shared store handles, and IndexName names that can collide. The persisted codecs are otherwise well done: bounded, fallible, version 1 only, strict on ordering and uniqueness, and verified against root hash and fingerprint. Enum values and equality keys are stored by stable IDs, so variant and type renames are safe. Overall risk is moderate-to-high, driven by the migration rename defect, which ordinary use of the generated migration plans can hit.

Strengths
  • Every persisted catalog codec (enum `ICYDBENX`, composite `ICYDBCMP`, bundle `ICYDBAEB`, root `ICYDBAER`) is bounded, checks magic and version (version 1 only), requires strictly increasing ids, rejects duplicates and trailing bytes, limits nesting depth (MAX_ACCEPTED_RECURSIVE_DEPTH), and re-validates after decode.
  • Bundle and root publication holds up: two root slots with CRC32C; the bundle's SHA-256 is bound into the root; the semantic fingerprint is recomputed and compared on every verified decode; new candidates are encoded and decoded again to prove a byte-exact match before publication; a torn slot is tolerated, but two valid slots at the same revision that differ are rejected.
  • Enum values are stored by (EnumTypeId, EnumVariantId), and the unit-enum equality/index key uses the same ids, so variant and type renames do not affect stored data or index keys.
  • Existing named types must match the proposal exactly (`matches_exact_definition`, shape equality), so an ordinary proposal cannot add, remove or change an enum variant or a composite shape under stored data.
  • Type removals re-validate catalog closure and check that no retained entity field or nested leaf refers to the removed type; the bundle then re-validates defaults, check literals and targeted rules.
  • Constraint and relation id allocators never reuse ids, use checked arithmetic, and are cross-checked by integrity (no id above the high-water mark).
  • describe/info/runtime_entity_catalog read only accepted snapshots and catalogs; I found no fallback to generated EntityModel/IndexModel. Runtime entity routing checks the store path and source binding, and rejects duplicate tags or paths across stores.
  • No panic!/unwrap/expect/assert in non-test code of the scoped modules; every failure is a typed InternalError.
Not covered

Query planner, access choice, plan validation, covering, continuation, ordering

query-plan1 critical1 high1 medium2 low2 info

I read the query-plan unit statically, since I couldn't build or run tests (read-only review). The core planner is carefully built. Filtered-index eligibility and nullable-index completeness use conservative implication proofs that fail closed. Expression-key paths are kept out of residual stripping. Candidate ranking breaks ties deterministically by index name. Reranking and cardinality tie-breaks rebuild each alternative through the same single-index planner, so they can't introduce routes the planner would reject. Construction work is budgeted almost everywhere, and production code has no unwrap, expect, panic or assert. The dangerous part is the set of "strip the predicate because the access path already proves it" optimizations. That layer has two confirmed ways to return wrong rows: - **Critical:** the primary-key "half-open range" proof treats `id >= a AND id < b` as exactly covered by `KeyRange{a,b}`. But KeyRange end bounds are inclusive at execution, so the predicate and filter expression are dropped and the row with id == b is returned, counted, or UPDATEd/DELETEd. - **High:** residual stripping for `Ne` and `NotIn` ignores the comparison's coercion. So `name = 'Alice' AND LOWER(name) <> 'alice'` on an indexed `name` returns the 'Alice' row. Two more issues: - Grouped validation accepts canonical grouped ORDER BY with mixed per-term directions, but grouped finalization sorts group keys with one direction (medium confidence). - The primary-key strip also drops the whole filter expression without checking predicate coverage (latent). Overall risk is high until the two stripping bugs are fixed. A property test comparing `eval(predicate, row)` against `access_contains(row) && eval(residual, row)` across access shapes and coercions would have caught both.

Strengths
  • Filtered-index eligibility and index completeness (nullable fields, nullable path ancestors) are proven through one conservative, fail-closed implication engine (planner/index_select.rs); unknown required clauses invalidate the proof, and an unsatisfiable query is correctly treated as a vacuous proof.
  • Residual stripping deliberately never uses expression key items: key_field_at() returns None for accepted expressions, so LOWER/UPPER prefix and range bounds can never discharge raw-field predicates.
  • Index-key literal lowering is centralized in key_item_match.rs; LOWER is the only expression admitted for TextCasefold lookup, and casefold_text and lower_text share one implementation, so index keys and evaluator semantics match.
  • Reranking by residual burden and exact-cardinality tie-breaking rebuild each alternative with the ordinary single-index planner and reject composite or mismatched outcomes, so they cannot bypass eligibility or completeness checks.
  • Ordering contracts are shared by the planner, covering and route (DeterministicSecondaryOrderContract), with explicit PK-tail stripping, Full-vs-Suffix classification, a full-order requirement for multi-lookup and branch-set paths, and an empty-non-unique-prefix guard.
  • Continuation signatures bind the access plan, predicate/filter, order, projection, and accepted schema revision/root fingerprint; grouped cursor-policy checks are enforced once at a single owner.
  • Budget accounting (PreparationWork/ConstructionBudget) is applied to essentially every allocation and proof step, and no production unwrap, expect, panic or assert was found in scope.
  • Branch-set and prefix candidates prune excluded values only when the exclusion's coercion matches the key item, which avoids a casefold/strict mixup at access-construction time.

I didn't review the unit-test files in depth, only enough to check what is and isn't covered. expr/ and semantics/ are out of scope; I read only the residual derivation in semantics/logical.rs and semantics/grouped_strategy.rs where they decide plan correctness. I didn't verify end to end whether the typed builder always emits NumericWiden for signed-integer equality (the input to info finding 6). Per the ground rules I built and ran nothing, so every finding comes from static tracing.

Plan expressions & semantics, query expr/filter, scalar expressions, numeric

query-expr2 high5 medium2 low

The query-expression layer is carefully built. It has one compiled-expression IR, arithmetic goes through a single checked numeric boundary, NULL propagates the same way in the evaluator and in literal folding, expansion of searched CASE is bounded by content size and charged to the request budget, input depth, node and byte limits are enforced up front, and the production code in this unit has no unwrap, expect or panic calls. The serious problems are semantic. They show up where two execution lanes or two rewrite stages disagree, and in the fixed-point Decimal arithmetic this unit relies on. (1) Evaluating a division can panic: `i128::MIN / -1` inside Decimal division is reachable from a plain SQL literal in WHERE while the plan is being built. (2) When SQL NOT is compiled into the two-valued predicate runtime, rows with NULL are admitted, while the expression lane correctly excludes them. So `NOT (x = 5)` and `NOT LIKE` return, update or delete NULL rows depending on which lane the planner picks. (3) In scalar WHERE, CASE is rewritten into AND/OR, but AND/OR evaluate both sides, so the standard CASE guard against division by zero stops working. (4) In nested-path filters, a missing subfield aborts the whole row, which breaks OR. (5) Decimal multiplication never normalizes or rounds, so ordinary products of scale-18 values or AVG results fail with 'overflow'. Medium issues: numeric-widen comparisons silently fail outside the Decimal range (tiny or huge floats, Nat128 values of 2^127 or more). The planner types integer arithmetic as Integer, but it is always Decimal at runtime, so `LEFT(name, LENGTH(name)-1)` passes planning and then fails. The affine rewrite in grouped WHERE turns integer literals into Decimal ones, which changes how the comparison is coerced. REPLACE with an empty search string behaves unlike other SQL engines, and text functions can blow up in size without being charged to the budget. Overall risk is high for query correctness. None of the findings corrupts persisted state by itself, but the NOT/NULL issue also affects which rows DELETE and UPDATE select.

Strengths
  • Single checked numeric boundary (db/numeric) with explicit Overflow/NotRepresentable taxonomy; U256 kept in its own fixed-width domain with no implicit widening.
  • Compiled-expression evaluator applies SQL NULL propagation consistently for arithmetic, comparison, unary NOT and the Kleene AND/OR truth tables; searched CASE and the special single-arm forms stay lazy.
  • Literal-only folding (preview.rs) swallows evaluation errors and leaves the subtree unfolded instead of failing planning, so folding cannot introduce errors on empty tables.
  • CASE-to-boolean expansion is size-bounded (8 arms, 256 units) and charges every clone and wrapper to PreparationWork before building it; normalization charges its steps and temporary bytes.
  • Caller input is depth-, node- and byte-admitted (MAX_QUERY_INPUT_DEPTH=128, 4096 nodes, 2 MiB) before recursive lowering; the SQL parser enforces MAX_SQL_EXPR_DEPTH as well.
  • No unwrap/expect/panic in non-test code in this unit's scope; the text functions use saturating/try_from conversions throughout.
  • The type inference that shapes planning checks both operand subtrees before letting NULL short-circuit, so a NULL operand cannot hide a bad sibling.
Not covered

Only skimmed or not read: plan/semantics/grouped_strategy.rs, group_distinct.rs, group_model.rs, access_projection.rs, pushdown.rs; plan/expr/projection.rs, aggregate_input.rs, cleanup.rs, canonicalize/ordering.rs (sort_bool_children details), type_inference/{source,aggregate,case,mod}.rs; the schema-side literal canonicalization called from filter.rs (canonicalize_filter_literal). I did not fully trace whether the literal left behind by the affine rewrite fails predicate validation or passes it and matches no rows (finding 8 has medium confidence for that reason). I did not check Candid decode-depth limits for FilterExpr before admission. Nothing was compiled or run (per the ground rules), so all findings come from static tracing. The Decimal primitive lives in icydb-schema, outside this unit, but I reviewed it where this unit's semantics depend on it.

Query intent/builder/admission/fingerprint/explain, predicates, cursors

query-intent3 high1 medium2 low2 info

I reviewed the query-intent unit statically; nothing was built or run. The continuation-token layer is the strongest part. HMAC-SHA256 covers the framing and payload and is checked before any value is decoded, the decoders are bounded and reject anything malformed, and scalar tokens are tied to the mode, the query signature (including bound values), the database incarnation, the accepted root and entity, the route pin, the window, the order terms and the page envelope, which exhaustive mode extends with the revision proof. The main risks are in public read admission, which in practice is looser than the contracts say. First, SortRequiresMaterialization can never fire, because the admission summary always reports `materialized_sort = false`. Second, any secondary-index route counts as bounded, including the planner's fallback that scans a whole index with no bounds. As a result a public page can do an effectively full-table scan on every call, limited only by the hard execution budget. Rows are not visibly wrong in the common case. Instead, cost grows with data size and pages eventually fail with budget errors, which is exactly what READ_ADMISSION and RESOURCE_MODEL say must not replace the planner's proof. Separately, the shared plan-cache key identifies literal values by a 128-bit XXH3 digest with a public seed whenever a filter has no parameter template. If an attacker can make one value's digest match another's (a second preimage), one caller would be served a plan built for another caller's filter; that part is unverified. Predicate normalization and simplification look semantically sound and conservative, but the AND simplifier restarts from the beginning after each rewrite, doing quadratic work on caller input with no metering. It runs before admission, on every filtered call.

Strengths
  • Cursor envelope: magic, version, variant and length are all covered by HMAC-SHA256, verified with a constant-time compare before any semantic decode; wrong variant, version or length, and trailing bytes, all fail closed (cursor/token/codec.rs:159-199).
  • The value codec used for cursors and stored job literals is bounded: nesting capped at 128, list/map counts checked against remaining bytes, big integers must be minimal with consistent signs, decimal scale is validated, and floats are checked (cursor/token/value.rs).
  • External Base64 decoding is strict: no padding, no nonzero trailing bits, and the length is capped before any allocation (cursor/string.rs).
  • Scalar tokens bind mode, signature, incarnation, accepted root, entity fingerprint, route pin, total limit and page profile, and order terms; exhaustive mode folds the revision proof into the signature, and tokens carrying lookahead state are rejected (session/query/dynamic.rs:282-356, 581-584).
  • The continuation signature binds actual literal values (tested in fingerprint/shape_signature). The access-plan hash frames children in postorder with counts, and the predicate fingerprint is SHA-256 over the full length-framed encoding.
  • Input admission checks depth before descending, shares one node/byte budget across all request components, and applies to the trusted lane too; dropping a deeply nested DynamicQuery filter is iterative, not recursive.
  • Predicate simplification is conservative: Strict comparisons require the same value variant, numeric widening compares exact decimals, numeric literals are rewritten only when integral, and OR-to-IN collapse requires the same field and coercion with scalar literals.
  • The reduced SQL predicate parser is depth-bounded, including the source depth of flat AND/OR chains; malformed persisted index predicates map to a typed corruption error.
  • No panic!/unwrap/assert in production code in scope (one infallible expect, noted below). No matching on error strings.

Executor aggregates, grouping, projection

executor-aggregate4 high4 medium2 low1 info

The executor aggregate/group/projection layer is carefully engineered in several respects. Resource accounting is centralized and fallible: every retained group, DISTINCT key and hash bucket is charged before a try_reserve allocation. Canonical key hashing is stable and frozen by test vectors. Decimal and float values are normalized for equality. The ordered-group fold fails closed on out-of-order input, and production code contains no panic, unwrap or assert. However, the generic grouped fold and its page finalizer have diverged from the dedicated grouped COUNT(*) path, and several of those divergences produce wrong results or failures under realistic use. (1) The generic hash fold's owned-key probe path never looks up existing groups. Any direct GROUP BY on an enum, unit, collection or composite field (reachable through the public fluent API, which does not check groupability) therefore creates one group per row. (2) Generic and ordered page finalization build the continuation cursor from the projected row, not the canonical group key. Non-identity SQL projections therefore fail with an internal invariant error, or resume at the wrong group. (3) The unbounded generic finalizer always sorts ascending, so ORDER BY key DESC without LIMIT comes back ascending. Mixed-direction group-key ORDER BY is admitted but executed with one leading direction. (4) Zero-key global DISTINCT fails on any NULL in a nullable target field. Smaller issues: grouped continuation never seeks and re-counts pre-cursor groups against the cumulative max_groups cap; zero-key aggregates return no row on empty input, unlike the global-DISTINCT and SQL paths; grouped FIRST/LAST depend on traversal direction and access path; the DISTINCT group seek hard-codes MissingRowPolicy::Error; grouped limit errors are not distinguishable as grouped-domain errors. Overall risk for grouped queries is high. The dedicated COUNT(*) path is noticeably more correct than the generic path, so parity tests between the two would catch most of these.

Strengths
  • Grouped state accounting is centralized in ExecutionContext (contracts/grouped/context.rs): group, byte and DISTINCT caps are checked before mutating counters, and allocations go through try_reserve_* after conservative backing charges (group/hash.rs). Failures are typed budget errors rather than OOM traps.
  • Canonical group-key equality and hashing are consistent. Decimal values are normalized in both hash (value/hash.rs write_to_hasher) and equality (Decimal PartialEq, canonicalize_value). Floats are finite with -0.0 normalized. Borrowed-probe hashes are built with the same list framing as owned keys, and a debug_assert cross-checks them. Stable hash vectors are frozen by test.
  • The ordered group fold (OrderedGroupFoldState::apply_row) checks key monotonicity and returns an executor invariant error on Ordering::Greater instead of silently merging or splitting groups. It also releases live-state reservations on group close.
  • No panic!/unwrap()/expect()/assert! in production paths of the reviewed modules. Slice indexing is guarded by length matches or by construction.
  • Per-group DISTINCT handling is correct: value-dedup DISTINCT skips NULL, FILTER is applied before DISTINCT admission, and the per-group and total caps are enforced in a deterministic order with tests (context.rs).
  • Projection DISTINCT is well structured. The adjacent strategy is selected only when projected slots form a leading order-equivalence prefix; otherwise a replayable global build with an offset is used. Cursor boundaries track the last duplicate of an emitted key.
  • Covering projection applies the scan-time offset only when row presence is planner-proven (shared.rs covering_scan_window gating), so stale index entries cannot shift pages.
  • The scalar MIN/MAX extrema fast path is restricted to non-nullable fields (load_plan.rs aggregate_execution_route_plan), avoiding a NULL-first early-stop bug.

I checked missing-row policy and offset/window handling, but not index-component decoding or the correctness of reorder_covering_projection_pairs. projection/eval/scalar.rs is mostly reader adapters; expression semantics live in query/plan/expr (another unit) and were not reviewed. The session-layer encoding of the DISTINCT output offset for global replay was not verified. No code was executed; all findings come from static tracing only, since I did not run cargo.

Executor streams, scans, pipeline, kernel, terminal/pagination

executor-stream2 high3 medium5 low

I reviewed the executor-stream unit statically; nothing was built or run. The low-level pieces are well built: the key-stream combinators (merge, flat merge, intersect, distinct, concat), the physical primary and index range leaves, strict primary-key resume, the scan loop and the page-unit reservation accounting. The code fails closed with typed invariant errors, uses checked arithmetic, and charges temporary memory before reserving it. The main risks are in how continuation interacts with index streams that are not ordered by primary key. (1) On resumed pages ordered by an indexed field over an IN-list lookup (IndexMultiLookup), a page fetch hint caps each branch at limit+1 keys counted from the start of the branch. The branch streams have no resume anchor, so rows past that cap are silently dropped and pagination can end early. This is a high-severity wrong-results bug. (2) DISTINCT over the same IN-list shape feeds branch-ordered keys into a de-duplication adapter that requires primary-key order, so the query fails with an invariant error. (3) The intersection stream reports no per-pull access bound, so any primary-key-ordered live page whose plan is a general intersection fails once the page-work envelope is active. (4) The scan loop pre-allocates a row vector sized from the caller's LIMIT, so a large LIMIT on a trusted or typed query can panic with capacity overflow (a trap on wasm32) or inflate the heap. (5) Resumed pages ordered by a non-primary-key field never reposition the physical stream, so each page rescans from the start of the range and deep pagination runs into the hard budget. Smaller issues: a lookahead row is scanned but thrown away (it breaks the contract that an exactly-full final page gets a null continuation, and makes one residual-retry check dead code), a latent seek bug in PrimaryRangeKeyStream, an offset inconsistency that cannot be reached today, and uncharged construction work in the branch-ordered prefix path. Overall risk is moderate to high: storage cannot be corrupted from here, but pagination can silently return incomplete results for a realistic query shape.

Strengths
  • Key-stream combinators check that each input stays in order (StreamSideState::validate_monotonicity) and suppress duplicates in both pairwise and heap-based merges. Heap ordering and ties between children are deterministic (composite.rs:360-373).
  • Temporary memory for combinator topology is charged before allocation, and allocations are fallible (reserve_stream_slots, intersect_all, FlatMergeOrderedKeyStream::try_new_with_comparator). The page-bound reasoning for FlatMerge is documented and holds up under inspection.
  • Primary-key continuation is applied to the raw range before the first pull (PrimaryRangeKeyStream::resume_strictly_after). It is strictly exclusive in both directions and marks the stream exhausted when the resulting range is empty. Materialized leaves apply the same boundary before paging (physical.rs:2073-2081).
  • ObservedOrderedKeyStream wraps outside the budget and limit wrappers, so a published physical anchor can never pass a key the row loop did not examine.
  • The exact-intersection probe checks that the number of physical entries equals the cardinality proof and rejects missing-row witnesses. This catches stale index state instead of hiding it. Falling back to the first child of an intersection is safe because composite access keeps the full predicate as a residual filter (index_select.rs:154).
  • Index-range LIMIT pushdown is correctly turned off for resumed pages (route.rs index_range_limit_pushdown_allowed = !requires_anchor || !applied), because index anchors are never threaded through.
  • Page-unit accounting reserves the whole inspection unit before any storage is touched, and commits the observed amount against that reservation (begin/finish_production_scalar_page_unit).
Not covered

Grouped fold, ordered-group, and grouped-cursor internals: they live in executor/aggregate, and I only read the pipeline wrappers. Covering-projection streams (covering.rs, which uses FlatMergeStream) and projection DISTINCT materialization. Route-planner internals beyond the paths I traced. The cursor token codec and the index envelope validation internals. Whether the raw data-key byte order matches PrimaryKeyValue Ord for variable-length key types such as Principal; this is a key-taxonomy question and a critical assumption behind merging PrimaryRange streams with materialized vectors. How index-prefix cardinality metadata is maintained; branch pruning trusts exact counts of zero. No tests or builds were run, so every finding comes from static tracing. For findings 1-3, the planner actually choosing the IndexMultiLookup or general-intersection shape was inferred from planner code, not executed.

Executor planning, mutation, prepared plans, budget, authority, explain

executor-core5 low1 info

The executor-core unit is careful work overall. No production code in scope uses panic!, unwrap(), expect() or assert!. The only deliberate stop is the documented ic_cdk::trap when a preflighted commit apply contradicts itself, and a trap rolls the marker back with everything else. Budget counters only ever grow: they saturate on overflow, keep charges for rejected work, and charge semantic bundles all-or-nothing across both the execution scope and the request scope. The mutation commit window finishes every fallible preflight before it publishes the marker. That preflight runs against a complete final-row overlay and enforces duplicate-key rejection, fixed work-unit caps and an identity-range preflight. Prepared plans freeze accepted-schema authority, the plan cache is keyed by runtime-root identity, revision and index visibility, and failed lazy builds are never cached. Route planning fails closed: residual filters, DISTINCT and descending non-unique secondary prefixes all fall back to materialized execution. The main weakness is instruction accounting. Every tracker measures instructions from its own first sample rather than against the whole message. So a mutation-job advance or a maintenance allowance always gets a fresh 30B allowance, whatever the message has already spent, and read executions do not sample at all until their 64th charge. Both can turn the intended typed exhaustion into an IC trap. Smaller issues: some checks after marker publication can return Err for a write that recovery will later commit; the commit path publishes index Ready for any store it touched, which is a latent hazard; the verbose EXPLAIN pushdown label is hard-coded. Native tests cannot catch the instruction problems because the counter stub always returns 0. Risk is moderate: I found no path to data loss or corruption, and the defects are about budgets and diagnostics.

Strengths
  • No panic!/unwrap()/expect()/assert! in production code across planning/, mutation/, prepared_execution_plan/, budget.rs, authority/, explain/ and the root executor *.rs files (verified by grep); failure paths return typed InternalError, and RefCell borrow conflicts map to invariant errors rather than panics.
  • HardExecutionBudgetTracker is monotonic and saturating, keeps charges for rejected work, and try_charge_budget_bundle preflights both the execution and request scopes before committing either, with a unit test proving atomicity (budget.rs:547-576, 1473-1518).
  • Nested read executions share the installed tracker instead of resetting it, request-scope counters survive derived sessions, retries and failures (tested at budget.rs:1520-1596), and MaintenanceConstructionBudget makes the first exhaustion sticky so a swallowed charge failure cannot turn into a published success.
  • The commit window finishes all fallible preparation before marker publication: from_row_ops seeds a complete final-image overlay, staged index overrides are merged in order with committed range scans, per-row and fixed work units are capped (16,384), identity ranges are preflighted for the whole owner set, and the instruction watermark is sampled just before begin_commit (commit_window.rs:548-601).
  • Commit apply wraps row and state-effect application in enforce_preflighted_apply, which traps in production, so a contradiction rolls back the whole message instead of leaving partial state.
  • The constraint scheduler rejects duplicate entity-qualified targets, requires each staged row op to match the evaluated after-image byte for byte, and evaluates unique-activation write barriers before row-local constraints.
  • Prepared plans bind AcceptedContinuationIdentity to the accepted schema authority, reject handoffs that lack the static planning contract, and publish lazy residents only after a successful build, with retention accounting that declines oversized entries without breaking execution.
  • Route planning fails closed: a residual filter forces materialized fallback before scan-budget hints can apply, DISTINCT and descending non-unique secondary prefixes force a materialized boundary, index-range limit pushdown under a residual filter is capped at 256 with bounded widening and an unbounded fallback in the kernel, and DISTINCT projection suppresses the scalar page before routing.
Not covered

I only skimmed or did not read: explain/descriptor/{load.rs, shared/mod.rs, shared/predicate.rs, aggregate.rs}, which I sampled only for the route-facts freeze and order-pushdown lines; planning/route/order_pushdown.rs; planning/route/contracts/*; planning/route/terminal.rs; planner/execution/{load_scalar, aggregate_non_count, aggregate_grouped}.rs; and the prefix-set / covering stream middle of covering.rs (about lines 140-930). I did not audit the in-scope unit tests beyond budget and maintenance. Several correctness questions end in modules outside this unit, and I traced them only far enough to rule out an executor-side bug. Those are: unique-conflict staleness handling (index/plan), delete-safety re-verification against the overlay (relation), the plan-cache staleness key (session/query/cache.rs, sampled), PK-order merge of multi-prefix streams (stream/access), projection DISTINCT, and the per-message count of mutation-job advances (session).
