Session write path, requests, accepted-schema session state, caches

session-write1 medium4 low3 info

I found no data-loss, corruption or wedge bugs in this unit. The core write owner, execute_accepted_structural_mutation_batch_inner (write.rs:1116-1595), holds up well under tracing. Every frontend (dynamic, typed-binding, mixed-batch, SQL, resumable) goes through one owner. That owner captures one accepted runtime root and one store, enforces the 4,096-operation, 64-entity and 16 MiB staged-byte bounds, and freezes one operation timestamp. It passes every after-image through the accepted constraint scheduler, which rejects duplicate entity-qualified keys (constraint_scheduler.rs record_target_key). Identity allocations publish only with a successful marker; a failed precommit leaves them unpublished, and the tests confirm this. Relation existence, delete-restrict and uniqueness are delegated to the final-overlay commit preflight, which re-resolves the current accepted fingerprint as a backstop. The accepted-schema root cache is revalidated on every access against each store's (revision, fingerprint, bundle hash) root, so it cannot serve stale schema after a publication. The findings are semantic mismatches with the contracts, not durability bugs: (1) resumable updates stamp UpdatedAt with a fresh clock reading on each advance, even though the continuation stores a frozen timestamp; (2) the structural lane rejects an explicit Default on database-owned insert fields, which SQL accepts; (3) replacing an existing row regenerates non-PK generated Ulid/Timestamp fields; (4) replace on a missing key lets callers write a generated ULID/Timestamp primary key themselves. Overall risk is low to moderate. Test coverage is extensive (recovery interruption points, identity ranges, overlay semantics, batch bounds), but nothing tests timestamp stability across resumable pages, generated fields under replace, or structural Default.

Strengths
  • One owner (execute_accepted_structural_mutation_batch_inner) handles every write frontend, so admission, constraint scheduling, staged-byte bounds and commit directives cannot drift between lanes.
  • Duplicate entity-qualified targets are rejected across every combination of operation kinds before commit (AcceptedMutationConstraintScheduler::record_target_key); insert conflicts, update-on-missing and delete-on-missing all fail closed.
  • Identity allocation is contained within the statement: a per-entity IdentityStatementCursor with checked ordinals, a post-materialization value/key/slot cross-check (validate_identity_materialization), treating a collision with a generated key as corruption, and publishing ranges only with the marker.
  • The accepted runtime root cache is revalidated against the compact per-store roots (revision + fingerprint + bundle hash) on every hit. After compiling, it re-captures the incarnation and roots before publishing, so the cache stays correct even without explicit invalidation.
  • Typed bindings are checked against incarnation, revision, fingerprint, layout generation and per-field accepted IDs/slots on every use. A stale binding returns None rather than writing to a remapped field.
  • Public result conversion and the exact Candid response-size check (mixed batch) run inside precommit, before the marker is opened, as ATOMICITY/TRANSACTION_SEMANTICS require.
  • Production code in scope has no panic!/unwrap/expect; all indexing is into vectors whose indices were just computed; errors are typed rather than string-matched.
  • The bounded prefix-packing mode is staging-exact and never admits a partial candidate; it is used only for update-only resumable pages, so an identity allocation cannot leak on a PageFull break.

I did not read the interiors of relation target-existence and delete-restrict checks (validate_delete_relations_with_reader, prepare_row_commit_with_context, PreflightStoreOverlay), the unique-index preflight, journal/marker publication or recovery replay. Those belong to the executor/commit units; I checked only that the session layer hands them a correct final-overlay batch, and I relied on the existing tests for the overlay semantics. ATOMICITY.md was not read in full. The session files mutation_job.rs, resumable_job.rs, read_set.rs and the session/query and session/sql trees were out of scope, except where they call the write owner (resumable_update.rs forward advance, SQL insert/update lowering). I skimmed rather than read the ~7k lines of write.rs test modules. Builds and tests were not run, per the ground rules; the CommitRowOp before-image canonicalization contract with commit prepare was not verified end to end.

Session query & SQL execution, resumable updates, SQL lowering

session-sql1 high2 medium8 low

The session-sql unit is well built overall. Write policies default to rejecting anything they don't recognize. The public primary-key and bounded proofs are conservative. Exact UPDATE uses a cap-plus-one selection limit plus a primary-only scan budget. RETURNING bounds are checked before commit. The resumable-update continuation format is bounded, CRC-checked, strictly version 1, and fails closed on any mismatch, and Forward pages commit target rows and the progress record atomically. The most serious problem is in lowering. `ILIKE` and `LOWER(field)` text predicates get two different meanings: the predicate lane casefolds both sides, but the expression lane (`STARTS_WITH(LOWER(x), '<raw prefix>')`) does not fold the literal. Resumable UPDATE evaluates its scope only through the expression lane, so it can report `Completed` after updating a different row set (often nothing) than exact or prefix UPDATE with the same SQL. The second high-risk issue is the SQL compiled-command cache. It is bounded by entry count only (1024 entries). Each entry keeps the full SQL text twice, plus decoded literal payloads such as blobs up to 1 MiB, so trusted INSERT traffic with large literals can push the canister heap past its memory limit. Medium issues: (1) a resumable job becomes permanently stuck in Active when one matching row deterministically fails write admission, for example a row-local CHECK constraint. It cannot be acknowledged or cancelled, and it holds a shared progress slot. (2) The hidden public SQL DELETE entry points skip the shared prepare/normalize phase, so the policy proof and the executed query can bind the same identifiers differently. The remaining findings are low: doc/code mismatches (placeholders, targetless DROP INDEX, positional INSERT), unknown columns reported as internal invariant errors, undocumented asymmetric write bounds, and Verify being unable to finish on busy entities.

Strengths
  • Resumable continuation codec (resumable_update.rs:250-371) is bounded (2 KiB), CRC32C-checked, strict version-1, validates phase/verify-revision consistency and checkpoint entity tag, and every advance re-binds entity tag, target allocation identity, schema fingerprint, scope and patch fingerprints and batch-policy identity (validate_resumable_update_bindings).
  • Forward checkpoint discipline is careful: a matching row's key only becomes the checkpoint after the packer requests the next mutation (pending_candidate_checkpoint), so a refused candidate is never skipped; target rows and the next progress record commit through one marker (WithMutationProgress); exact replay is served before any budget charge.
  • Batch-policy identity is a const FNV fold over every numeric bound and component revision, with a test proving each input participates.
  • Write-shape policies are conservative: PK-only requires a complete primary-key equality conjunction with no duplicates; bounded requires canonical ascending PK order, 0 < LIMIT <= 100 and no OFFSET; exact update uses a cap+1 selection limit plus an executor-enforced cap+1 scanned-key probe over a primary-only plan; RETURNING row/byte bounds are validated inside precommit, before commit.
  • Generic mutation dispatch rejects UPDATE (MutationRequiresExplicitUpdateIntent), and the query surface rejects every write family before compilation.
  • Compiled-command cache keys include surface, entity path, runtime-root identity, schema revision/version/fingerprint and raw SQL; execution re-checks that accepted authority is still current; bound invocations bypass the text cache.
  • No production panic/unwrap/expect in scope; lowering charges PreparationWork budgets throughout.
Not covered

These were only skimmed or not read: sql/lowering/aggregate/* (strategy, terminal, grouped validation, command binding), select/projection.rs, select/order.rs, select/aggregate.rs, analysis.rs, copy.rs. In session/query: cardinality_tiebreak.rs, grouped.rs, projection.rs, cache/template.rs, and the rest of cache.rs. In session/sql/execute: global_aggregate.rs, aggregate_plan.rs, aggregate_request.rs, metadata.rs, write_returning/projection.rs, and the rest of exact_aggregate.rs (index-metadata fast paths). The dynamic scalar-page cursor/token flow was read but not verified in depth. Several things sit outside this unit and were not reviewed: the CanonicalMutationIntent and MutationJobRecord codecs and progress-store CAS semantics (db/mutation_job.rs, db/integrity), journal revision prediction correctness, and how the query planner picks index access for casefold predicates. Nothing was built, run, or tested. Every finding comes from static tracing.

SQL parser, DDL frontend, input, shared SQL utilities

sql-parser5 medium6 low

The SQL frontend (lexer, parser, DDL binder, input validator) is mostly careful. Lexing takes linear time and has hard limits: 2 MiB of input, 32,768 tokens and 1 MiB per blob literal. Quoted identifiers and unknown bytes are rejected with typed errors. The main expression parser limits recursion depth and binary-chain length, and SqlExpr is dropped iteratively so deep trees cannot overflow the stack on drop. A shared node/byte/depth budget is checked after parsing, and the BETWEEN rewrite is checked before its left side is cloned. The biggest defect is that the ORDER BY arithmetic sub-parser (arithmetic.rs) has no depth guard at all. A deeply parenthesised ORDER BY term therefore overflows the stack instead of returning ExpressionDepthLimit: a trap on wasm and a process abort on native hosts. Beyond that, most issues are about semantics and the contract. (1) Identifier-scope normalization quietly rewrites record paths whose middle segment matches the entity name or alias, so reads and writes can hit the wrong column. (2) Scientific and hex numbers are silently split into a number plus an implicit projection alias (`price * 1e3` returns price*1). (3) DDL accepts dotted column names. (4) CREATE INDEX predicate identity compares raw token text, so IF NOT EXISTS and duplicate-contract checks are fragile, especially after RENAME COLUMN re-renders every stored predicate. (5) Flat AND/OR chains longer than about 127 terms are rejected as 'depth', which contradicts READ_ADMISSION.md. (6) SQL_SUBSET.md has drifted from what the parser accepts and requires, e.g. the mandatory EXPECT/SET SCHEMA VERSION clauses. Overall risk is moderate. Nothing found here corrupts durable state directly, but wrong-column rewriting in UPDATE/DELETE predicates is a realistic way to mutate the wrong rows.

Strengths
  • The lexer is single-pass and linear, with hard input limits (2 MiB + 4 KiB), a token limit (32,768) and a decoded-blob limit (1 MiB). String-literal slicing only cuts at ASCII quote positions, so it is UTF-8 safe. Quoted identifiers, `--` comments and unknown bytes all fail with typed errors.
  • The main expression parser (parse_sql_expr/prefix) limits both recursion depth and binary-chain length, and the tests cover both limits.
  • `impl Drop for SqlExpr` uses an iterative cleanup (model/cleanup.rs), so deep or rejected trees cannot overflow the stack while being dropped.
  • validate_sql_statement_input checks depth before it descends and shares one node/byte budget. The BETWEEN rewrite is pre-validated (validate_sql_between_input) before `left.clone()`, which stops exponential growth from chained BETWEEN.
  • No panic!/unwrap/expect in production parser, DDL-binding or shared-lexer code. Errors are typed enums (SqlSyntaxErrorKind/SqlFeatureCode) and nothing matches on error strings.
  • The CREATE INDEX predicate text is rebuilt from tokens, with string literals re-escaped, never cut from the raw input. It is then re-validated through parse_sql_predicate and bound against the accepted schema, so predicate-text injection is not possible.
  • DDL binding always resolves against the AcceptedSchemaSnapshot and hands off to schema-owned candidate and admission functions, so schema mutation stays catalog-native.
  • Unsupported SQL families (JOIN, UNION, WITH, window functions, CAST, subqueries, multiple statements, transaction control) reliably fail closed, most of them with a specific feature code.
Not covered

I did not review the rest of sql/lowering (aggregate, select binding, predicate lowering, bindings.rs) apart from the identifier-normalization path. I did not review the reduced predicate parser (db/predicate/parser) apart from its depth guard and IN-list handling, or the session SQL dispatch and write-policy code. I skimmed model.rs rather than reading all of it (the SqlScalarFunction call-shape tables and surface admission matrix were not checked exhaustively), and only skimmed ddl/report.rs. Per the ground rules I did not build, run tests or fuzz. So the stack-overflow threshold for the ORDER BY recursion is estimated from frame sizes, not measured. I only partly traced the downstream effect of re-rendering predicates on RENAME COLUMN for generated filtered indexes (the transition/compatibility text comparison at reopen); treat it as a low-confidence cross-unit lead.

Integrity progress, relations/reverse index, startup, diagnostics

integrity-relations5 medium4 low1 info

I reviewed the integrity-relations unit (Deep integrity jobs, progress store and codec, reverse-index maintenance, delete-restrict, startup readiness, diagnostics) by static reading only. I did not build or run tests. The core relation logic looks correct. I checked the reverse-index delta merge and it is sound: target keys are sorted by RawDataStoreKey, and that order matches the reverse-key comparator. Same-store batches use one final-image overlay, and delete-restrict plus source-side target checks both read it, so the batch semantics in REF_INTEGRITY §4.1 hold logically. Persisted decoding (progress codec/store, startup receipt) is bounded, checksummed, version-1 only and fail-closed. The main risks are liveness and capacity, not data corruption. (1) Startup failure receipts are bound only to durable state, never to the code build. Invariant-class codes (STORE/RUNTIME_INVARIANT_VIOLATION) count as terminal, so a code bug during recovery or reconciliation leaves a durable receipt that a fixed upgrade cannot clear, and the canister stays wedged. (2) Integrity progress records for abandoned or expired jobs are never retired unless the original owner walks the acknowledgement protocol. Capacity (8 per owner, 64 global, which also gates mutation and resumable jobs at 56) leaks permanently. (3) Relation budget accounting has two structural problems. Delete-restrict re-projects and re-charges a surviving source once per deleted target, which is quadratic. Updates charge the before and after images against a batch limit equal to the per-image limit. Together these reject realistic batches the contract promises, and can make large-fanout rows impossible to update. (4) Proving a removed relation's reverse domain is empty scans the whole target index store, capped at 262,144 entries. Smaller issues: a derived-phase livelock on oversized corrupt rows, heap-source reverse keys that live only in a journaled target's unjournaled overlay, retention errors masking results, and diagnostics accuracy and cost.

Strengths
  • Reverse-index delta computation is canonical: target keys are sorted and deduped (reverse_index.rs:1605-1608) in an order that matches the decoded-segment comparator of RawIndexStoreKey (key_taxonomy.rs:1418-1434). merge_relation_entries emits only real old/new differences, and duplicate references inside one row collapse correctly.
  • Same-store batch semantics are sound: PreflightStoreOverlay::from_row_ops exposes every final data image before any storage-backed check (commit_window.rs:283-305). Delete-restrict, source-side target existence and the per-batch target-lookup cache all read the same immutable final view, so 'source before target insert' and 'update-away plus target delete' behave correctly.
  • Persisted decoding is careful. The progress_codec counts are bounded both by constants and by remaining bytes, tags are closed, records use a CRC-checked envelope with the payload length verified, IntegrityJob::validate enforces cross-field invariants, the startup receipt has a checksum, fixed cell size and fact-schema validation, and every format uses exactly version 1 with no fallbacks.
  • Deep integrity uses a typed A/B proof vector captured before and after every page, idempotent replay keyed on the acknowledged sequence, and owner plus incarnation authorization. The row phase always makes progress because the first row of a page is exempt from the byte budget.
  • Startup observation is a pure read-only set. The lifecycle participant latch and watchdog registration run before application callbacks. No panic!/unwrap/expect appears in the production paths I reviewed (only debug_assert and test code).
  • Relation work is budgeted per image and per batch with typed errors, never traps, and the limits are backed by the documented 0.253 measurements.
Not covered

Static reading only. Nothing was built or run, including tests. Not covered or only skimmed: journal/commit internals beyond the relation and recovery touchpoints (journal batch encoding, fold and retirement correctness); relation staging in the migration lane (schema/migration_execution.rs, migration_validation.rs); the mutation_job and resumable_job payload codecs, and how SQL mutation-job pages react to relation-budget errors; whether the watchdog, stopped on SCHEMA_MIGRATION_IN_PROGRESS (store.rs complete_generated_schema_handoff), is reliably woken when the explicit migration finishes; the worst-case instruction cost of one Deep row or derived page (not measured; estimates suggest it stays under 40B, so not reported); JournalTailStore::inspect_page; entity-rename interactions with integrity job reloads; model.rs diagnostics DTOs beyond memory_bytes semantics; memory_allocations tests.

Value model, core types, errors, metrics, core lib root

value-types-error3 high2 medium3 low2 info

The core value model is well built. Ord, Eq and Hash agree for every scalar variant. The Float wrappers reject NaN/Inf and turn -0.0 into 0.0 at construction. Decimal Eq, Ord and Hash all normalize first. Canonical hashing normalizes decimals and sorts map entries, and the rank/tag tables are centralized and tested. The error taxonomy is fully typed, carries no strings, and validates facts against a per-code schema. In-scope production code has no panic!/unwrap/expect. The real problems sit where values meet numeric semantics and security material. (1) On wasm32 (the IC) the scalar-cursor HMAC key comes from the ULID generator, which has no entropy there, so the key can be derived from the database creation time. The 'authenticated, fail-closed' cursor contract therefore does not hold on the target platform. (2) Numeric-widening comparisons send floats (and Nat128 values ≥ 2^127) through a lossy i128-mantissa Decimal conversion. Values outside that range compare as 'unknown', so ordinary SQL range filters on float columns silently drop rows, and float arithmetic/comparison in expressions returns an error. (3) Decimal division panics on i128::MIN / -1, which callers can trigger through SQL arithmetic. (4) Decimal multiplication does not normalize its operands first. Admission pads fixed-scale fields with trailing zeros, so multiplying two Decimal(scale=18) fields fails with Overflow for values as small as 20 × 20. (5) Id::subaccount() ignores the entity, so the same key in two entities gives the same ledger subaccount. The overall risk is moderate to high: no durable-corruption path turned up in this unit, but there are realistic wrong-result and DoS paths and one weakened security control. Several root causes (Decimal arithmetic and float conversion) live in icydb-schema's Decimal, which the core re-exports and depends on.

Strengths
  • Float32/Float64 wrappers enforce finite-only values and turn -0.0 into 0.0 at construction and on every decode path (serde, bytes, try_from_f64), so derived Eq, to_bits Hash and total_cmp Ord agree
  • Decimal PartialEq, Ord and Hash all go through normalized (mantissa, scale); the canonical value hash also normalizes decimals, so 1.0 and 1.00 agree on every surface
  • The canonical tag/rank tables are one source of truth; canonical_cmp is total, with a debug assertion that ranks stay unique across variants; map hashing sorts entries by canonical order so a map built in any order hashes the same
  • The single-list fast hash path for grouped keys excludes non-identity-canonical variants (Decimal, containers) and has a test proving it matches the generic path
  • Error taxonomy is typed and compact: (class, origin, detail), numeric facts checked against per-E-code schemas, a safe InvariantViolation fallback instead of emitting invalid facts, constant Display messages; no matching on error strings found anywhere in core or facade
  • No panic!/unwrap()/expect()/assert! in in-scope production code (only in tests); big-integer decimal formatting admits scratch/work up front and uses fixed stack buffers
  • Value::from_map and the accepted admission path (normalize_map/normalize_list) canonicalize and reject duplicates using canonical_cmp consistently with Eq
  • Metrics: bounded report size (64 entities / 64 KiB paths), window id never wraps, and non-replicated (query) execution is excluded so heap-only counters are not polluted

I only skimmed error/mod.rs constructor bodies (roughly lines 620-2030) through its outline, so origin/class choices were not checked constructor by constructor. I also skimmed error/tests.rs, value/format/tests.rs, value/hash/tests.rs, types/account/tests.rs and types/ulid/tests.rs. I did not read the Ulid, Timestamp, Principal, Date, IntBig/NatBig and U256 implementations in icydb-schema, and did not audit their Ord/byte-order agreement. I did not confirm whether SQL admits literal-only arithmetic in projections. Stored-field and binding routes to the Decimal division panic were traced; the literal route was not confirmed at the admission level. I did not verify whether index-range access paths chosen for NumericWiden predicates return different rows than the residual filter would; that could make the float finding plan-dependent. I did not trace what, beyond row window/progress, a forged cursor could reach in the scalar/grouped token decoders or the exhaustive-proof checks. Public icydb facade crate and diagnostic-code crate

facade1 medium6 low1 info

The facade (crates/icydb) and the diagnostic-code crate are in good shape. The facade is a thin layer that converts types and wires endpoints over icydb-core, and most invariants are enforced in code rather than by convention. The diagnostic registry is checked for exhaustiveness at compile time. Fact schemas are validated when an error is built in core and again at the facade boundary, and a mismatch collapses the error to a compact failure instead of passing unvalidated data through. The endpoints! macro proves it sits at the crate root, rejects duplicate declarations through statics, gives a compile error when a declared endpoint's Cargo feature is off, and has trybuild coverage. Guarded reads reject anonymous callers before the application guard runs, and the guard runs before any request root is built. Request execution roots are installed per poll with RAII restore and are reused when nested, so an application cannot reset its budget by nesting calls. I found no data-corruption or authorization-bypass bug in this unit. The main risks are integration footguns and operator-tooling safety. First, participant lifecycle mode suppresses dead_code, so an app that forgets to call the participant hook compiles cleanly and leaves the database stuck in Recovering indefinitely. Second, the public SQL table renderers print stored user text verbatim, which allows terminal-escape injection and forged rows in the CLI. Third, bootstrap and grant misconfiguration (including the upstream Reserved default of ic_memory_range!, re-exported unchanged) collapses to an opaque E23 with no facts. Smaller items: one production assert! in RequestExecutionFuture, a SQL reply cap that fits only non-replicated queries, a stale crate README, a missing compile-fail test for the metrics feature, and (unmeasured) repeated binding work in typed batches.

Strengths
  • Compile-time-exhaustive public error registry: DiagnosticDetail::diagnostic_code is generated without a wildcard arm, so every detail-enum variant must have a registered code; tests enforce contiguous raw codes 1..=275 and round-trip reconstruction.
  • Numeric fact schemas are validated twice, in core InternalError::with_diagnostic_facts and in the facade's Error::from_diagnostic_facts_and_query_field. A mismatch collapses to a compact InvariantViolation instead of emitting unvalidated facts. The query_field echo is capped at 256 bytes and allowed only on QUERY_PLAN.
  • endpoints! proves crate-root placement via marker bindings and detects duplicate or conflicting declarations through per-endpoint #[used] statics that respect cfg. A declared endpoint whose Cargo capability is missing gives a compile_error; a compiled capability without a declaration exports nothing. All exported methods use icydb_* names. trybuild covers the guard ABI and the declaration syntax.
  • Read guards: the ReadAuthorizationGuard fn-pointer type forces a synchronous guard with no captures. Anonymous callers are rejected before application code runs, and the guard executes before the request root is built, startup admission runs, or SQL is parsed, matching docs/contracts/READ_ADMISSION.md.
  • Request-execution scoping is sound for ordinary use. The RAII guard restores the previous scope on return and on unwind. Nested entry and lazily-rooted futures reuse the active counters, which closes the budget-reset escape. An explicit root that conflicts with the active one fails closed with a typed error.
  • Memory admission (prepare_memory_bootstrap) enforces a closed icydb.* role grammar, complete control and store quartets, namespace-authority matching, and rejection of removed namespaces. It keeps only omitted historical journals under known-only selection, and tests/memory_admission.rs covers it extensively.
  • Typed adapters re-check binding currency, validate record outputs as exact permutations before exposing any member, and use sealed per-builder batch handles with single-consumption rows.
  • The SQL reply guard measures the exact Candid Result envelope and returns a small typed error instead of letting the replica reject an oversized reply.

Proc macros: schema authoring, codegen, request_execution

model-macros2 medium9 low

icydb-model-macros is well built overall. Parsing is strict: most errors carry spans, duplicate arguments are rejected, and the reduced-SQL predicate parser has byte, token, depth and membership limits. Crate-path resolution handles renamed dependencies and rewrites string-literal paths. The request_execution and test attributes are small and correct: early returns and `?` behave the same inside the closure or async-block wrapper. Generated runtime code checks lengths before indexing and returns typed errors instead of panicking. This crate generates no canister endpoints and no controller/guard logic; that code lives in the icydb `start!` macro and the icydb-model build actor, which are outside this unit. The main risks are semantic gaps between what the authoring grammar accepts and what the generated code actually does. (1) Normalizers and validators declared in several accepted positions are silently never run: item-level normalizers on list/set/map/tuple/enum payloads, item validators on tuple and enum payloads, and `ty(...)` normalizers/validators on entity, record, enum and tuple. (2) `IS TRUE` / `IS FALSE` in check constraints is lowered to `= TRUE` / `= FALSE`. Under the three-valued check evaluator this lets NULL through on nullable fields. (3) The redundant-prefix index check points the wrong way for unique indexes and ignores predicates. The remaining findings are compile-time: hygiene and name-collision problems, a runtime-detection false positive from proc-macro-crate, proc-macro panics with poor diagnostics, and silently discarded user attributes. Nothing reachable at runtime can corrupt durable state or wedge a canister from this crate.

Strengths
  • Authoring grammar is strict and fail-closed: unknown args, duplicate args, missing required args, reversed ranges and zero divisors all reject. Most errors carry precise spans (store, index, relation, pk, constraint, migration parsers).
  • The predicate parser (src/predicate.rs) is bounded by byte length, token count, recursion depth and IN-list size, so hostile schema text cannot blow the proc-macro stack.
  • crate_path.rs resolves package owners through proc-macro-crate, supports renamed `icydb` dependencies and an explicit `model_crate` override, and also rewrites string-literal paths in `candid_path` and `serde(crate = ...)` attributes.
  • request_execution.rs is minimal and correct: sync bodies are wrapped in `|| body` and async bodies in `async move body` passed to `with_request_execution_async`, so `return` and `?` keep their meaning. Arguments are rejected, and `#[icydb::test]` rejects async functions and functions with parameters.
  • Generated composite-key codecs check component counts before indexing (`values.len() != N` and `composite.len() != N`). `EntityKeyBytes` validates the exact buffer length before `split_at_mut`. Decode failures return typed Corruption / ShapeMismatch errors, not panics.
  • The trait policy table (trait_kind.rs) checks at validation time that every selected trait has a derive or impl strategy, and required traits cannot be added or removed.
  • Generated identity and managed-timestamp fields are left out of typed Insert/Patch/Replace structs, so typed writes cannot supply database-owned values.
  • Accepted-schema authority is respected: generated typed adapters bind through `TypedEntityBinding` and decode rows by source name. Nothing in the macro output rebuilds schema at runtime.
Not covered

Generated endpoint authorization (controller gating, guards, icydb_* exports) is not generated by this crate. It lives in the crates/icydb `start!` macro_rules and the crates/icydb-model/src/build actor generator, so I did not review it here. I checked icydb-model build-time lowering and validation only where it bounds a macro finding (default parsing, duplicate index names, stable-key validation). I did not verify how filtered-index membership evaluates NULL at runtime (the query evaluator is two-valued, the check evaluator three-valued), so the index-filter half of finding 2 is unverified. The trybuild compile tests (crates/icydb/tests/pass*, fail*) were not run, per the ground rules; compile-error claims come from static reading of the emitted tokens and Rust type rules. I skimmed rather than fully read src/node/entity/tests.rs, src/node/item/tests.rs and src/node/field/tests.rs, and the parts of collection_protocols.rs and index.rs past the lines cited. icydb-model and icydb-schema crates

model-schema-crates1 high6 medium5 low

The low-level codecs in icydb-schema are well built. The ICYF/ICYP/ICYM wire reader is bounded and checked, allocation happens only after count/remaining checks, and decoding does a full re-encode comparison, so any non-canonical input bytes are rejected. The bigint LEB128 encoder and the tagged byte bodies are correct and are tested exhaustively against Candid's own encoder. There is no LEB128 decoder in scope, and I found no overflow or non-canonical acceptance paths. The main risks are in numeric semantics and in schema-model completeness, not in byte decoding. Decimal's operator traits mistake a scale overflow (more than 28 fractional digits) or an alignment overflow for a magnitude overflow, and then saturate. Examples: `(1/3)*(1/3)` returns about 1.7e10, and `1e21 + 1e-18` returns about 1.7e20. The same flaw in `Rem` makes the MultipleOf application validator bypassable. Every Decimal newtype (Usd/E8s/E18s) inherits the flaw through derived operators. The `Account` atom has two distinct encodings for the same ICRC account (no subaccount vs. an all-zero subaccount). Core stores and indexes them differently, which breaks uniqueness and text-literal lookups. In icydb-model, nested-relation lowering silently skips relation leaves that are reachable only through a recursive type, although the authoring guide says such schemas are rejected. Build-time codegen never composes the fragment with the migration plan, so a mismatch such as a version gap shows up only on the canister, where it persists a startup failure. Overall risk is moderate. There is no persisted-state corruption in these crates, but there are several realistic wrong-result and integrity gaps.

Strengths
  • WireReader/WireWriter: checked offset arithmetic; every count is bounded by an explicit max and by the remaining input before try_reserve; string lengths are capped; decode always ends with a trailing-byte check plus a full canonical re-encode comparison (decode_schema_fragment/proposal/migration_plan).
  • Pre-1.0 versioning is followed for the transport forms: exact headers (ICYF/ICYP/ICYM/ICYS \x01), proposal contract version 1, migration program version 1; future versions fail closed with typed errors and no legacy fallback.
  • Bigint LEB128 streaming encoder and exact leb128_len (including the negative power-of-two boundary) are verified against Candid's encoder for all bit boundaries 0..=2048 and random limbs; tagged unsigned/signed bodies enforce minimal encoding and match Candid's visit_byte_buf convention.
  • U256: bounded decimal parse (at most 78 ASCII digits), fixed-width stack-only formatting, checked arithmetic only; Candid ingress rejects values of 2^256 or more.
  • Every fragment type is canonicalized by rebuild-and-compare; source keys have a charset and 128-byte bound; field-type depth is bounded during both decode and encode; check expressions are stack-validated and capped at 1024 instructions.
  • Deterministic compact heapsort with a correct permutation-cycle application; duplicate keys are rejected after sorting, so unstable tie order is never observable.
  • Entity source digest is deterministic (BTree ordering, length-prefixed, domain-separated SHA-256), excludes the declared version, and handles rename-induced target reordering and collisions.
  • Typed adapter narrows via try_from (i8/u8/etc.), and duplicate set elements and map keys fail with ShapeMismatch instead of silently collapsing.
  • Stable-memory key namespacing cannot collide (segments cannot contain dots; duplicate journaled store keys per canister are rejected); type names are globally unique before lowering, so name-keyed dedup in lower_reachable_types is safe.
  • Date/Timestamp/Duration parsers are strict, fixed-width and overflow-checked; Float atoms reject non-finite values and normalize -0.0.
Not covered

The icydb-model-macros crate is out of scope and was consulted only for derived operators and the map-key relation check. Core-side behavior was verified only where a finding depended on it (numeric evaluation, Account encoding/admission, SQL literal canonicalization, index arity, PK integrity). The core PK-shape check was not traced fully, which is why that finding has low confidence. I did not build or run tests, per the ground rules.

icydb-cli

cli7 medium13 low

icydb-cli is small (about 9k lines), neatly layered, and careful in the places that usually go wrong. It never shells out: every icp invocation is built as an argv array with stdin set to null. Destructive migration operations require --yes. Migration commands carry exact database/head/plan identities. Offline diagnostic inputs are size-bounded, version-1 exact and deny_unknown_fields, and production code has no panic, unwrap or expect. The serious defects sit in the operational workflows rather than in input handling. (1) `icydb schema migration run`, the documented controller workflow, uses exact status-page equality as its progress check. The core emits identical status pages on legitimate progress steps: multi-page FinalValidation (any migrated entity set over 256 rows) and prior-journal draining while Idle. So `run` fails with "made no bounded progress" on realistically sized data. (2) `icydb canister refresh` runs `icp deploy --mode reinstall --yes` against whatever environment is selected, including one picked up implicitly from ICP_ENVIRONMENT. There is no local-only guard and no confirmation, so it can wipe a production canister's stable memory. (3) Exit codes are unreliable for scripting. One-shot `sql` prints canister errors to stdout and exits 0. Migration `run`/`abort` exit 0 on Rejected, and abort also exits 0 when the migration had already been Applied. Smaller issues: the interactive shell alters multi-line string literals, executes a half-typed statement on Ctrl-D even though the banner calls Ctrl-D quit, and misreads backslashes as escapes. Canister text reaches the terminal without escaping. `canister upgrade` installs a wasm from a hard-coded, environment-independent path. Errors are classified by substring matching, and some docs are stale. Test coverage is almost all argument parsing and rendering. The migration loops, SQL exit-code behaviour and lifecycle safety guards are untested, which is how finding 1 got through. Overall risk: medium-high for operators. Nothing here corrupts data by itself, but the refresh foot-gun can destroy data and the migration runner fails on normal-sized tables.

Strengths
  • All external process execution uses std::process::Command with discrete argv elements and Stdio::null() stdin; no shell interpolation, so SQL/canister/environment values cannot inject shell commands.
  • SQL is routed client-side via the core parser (sql_statement_shell_surface) to fixed icydb_* endpoints, and the Candid text-literal escaping is correct for the candid_parser lexer (raw control chars are legal there).
  • Candid decode types for every endpoint (Result<SqlQueryResult|StorageReport|MetricsReport|Vec<EntitySchemaDescription>|SchemaMigrationStatusPage, Error>) match the generated endpoint signatures in crates/icydb/src/lib.rs, with decode-shape tests.
  • Migration commands are compare-and-swap style: each Advance/Abort/Adopt carries expected database identity, accepted head and plan digest from fresh status, and the loops re-verify database/plan identity every iteration; abort/adopt require explicit --yes.
  • Offline inputs are bounded and fail closed: error JSON is capped at 64 KiB and must be an object; diagnostic artifacts are size-capped, deny_unknown_fields, exact format/version 1, count/length validated, and written with create_new (never overwrite).
  • No panic!/unwrap()/expect() in production code; every failure path returns Result and main maps Err to ExitCode::FAILURE with an ERROR: prefix on stderr.
  • Diagnostic rendering escapes control characters in caller-supplied query field names (escape_query_field) and validates fact schemas before trusting them for name resolution; provenance mismatches withhold names instead of guessing.
Not covered

I only skimmed the large exhaustive text-mapping tables in diagnostic.rs (about lines 470-1686; they are compile-checked, exhaustive matches) and read only the start of its test module; observability tests were skimmed. I did not check icp-cli's real flag names or output formats against icp-cli source: `--output hex`, the "response (hex):" label, `--id-only`, the `canister list --json` shape, the "Cycles:" status line, and whether `canister call` types Candid text arguments from canister metadata. Findings that depend on those behaviours are marked medium/low confidence. Per the ground rules I did not build or run tests. Candid decoding quotas on canister responses are not reviewed in depth (host-side and operator-chosen targets).

Canisters, schema fixtures, testing harnesses, CI, Makefile, scripts

canisters-testing-ci4 medium7 low1 info

The test infrastructure is sophisticated. The PocketIC harness really performs upgrades, checks that a trapped message rolls back stable memory (via stable-memory fingerprints), replays pending markers across upgrade, reinstalls, and runs migrations. Release tooling binds a tested commit to a version-only diff, and the nightly Tier C generated differential cannot pass vacuously. The main risk is that PR CI enforces much less than the repo claims. The two "Tier A" SQLite/mutation oracle lanes filter on test-module paths that no longer exist, so they run zero tests and pass. Every PocketIC test for durability, upgrade, migration and application-guard authorization is excluded from PR CI; about 21 test targets are not even compiled on PRs. Those tests only run when a maintainer runs `make test`/`make patch` locally, and AGENTS.md forbids agents from running full suites. The dependency-MSRV job is also vacuous: the repo's rust-toolchain.toml (1.98.1) overrides the toolchain the dtolnay action sets with `rustup default 1.88.0`. Smaller issues: tautological instruction-budget assertions, a frozen artifact policy that only inspects `icydb_*` exports, docs that contradict each other, source-text contract tests that TESTING.md prohibits, and name-based invariant scans with blind spots. The test canisters themselves are mostly well gated: generated admin endpoints are controller-gated, and Tier B verifies that outsider calls are rejected.

Strengths
  • Real IC-level evidence exists: recovery_closeout.rs proves a trapped recovery message rolls back stable memory byte-for-byte (blake3 fingerprint) and that the canonical watchdog then retries; logical_memory.rs replays a genuine production pending marker across upgrade and proves store-removal is rejected without control publication.
  • The Tier C nightly generated differential writes per-shard receipts and a merged receipt, and the Makefile checks them with `test -s`, so a filter that matches nothing cannot pass. Minimized failures are replayable.
  • The release flow is fail-closed and auditable: release-candidate-receipt.sh binds the tested candidate commit to a version-only diff hash, verify-staged/verify-commit re-check it, the push is atomic and names exactly one tag, and publish-workspace.sh validates crate order against the manifests.
  • Workflow hygiene is enforced mechanically by check-ci-workflow-invariants.sh: actions pinned by 40-char SHA, persist-credentials false, top-level permissions, timeouts on every job, fixed runner image.
  • The Binaryen optimizer is pinned by archive SHA-256 and binary SHA-256 and re-verified at use (wasm_optimizer.rs), which makes the post-link pipeline deterministic.
  • Generated endpoints (crates/icydb/src/lib.rs endpoints! arms) always apply controller or guard authorization; fixture endpoints raise a compile_error! without the test-admin-api feature; Tier B (sql_canister.rs ~3487-3546) asserts outsider rejection for every generated admin surface.
  • run-validation-targets.sh uses pipefail correctly, keeps collecting failures across targets, and retains full failure logs.

CROSS-CUTTING: security & trust boundaries

xc-security1 high1 medium5 low1 info

IcyDB's caller-facing surface holds up well. Nothing is exported unless it is declared through the closed `endpoints!` grammar. SQL and DDL endpoints require a controller by default. A read guard rejects the anonymous principal before any application code runs, and before request, startup or parse work. Query, mutation and DDL lanes are separated in one place. Public reads go through planner admission, page envelopes and hard execution budgets. Public errors carry only numeric codes. The most serious issue is cryptographic: on the only production target (wasm32/IC), the HMAC key that authenticates continuation cursors comes from the IcyDB ULID generator. On wasm that generator is entirely deterministic (message time in ms plus a process-local counter). Anyone who holds one cursor can recover the key offline and forge cursors. That breaks the CURSOR.md promise that modified tokens fail closed. It also lets a caller bypass an authored total LIMIT and seek anywhere inside the query envelope. Envelope and contract checks keep forged cursors from exposing rows outside the query's predicate. Native tests use getrandom, so this path is never exercised. Second, the generated startup watchdog classifies deterministic schema-migration planning errors (for example a version gap, downgrade or unadopted lineage) as non-terminal. It then replans every round with no backoff, no log and no receipt, while ordinary work stays gated as 'recovering'. This contradicts the migration guide's statement that the watchdog does not keep retrying. The rest are low-severity items: gaps in admission semantics and docs, unbudgeted diagnostics, predictable generated ULID keys, and reply-size assumptions.

Strengths
  • Endpoint exposure is explicit and closed: `endpoints!` accepts only a fixed grammar (unknown declarations are compile errors), generated actor code contains no ic_cdk export attributes (asserted by tests), SQL/DDL/update/integrity/snapshot/migration endpoints default to controller checks, and `icydb_schema`/`icydb_metrics` require an explicit authorization choice.
  • Read guard ordering is correct: `authorize_read` denies anonymous before calling application code and runs before `with_request_execution`, startup admission, and SQL parsing; guard authority replaces controller authority with no implicit union (crates/icydb/src/guards.rs, crates/icydb/src/lib.rs).
  • Lane separation is centralized in `ensure_sql_statement_supported_for_surface` (query lane rejects INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE/DDL; mutation lane rejects reads/introspection), and the generated query dispatcher has a separate introspection gate.
  • Public read admission rejects full scans, KeyRange, Union/Intersection, unbounded row bounds (>100), and oversized PK input. Public live pages add a per-page work envelope (10k key visits, 100 rows), and all reads sit under hard execution budgets that return typed exhaustion errors instead of trapping.
  • Cursor tokens use bounded decoding (8 KiB, value depth 128, 4 KiB boundary), check the MAC before any semantic decode with a constant-time comparison, strictly validate signature/authority/window/order/route-pin against the current plan, and enforce anchor containment in the index envelope.
  • Public errors are compact numeric codes and facts with no row values or internal paths; the SQL query lane checks the encoded reply size before returning.
  • The migration endpoints bypass the ordinary readiness gate but still run `ensure_recovery_admitted`; sampled production executor paths contain no reachable unwrap/expect/panic.
Not covered

These were not reviewed in depth: - DDL execution internals and index-build paging behind `icydb_ddl`. - Write-admission internals. - Correctness of journal/commit-marker replay. - ic-memory allocator internals, beyond the IcyDB bootstrap/admission wrappers. - Grouped executor and grouped-cursor validation code. - Binding of the exhaustive-page ReadSetRevisionProof. - Integrity Deep job ownership and replay. - Mutation-job continuation custody. - SQL lowering and semantic-compiler details. - Model macros outside endpoint and actor generation. - CLI, apart from argument construction. - Metrics recording internals. The panic sweep was heuristic, filtering out test modules; it was not exhaustive. Nothing was built or run, so the following are unverified: - the startup hot-loop cycle cost; - the IC reply-size limits (based on documented platform limits); - the exact observed error code for each SchemaMigrationCode path.

CROSS-CUTTING: contract conformance

xc-contracts1 medium8 low1 info

I checked the load-bearing MUST claims in ATOMICITY, DURABILITY, TRANSACTION_SEMANTICS, CURSOR, READ_ADMISSION, WRITE_ADMISSION, REF_INTEGRITY, RESOURCE_MODEL, IDENTITY_CONTRACT, GROUP-BY, SQL_SUBSET and the two PERSISTED_FORMAT docs against icydb-core, and also compared 1.0-FEATURES/1.0-TODO with what the code does. The code matches the contracts unusually well. Every numeric ceiling I checked equals its compiled constant, the version-1 hard-cut rule holds, cursor/journal/marker decoders are bounded and verify authentication before decoding, and ordinary entrypoints only check recovery state. My panic-family scan (a heuristic script) found no panic!/unwrap/expect in production icydb-core outside const-eval and infallible conversions. The one real behavioural contract violation: exhaustive (revision-strict) pages over heap stores can be resumed across a canister upgrade. The heap store's revision counters restart from deterministic values, so an old continuation plus its proof can validate against a completely different row set and report "complete under an unchanged proof". The second notable issue is in 1.0-TODO: it lists CLI SQL INSERT/DELETE as done, but the CLI sends those statements to the read-only `icydb_query` query method, which always rejects them. The rest is contract drift and latent hazards. Several normative docs contradict each other or the code: SQL placeholders, the resumable-update timestamp rule, checksum policy, stale index-entry repair, and NULL ordering. The atomicity contract says an error means nothing was written, but a few normally returned post-marker errors leave the marker in place so recovery commits the write later. Recovery traps on an 'impossible' preflight/apply contradiction; if that ever happens it recurs deterministically and wedges the canister without writing a startup failure receipt. Overall risk is low-to-moderate: I found no reachable corruption or authorization bypass through this lens.

Strengths
  • State-only recovery admission (`ensure_recovery_admitted`) is applied uniformly through `recovered_store`/`ensure_recovered_state`, including storage reports, accepted-root cache construction, integrity proofs and schema application. The heap-only marker-presence hint fails safe (unknown means re-check stable memory).
  • Contract numeric ceilings match compiled owners exactly: the READ_ADMISSION/RESOURCE_MODEL table (100 rows / 1024 PK terms / 64 KiB / 100 groups / 64 KiB group bytes), batch bounds (4,096 ops, 64 entities, 16 MiB staged, 4 MiB rows, 1 MiB results), cursor caps (8 KiB binary, 10,923-char text, depth 128, 32 terms / 4 KiB boundary), marker limits (16 MiB, 4 control ops, 257-page region without overlap).
  • The pre-1.0 version-1 hard cut holds: no format version constant other than 1 and no V2/legacy decode paths in icydb-core production code.
  • Persisted and wire decoders bound counts before allocating (journal record_count, proof vectors, cursor term/map lengths); the journal SHA-256 fingerprint and cursor HMAC are verified before any semantic decoding.
  • Exhaustive continuation tokens bind the canonical proof bytes into the signature, so a caller cannot swap in a freshly captured proof. Durable resumable jobs and Deep integrity correctly require journaled stores.
  • Durable-source to volatile-target relations are rejected in both the model macros and at runtime, the `*_id`/`*_ids` relation naming rule is enforced at compile time, and relation write violations use the documented InvariantViolation/Executor class.
  • Generated endpoints consistently use `icydb_*` names and controller/guard gating; `icydb_update` is opt-in and controller-gated.
  • Grouped results without ORDER BY are finalized in canonical key order (sorted or top-k ranked), consistent with GROUP-BY §3.1 determinism.

Only skimmed: SQL_SUBSET sections beyond DDL/UPDATE (functions, expression typing, numeric semantics, RETURNING), and QUERY_CONTRACT/QUERY_PRACTICE/NESTED_STORAGE. Not traced end to end: the migration-feature lifecycle (DURABILITY's ReadyToRewrite/terminal-replacement claims), constraint activation promote/abort, Identity range recovery proofs, and relation delete-safety through the reverse index. Not verified: grouped cursor signature composition (whether it binds accepted-root identity), GROUP-BY null-group semantics for optional record paths, and RESOURCE_MODEL §6 scan-budget gating. Not checked: IDENTITY_CONTRACT's Nat-kind/sole-PK validation, which lives in icydb-schema. The panic-family scan was a heuristic script over icydb-core only; other crates were not scanned. CROSS-CUTTING: panics, overflow, unbounded allocation in production code

xc-robustness3 medium2 low

Through a panic/overflow/allocation lens, IcyDB's production code is unusually well hardened. After stripping #[cfg(test)] items and cfg(test)-gated module files (about 237k production lines across icydb-core, icydb and icydb-schema), there are zero .unwrap(), zero panic!, 3 .expect(), 3 unreachable!, and 5 assert! outside debug_assert!. All of them are infallible, const-evaluated, or documented `# Panics` APIs. The persisted-byte decoders (ByteReader, WireReader, SnapshotReader, journal/control-slot/receipt/progress/row/index/key codecs) consistently use checked offsets. They bound every count by both a max and the remaining bytes before calling with_capacity, apply depth limits to recursive values and expressions, and check sizes before every stable-memory read. Storable::from_bytes impls never panic. The wasm-release profile has no overflow-checks, so arithmetic wraps silently, but journal, commit and startup code uses checked/saturating arithmetic almost everywhere. The residual risk is in expression evaluation and executor preallocation, not in decoding. There are three real defects there: (1) a signed-division-overflow panic in Decimal division (`i128::MIN / -1`), which bypasses the checked-arithmetic contract and panics in the public `Decimal::checked_div`; (2) an unclamped `Vec::with_capacity(offset+limit+1)` in the scalar page kernel, which traps on large OFFSET/LIMIT; (3) REPLACE with an empty search string, which does unbounded, unaccounted allocation and also diverges from standard SQL semantics. Reachability of (2) and (3) is mostly via the guard-gated trusted SQL lane and trusted typed APIs, because public lanes cap LIMIT at 100 and cannot set OFFSET. Lesser items: the data/index/journal/schema/progress stores open through ic-stable-structures' `BTreeMap::init`, which silently reinitializes on a bad header and panics on a bad version (unlike the pre-validated schema control store), and the IntBig/NatBig `Div` operators panic on a zero divisor without `# Panics` docs. Overall risk from this lens is low-to-moderate: none of the findings can corrupt durable state or brick a canister, because traps roll back and startup runs from a watchdog timer, not synchronously in post_upgrade.

Strengths
  • Production code essentially follows the AGENTS no-panic rule: no unwrap()/panic! in shipped code. The remaining expect/unreachable/assert sites are provably infallible, const-evaluated (resumable_update.rs:86, startup/receipt.rs:45, database_format/convergence.rs:32), or documented `# Panics` public APIs (Decimal::new, Decimal::from_i128_with_scale, Principal::from_slice, RequestExecutionFuture::poll).
  • Single checked primitive readers (db/codec/reader.rs ByteReader, icydb-schema codec/wire.rs WireReader) are used everywhere. Every count read is bounded by a named max and by remaining bytes before allocation (e.g. journal/codec.rs:751-752, commit/store/control_slot.rs:388-392, integrity/progress_codec.rs, icydb-schema WireReader::read_count).
  • Recursive decoders and encoders carry explicit depth and node limits: cursor tokens (MAX_VALUE_NESTING_DEPTH=128), structural value storage, CHECK expressions (schema/codec/constraint.rs:342), mutation-job expressions. SQL parsing bounds input bytes, tokens and expression depth, including left-assoc binary chains.
  • Stable-memory reads are always preceded by size/length validation (commit/store/mod.rs:476-492, 682-694; database_format inspect_boot_record; startup/receipt.rs decode_cell). Storable::from_bytes impls fall back instead of slicing blindly (journal/store.rs:456-473, schema/store.rs:305-318).
  • Commit apply after a complete preflight uses a deliberate ic_cdk::trap fail-stop (commit/recovery.rs:1354-1357, executor/mutation/commit_window.rs:707-710), so partial mutation is rolled back rather than persisted. This is a correct atomicity design for IC.
  • Allocation-before-admission discipline is visible in many places: value/decimal.rs chunks_from_limbs admits budget before allocating, executor/stream/access/traversal.rs:496-505 charges TemporaryBytes before Vec::with_capacity, and most executor preallocations clamp to small caps (LIMITED_SCAN_PREALLOC_CAP=32, BOUNDED_ORDER_INITIAL_CAPACITY, limit.min(32)).
  • Sort comparators are total: Float32/Float64 are finite-only and use total_cmp, and keep_count==0 is guarded before `select_nth_unstable_by(keep_count - 1)` (executor/order.rs:143).
Not covered

I skimmed rather than traced every one of the ~390 production with_capacity sites. I triaged them by grep, verified the decoder- and LIMIT-derived ones, and assumed plan-shaped capacities (compiled projection/terminal counts, contract.field_count) are bounded by the accepted schema. Not deeply read: grouped aggregation state accounting (executor/aggregate/**), DISTINCT/grouped live-memory charging, schema mutation/DDL paths (schema/sql_ddl.rs, migration_execution.rs, constraint_activation_runner.rs), relation/reverse_index maintenance, the integrity deep verifier, and the full SQL lowering tree beyond predicate normalization. I did not verify candid's own recursion/decoding quotas for generated endpoint arguments (upstream). Generated canister code in icydb-model is outside this unit's scope; I noted but did not report its `.expect("ic-memory committed allocation unavailable")` in thread_local store initializers and the lifecycle ic_cdk::trap calls, which look fail-safe because a failed post_upgrade reverts. I did not examine upstream ic-stable-structures BTreeMap node-decode panics on corrupted node bytes; they are inherent to the dependency. No code was compiled or run. The wasm32 capacity-overflow and division-overflow conclusions rest on Rust semantics: signed `/` overflow panics regardless of overflow-checks, and Vec::with_capacity panics when the byte size exceeds isize::MAX.

CROSS-CUTTING: architecture, layering, duplication, complexity, dead code

xc-architecture1 high8 low2 info

IcyDB's architecture is carefully governed, and most cross-cutting rules hold up. Every persisted or wire format constant is exactly version 1. Production code outside tests has no unwrap/expect/panic apart from const asserts and two provably infallible expects. Neither production code nor tests match on error strings. The facade imports only root re-exports, and SQL INSERT/UPDATE, dynamic and typed writes all converge on one structural mutation coordinator. The main defect found is filtered-index predicates. The binder builds a typed, field-ID-bound AcceptedCheckExprV1, then renders it to SQL text with field and enum-variant names and throws the typed form away. At runtime that text is re-parsed by a different grammar (the reduced predicate DSL on the shared SQL lexer). This loses literal types: Nat, Int128, Decimal, Float and enum equality or IN never match at write time. The planner's numeric-or-strict implication still treats the filtered index as usable, so queries can return missing rows and filtered unique constraints go unenforced. Fields whose names are SQL keywords (count, order, index, min, max, end, default…) make generated schema publication fail at startup. The same text representation drives name-based relabeling, text-equality duplicate and compatibility checks, and a migration relabel that depends on rename order. Other issues are architectural: the resource-budget vocabulary lives in the query/executor/session layers, which inverts the import graph for index, access, schema and codec. The catalog-native schema layer depends on SQL-frontend request types. Several cfg(test) forks make unit tests exercise code paths that production never runs. There is also some dead or over-broad surface: a stale CLI error-string match and a public, uncalled, non-durable IndexStore::clear. Beyond the filtered-index issue, overall risk is moderate-to-low and mostly about maintainability.

Strengths
  • Hard-cut discipline is visible: every persisted/protocol format version constant (commit marker, journal batch, schema snapshot, bundles, cursor token, progress stores, receipts, etc.) is exactly 1; no V2/legacy decoders found.
  • Production panic hygiene is good crate-wide, not just in the gated executor directory: only const asserts, two infallible expects (access/plan.rs:337 Infallible map, scalar_projection.rs:77 write-to-String) and a facade misuse assert remain.
  • A shared bounded ByteReader (db/codec/reader.rs) with checked offset arithmetic exists; the private readers that remain also bound spans correctly (checked_add or saturating end + get()).
  • Structural mutations from SQL INSERT/UPDATE, dynamic, typed, and batch APIs converge on one coordinator (session/write.rs execute_accepted_structural_mutation_batch_inner) and one commit window.
  • Index key contracts and check constraints are field-ID-bound (PersistedIndexKeySnapshot::references_field, AcceptedCheckExprV1), consistent with accepted-schema authority.
  • The accepted runtime root cache revalidates compact store roots on every hit (session/accepted_schema.rs:436-443), so explicit invalidation after DDL is only an optimization, not a correctness dependency.
  • Visibility is mostly narrow (pub(in crate::db) dominates, no deep pub mod trees); the facade uses only icydb_core::db root re-exports.
  • No error-string matching in core/facade production code or tests; a structured diagnostic-code crate carries error identity.
  • Many cross-cutting rules are backed by CI invariant scripts (layer authority, persisted format, read admission, schema-model boundary, executor panics).
Not covered

I did not run cargo build/test or anything else dynamic; every trace is static. Systems I only skimmed or left to other reviewers: detailed journal fold/recovery page logic, integrity deep/quick jobs, cursor token codec internals, SQL lowering and parser beyond the predicate/DDL paths, grouped/aggregate executor internals, mutation_job/resumable_update execution, relation/reverse-index maintenance, identity allocation, the ic-memory bootstrap and generated actor codegen, the CLI beyond shell/call.rs, and the testing/ and canisters/ crates. My module-graph analysis used a heuristic import parser over use statements and inline crate::db:: paths, so a few edges may be over- or under-counted. For the filtered-index finding I traced the write-membership and planner-implication paths end to end. I did not trace planner cost/tie-break selection to prove which concrete query shape picks the filtered index over its alternatives.

CROSS-CUTTING: instruction-count & wasm-size efficiency

xc-performance4 medium9 low2 info

I reviewed IcyDB's hot paths for IC instruction cost and wasm size: row decode, the executor scan and ordering loops, value comparison, the session write path, commit prepare/apply and the store traversals. The design is sound. The runtime is structural rather than generic per entity, row readers are erased behind `dyn` callbacks, slot decode is lazy, and scans are bounded and chunked. The problems are mostly constant factors in shared primitives, and a few of them are large. The two most serious: 1. **Numeric comparisons go through `Decimal`.** `canonical_value_compare` converts even same-type integer and timestamp values to `Decimal` first. `Decimal::cmp_decimal` then turns both mantissas into decimal digit strings using u128 division (a slow library call on wasm32). `Float64` values are formatted to text and parsed back on every comparison. This comparator drives ORDER BY, top-K, cursor boundaries and MIN/MAX. 2. **Top-K is O(N·K).** The bounded top-K window rescans all K kept rows whenever a row is replaced, and charges K+1 comparisons per row once full. So a query like `ORDER BY <non-indexed column> LIMIT 1000` over roughly 33k+ rows always fails with a SortComparisons budget error, whatever the data order. The write path repeats work heavily. Each row is fully validated 4–6 times, re-encoded to canonical form at commit even though it was just encoded, and copied several times. The accepted row decode contract is rebuilt and deep-cloned 4–5 times per batch item. Full-row reads (SELECT * and typed pages) validate every slot, throw the result away, then decode again, which contradicts the rule written in `data/persisted_row/contract.rs`. Primary-range scans for full-row strategies do a key-only walk plus a separate B-tree lookup per row; the single-pass path only covers slot-only, ascending scans on stores with no pending live overlay. The rest are low-severity per-row allocations, redundant full scans in diagnostics and preflight, and an unmeasured wasm-duplication risk in the generic store visitors. All magnitudes are estimates from reading the code; nothing was measured, because builds were out of scope.

Strengths
  • The executor runtime is structural rather than generic per entity: `execute_kernel_row_scan_with_readers` erases row readers behind `&mut dyn FnMut`, and the facade crate's generics are thin, which limits monomorphization.
  • `StructuralSlotReader` uses per-slot `OnceCell` caches for validation and materialization. Dense, sparse and single-slot direct decoders avoid the cache entirely, and the one-slot path even avoids the per-slot span vector (`SparseRequiredRowFieldBytes`).
  • `DecodedDataStoreKey` caches its raw key in a `OnceCell`. Physical scans refill in bounded chunks of 64 entries with page-local entry caps, so the store is never borrowed for an unbounded stretch.
  • The sort paths are carefully built: inline two-value order tuples, sorting an index permutation instead of moving large rows, borrowed comparisons for direct-field orders, and ordering values cached once per row for expression orders.
  • Commit prepare shares accepted-schema setup across a batch through `CommitPrepareContextCache`.
  • Every hot loop charges typed hard budgets, so runaway work returns an error instead of trapping mid-message; a data-dependent trap would be worse.
Not covered

Nothing was measured: builds and tests were out of scope, so every instruction and wasm-size figure is a qualitative estimate from reading code. The following areas were not reviewed or only skimmed. SQL parser/lowering/planner cost (e.g. `index_select`, `plan/pipeline`). Covering-index projection in depth (`covering.rs`, `projection/covering/*`). The grouped aggregation fold and finalize internals beyond the equality/bucket helpers. Journal codec/store, fold and convergence cost (`journal/*`, `commit/convergence_candidate.rs`), commit marker serialization size, and recovery replay. Migration, schema application beyond one preflight, constraint activation, relation reverse-index maintenance. SQL `resumable_update`. Index key encoding (`index/key/*`) and prefix-cardinality maintenance. Value hashing (xxh3) cost beyond a skim. Budget and page-unit overhead was estimated, not measured. I did not verify how rustc/LLVM optimizes the u128 digit loop in `Decimal::cmp_decimal` or the `PageWork` merge chains on wasm32 at the release profile.

CROSS-CUTTING: documentation accuracy & public API ergonomics

xc-docs-api13 low

Documentation quality is high in the places that matter most. I resolved every API name in docs/guides/public-facade-api.md and read-intent.md to a real public method with a matching signature. Every numeric limit I checked matches the code constant: 64 entities, 4,096 ops, 16 MiB and 1 MiB per batch; 240 rows and 4,096 keys per mutation-job step; 100 rows per public page. The migration macro syntax, CLI subcommands, memory-profile table and E-codes quoted in the guides also match. The compiled fixture that README points to exists and is exactly what the docs describe. The real problems are at the edges. The biggest is a CI evidence gap: the Tier A SQLite and mutation-reference lanes (also given in INSTALLING.md as the 'SQL evidence' commands) filter on test modules that no longer exist, so they pass with 0 tests. The main API hazard is that `.limit()` on the same builder means 'cap on the whole traversal' for scalar reads but 'page size, with a continuing cursor' for grouped reads, while its rustdoc says neither. Beyond that, several onboarding documents have drifted from the code. INSTALLING.md says the CLI defaults to the `demo` environment, but the code defaults to `local`. The crates.io README for `icydb` says model macros are not re-exported, but they are. TESTING.md and SECURITY.md describe a test layout and a git hook that no longer exist, and one 'complete starting declaration' link is dead. The endpoint-declaration macro has constraints that user-facing docs never state. I found no runtime correctness or durability defects through this lens. Overall risk from this unit is low to moderate: mostly developer-experience issues, plus one real loss of CI coverage.

Strengths
  • The public facade guides are accurate against the code: every referenced method exists with a matching signature. Examples include execute_live_page, advance_live_page/LivePageStep::commit, execute_exhaustive_page, capture_read_set_revision_proof, compare_proof_and_advance, trusted_typed_write_batch/push/execute/row, execute_trusted_structural_mutation_batch_rows, bind_typed_input and the mutation-job APIs.
  • Numeric limits quoted in guides match core constants: batch 4,096 ops / 64 entities / 16 MiB staged / 1 MiB result (core session/write.rs:173-179); mutation job 4,096 keys / 240 rows (commit_window.rs:56, asserted = 240); public page 100 rows (coordinator.rs:75); memory profile page sizes; E274/E275/E25/E261/E221 code numbers.
  • The endpoints! macro is defensive: it rejects unknown declarations with compile_error, detects duplicate declarations through per-endpoint #[used] statics, raises feature-gated compile errors for missing capabilities, and uses crate-root binding markers to prove that start! and endpoints! sit at the canister root.
  • The read-guard design is sound and well documented in rustdoc: anonymous callers are rejected before application code runs, the allowlist helper is bounded, and guard authority replaces controller authority rather than being unioned with it.
  • README's compiled single-package example (testing/model-facade-only) exists, exercises exactly the pattern the docs describe (renamed dependency, ic_memory_range with mode = Allowed, typed write and read), and is part of make test-documentation.
  • MSRV 1.88 for the public dependency path is enforced by a dedicated CI job (dependency_msrv), and a documentation script validates relative link targets.
  • Public error types are compact and validated: facts are checked against the known fact schema before an Error is built (error.rs:183-207), and query-field context has a validating accessor.
Not covered

Nothing was compiled or executed, so doc snippets were checked against signatures by reading, not by building them. Contract documents (docs/contracts/*.md) were consulted only for the sections relevant to the guides, not audited in full. The icydb-model-macros README and its full rule grammar were not verified. icydb-core's own public API surface was reviewed only where the facade re-exports or wraps it. CLI runtime behavior beyond argument parsing and environment resolution was not traced. docs/design, docs/reports, docs/audits, docs/governance and CHANGELOG were not reviewed. Rustdoc rendering of #[doc(hidden)] glob re-exports (the prelude's `types::*`) was not confirmed empirically. Git history could not be consulted because git is blocked by the Xcode license prompt on this host.

Strengths

  • The version-1 hard cut is followed rigorously. Every persisted and wire format (commit marker, journal, snapshot, bundles, catalogs, cursor, progress, receipts, migration records, ICYF/ICYP/ICYM transport) is exactly version 1, with no V2 or legacy decode paths.
  • Persisted decoding rejects bad input safely throughout. Shared checked readers (ByteReader, WireReader) are used, counts are bounded by both a maximum and the remaining bytes before try_reserve, recursion depth and node counts are capped, trailing bytes are rejected, and canonical re-encode checks are performed. The journal SHA-256 fingerprint and cursor HMAC are verified before any semantic decode.
  • The commit protocol is sound. The control slot is framed and CRC-checked. Marker publication is compare-and-swap style (prepare, Gate-2 backlog admission, publish only if the proof is unchanged). The database commit sequence only increases. Recovery is staged (Replay, Fold, Verify) and idempotent under heap loss. Fold validates everything before any stable write. The marker is cleared only after its own effects are verified.
  • Atomicity fits the IC: every fallible preflight finishes before the marker is published, and a contradiction after preflight deliberately traps, so the whole message rolls back instead of persisting a partial mutation.
  • Production panic hygiene holds across the whole crate: no unwrap/panic in shipped code. The remaining expect, unreachable and assert sites are infallible, const-evaluated or documented. Errors are typed, with an exhaustive diagnostic registry and fact schemas validated twice. No code matches on error strings.
  • Accepted-schema authority is respected. There is no runtime fallback to generated EntityModel/IndexModel. The runtime-root cache is revalidated against per-store roots on every hit. Typed bindings are checked against incarnation, revision and field IDs. Existing-head lowering rejects any change to kind, nullability or codec.
  • One write coordinator serves every frontend (SQL, dynamic, typed, batch, resumable), with uniform bounds, duplicate-target rejection, identity allocations published only with the marker, and relation and uniqueness checks against a complete final-row overlay.
  • The caller-facing trust boundary is well designed. `endpoints!` is a closed grammar and controller-gated by default. The read guard rejects anonymous callers before any application, startup or parse work. Query and mutation lanes are separated in one place. Public errors are compact numeric codes.
  • Resource accounting is centralized, monotonic and fallible. Budget bundles are charged all-or-nothing across execution and request scopes. Grouped state is charged before try_reserve. The first exhaustion is sticky, so runaway work returns typed errors instead of trapping.
  • The core value model is consistent. Floats are finite-only with -0.0 normalized, Decimal Eq, Ord and Hash normalize, canonical ranks and tags have a single source, key-stream combinators check monotonicity, and the order-preserving encoders for integers, floats, decimals, bigints and text are covered by property tests.
  • The release and CI hygiene tooling is serious. Actions are SHA-pinned and checked by invariant scripts. Release receipts are bound to a version-only diff. Binaryen is pinned by checksum. The nightly Tier C differential cannot pass vacuously. The PocketIC suites that exist really do exercise trapped-recovery rollback and marker replay across upgrades.

Method and limits

Round one split the workspace into 25 subsystem areas and 6 cross-cutting lenses: security, contract conformance, panic and overflow paths, architecture, instruction-count and wasm-size efficiency, and documentation and API. Each reviewer read the code statically and reported findings with a file and line, evidence, a concrete failure scenario and a recommendation.

Every critical, high and medium finding then went to an adversarial verifier instructed to refute it. Confirmed critical and high findings went to one or two further skeptics with fresh context: one traced reachability from a real entry point, the other checked intent against the contracts and design docs. Verified means a finding survived all of them. Disputed means a skeptic refuted it after the verifier confirmed it. Low and info findings were not verified and are marked unverified.

A completeness critic then named the areas round one covered least, and round two probed ten of them with the same verification. Finally, the most important findings were retested by writing focused tests in throwaway git worktrees and running them with cargo against the current commit. Only the named tests were run, never the full suite.

The reproduction pass is also a calibration check on the static review. Of 28 findings tested, 26 reproduced exactly and 2 partially, including one finding a skeptic had disputed. That suggests the verified findings that were not retested are also reliable, though each still deserves a test before it is fixed.

Limits: nothing was measured on the Internet Computer, so instruction and cycle figures in findings are estimates from reading code. Upgrade scenarios were approximated natively by reopening stores with changed registries, not with PocketIC. The dependency advisory scan (cargo audit) found no vulnerabilities and two unmaintained crates: paste, which comes in through candid, and serde_cbor, which is dev-only.
